title: Perceptual Image Hashing
description: Compute average-hash fingerprints from downsampled grayscale data and compare them by Hamming distance so near-duplicate images are detected without byte equality.
body: Perceptual Image Hashing Category: Multimodal | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Byte hashes cannot recognize the same picture after a resize or re-encode. A perceptual hash captures visual structure: downsample to a fixed grid, threshold each cell against the grid mean, and pack the bits into a fixed-width fingerprint. Two images then compare by Hamming distance, and a declared threshold turns that distance into a duplicate decision. Face or semantic similarity is out of scope; this is structural near-duplicate detection. When to Use Use when a corpus must be deduplicated against resizes, crops, and re-encodes, and the decision must be explainable as a measured distance against a declared threshold. Do not use for semantic matching — different scenes with similar histograms compare equal; use classification or embedding retrieval for meaning-level search. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Downsampled grayscale values in row-major order | | | | Yes | Hamming distance at which two hashes count as duplicates | | | | No | Bits per hash; derived from grid length when omitted | Procedure 1. Downsample every image to the same fixed grayscale grid before hashing; grid mismatch makes hashes incomparable. 2. Compute the grid mean and threshold every cell to one bit, using a strict greater-than comparison. 3. Pack the bits in row-major order into a fixed-width integer fingerprint. 4. Compare fingerprints by Hamming distance — popcount of the XOR — never by string similarity. 5. Apply the declared duplicate threshold and record the distance, not just the verdict. 6. Treat dark, flat, or synthetic grids as unhashable noise: their bits carry no structure and produce false matches. 7. Never edit images to force a match; if distances sit at the threshold, collect more evidence instead. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The perceptual fingerprint of the grid | | | | Hamming distance between two hashes | | | | Threshold-applied verdict, recorded with its distance | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | False positives | Flat or low-contrast images hash to noise | Flag degenerate grids and exclude them from matching | | Grid mismatch | Images hashed at different resolutions | Downsample everything to one fixed grid first | | Threshold guessing | Cutoff tuned on unlabeled data | Calibrate the threshold on labeled pairs and record it | | Bit-order drift | Cells packed in inconsistent order | Pack row-major in one documented order everywhere | | Semantic overreach | Different scenes counted as duplicates | Keep the decision structural and confirm borderline pairs | Security and Authority Boundary Perceptual hashes are derived features of their source images; they inherit every access restriction of the source. A hash that survives deletion of the original can still identify it, so retention policy must cover hashes too. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia’s overview of perceptual hashing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perceptual_hashing). 2. Python’s statistics module documentation for mean computation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/statistics.html). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Subtitle Generation
description: Build well-formed WebVTT subtitle cues from timestamped transcript segments with monotonic ordering, overlap detection, and exact timestamp formatting so captions render correctly and validate mechanically.
body: Subtitle Generation Category: Multimodal | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A caption file is a format contract: cue timestamps must be ordered, non-overlapping, and formatted to the millisecond, or players drop or smear cues. This skill turns timestamped segments into a validated WebVTT payload — exact formatting, overlap detection, and a deterministic builder that never emits an invalid cue. Content quality of the translation itself is out of scope; this is the timing-and-format contract. When to Use Use when transcript segments with start and end times must become a caption track that players and validators accept as-is. Do not use to align audio to text from scratch; alignment belongs to transcription tooling, and this skill consumes its timestamped output. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Timestamped transcript segments in seconds | | | | No | Longest single cue allowed before splitting | | | | No | Per-cue character cap applied by re-segmentation | Procedure 1. Format every timestamp as HH:MM:SS.mmm computed from seconds with integer millisecond rounding. 2. Reject any segment whose end precedes or equals its start; malformed timing never reaches the output. 3. Detect overlaps between consecutive cues and fail closed instead of silently emitting both. 4. Split cues exceeding the duration or character caps before formatting, in reading order. 5. Emit cues in a fixed order: header once, then timing line, text, blank separator per cue. 6. Round-trip the payload: re-parse the emitted cues and assert the turn count and ordering match the input. 7. Keep the builder deterministic — identical segments produce byte-identical output. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The complete WebVTT payload with header and cues | | | | Number of cues emitted | | | | Input segments rejected for timing or overlap reasons | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Overlapping cues | Segments overlap after alignment | Detect overlaps and fail closed or split on evidence | | Smearing timestamps | Floating-point drift in formatting | Round to integer milliseconds from seconds | | Zero-length cue | End time not after start | Reject malformed segments before emission | | Player rejection | Missing blank line between cues | Emit the separator line after every cue | | Silent split drift | Long cues exceed player caps | Apply duration and character caps deterministically | Security and Authority Boundary Caption generation processes potentially private spoken content. title: Thumbnail Generation
description: Derive bounded thumbnail dimensions from source width and height using integer-only aspect-ratio arithmetic so preview sizes are exact, reproducible, and free of rounding drift.
body: Thumbnail Generation Category: Multimodal | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A thumbnail pipeline needs one deterministic answer per input: given a source size and a bound, what target box does every runtime agree on? This skill defines that answer with integer math — scale by the limiting side, floor to whole pixels, never upscale past the bound — so galleries and indexes render identical sizes everywhere. Pixel resampling quality is out of scope; this is the sizing contract. When to Use Use when generating preview images for galleries, feeds, or search results where the target box must be computed, not guessed, and must match across implementations. Do not use for art-directed crops; creative sizing belongs to image editing, not to this mechanical contract. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Source image width in pixels | | | | Yes | Source image height in pixels | | | | Yes | Largest permitted thumbnail dimension | | | | No | Whether already-small sources may be enlarged; default false | Procedure 1. Reject non-positive width, height, or maxside before any math runs. 2. Compute the scale as the minimum of maxside/width, maxside/height, and 1 when upscaling is disabled. 3. Apply the scale to both dimensions and floor to whole pixels, flooring identically in every implementation. 4. Clamp each result to at least one pixel so degenerate inputs never yield an empty box. 5. Return the box together with the computed scale so callers can verify the bound was respected. 6. Keep the operation pure: same inputs, same box, no environment state. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The integer thumbnail dimensions | | | | The limiting scale factor applied | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Aspect distortion | One dimension rounded independently of the ratio | Scale both dimensions by the same limiting factor | | Upscaled previews | Small sources enlarged and blurred | Cap the scale at 1.0 unless upscaling is explicitly enabled | | Zero-size box | Degenerate source or flooring to zero | Clamp each dimension to at least one pixel | | Cross-runtime drift | Float rounding differs by platform | Floor with integer truncation in a fixed order | | Unbounded thumbnails | maxside not validated | Reject non-positive bounds before computing | Security and Authority Boundary Thumbnails inherit the access state of their source image. Generating a preview grants no new viewing rights; protected media must keep its protection at every derived size. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. title: Agent Checkpointing
description: Persist an agent run as resumable checkpoints — state, memory, pending actions — so a failure or restart continues from a recorded point instead of from scratch.
body: Agent Checkpointing Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A long agent run that cannot resume is a long agent run that will eventually be repeated. This skill treats the run as a sequence of durable states: after each completed step, the run writes a checkpoint — conversation state, working memory, pending tool calls — and a restart restores the latest one before doing anything else. The design question is granularity: checkpoints cost writes, and restarts cost rework, so the checkpoint cadence is chosen by what re-execution is actually allowed to cost. When to Use Use for long-running or stateful agent work — multi-step plans, sessions holding tool state, pipelines vulnerable to timeout or restart. Do not checkpoint every intermediate token of fast, cheap runs; when re-execution costs less than persistence, the checkpoint is pure overhead. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Conversation, memory, and pending actions to persist | | | | Yes | Checkpoint after every step, on demand, or on a schedule | | | | Yes | Latest checkpoint, or a specific recorded point | Procedure 1. Choose the checkpoint unit — step, tool call, or plan stage — based on what re-execution of that unit is allowed to cost. 2. Serialize complete state, not deltas alone: a checkpoint that needs every prior checkpoint to restore is a chain, not a checkpoint. 3. Write the checkpoint atomically, so a crash mid-write leaves the previous checkpoint intact rather than a torn one. 4. On restart, restore the latest checkpoint first and reconcile with reality — replay tool side effects only where the tool contract allows it. 5. Version the checkpoint schema; a restored run must refuse to continue on a state format it cannot fully interpret. 6. Prune old checkpoints on a retention rule, and record the retention decision so the pruning is explainable later. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Durable run states with timestamps and step markers | | | | The checkpoint a restart continues from | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Torn writes | A crash during checkpoint serialization | Write atomically; keep the previous checkpoint valid | | Delta-only state | Restoring requires the entire history | Serialize complete state per checkpoint | | Stale resume | Restored state disagrees with the world it mutated | Reconcile with external state before continuing | | Unversioned schema | A restored run misreads an old format | Version schemas and refuse unknown formats | | Checkpoint storms | Persisting on every token, starving the work | Choose cadence by re-execution cost | Security and Authority Boundary A checkpoint is a complete, portable copy of agent state — credentials in working memory get persisted with it, so checkpoints must inherit the encryption and access scope of the run itself, and the pruning policy must respect data-retention obligations, not just disk budgets. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The arXiv paper on human-in-the-loop agent oversight (https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657). 2. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework overview (https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Agent Failure Taxonomy
description: Classify agent failures into a shared, evidence-based taxonomy — planning, retrieval, reasoning, execution, environment — so fixes land at the right layer.
body: Agent Failure Taxonomy Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Agents fail in characteristic ways, and a fix aimed at the wrong layer is a fix that did not happen. This skill gives the failures names: a plan that never fit the goal, retrieval that brought back wrong evidence, reasoning that misjoined what it had, execution that fumbled a working plan, environment that changed under the run. Classification comes from traces — where the first wrong step appears — and the taxonomy pays for itself by making postmortems comparable across incidents instead of anecdotal. When to Use Use when reviewing a failed agent run — incident triage, postmortem, quality review — before anyone decides what to change. Do not skip classification and jump to the most recent failure; without a layer verdict, fixes become folklore and the same class recurs. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The observable steps of the failed run | | | | Yes | What the run was supposed to accomplish | | | | Yes | The failure classes and their diagnostic criteria | Procedure 1. Reconstruct the run from its trace: what was asked, what was retrieved, what was decided, what was executed. 2. Locate the first wrong step — the earliest point where the run departed from a path that could still reach the goal. 3. Classify by layer: planning, retrieval, reasoning, execution, or environment, using the criteria of the taxonomy rather than intuition. 4. Distinguish root cause from symptom: a wrong answer is a symptom; the layer that injected the error is the cause. 5. Record the classification with its evidence — the trace excerpt that supports it — so the verdict is reviewable. 6. Aggregate over incidents: recurrence by class is the signal that directs where the next fix budget goes. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Failure class, layer, and supporting trace evidence | | | | Cause, fix target layer, and recurrence tracking | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Layer guessing | Verdicts assigned without trace evidence | Classify from the first wrong step, with excerpts | | Symptom fixes | The visible error fixed, the cause untouched | Separate the root cause layer from the symptom | | Folklore drift | Each postmortem invents new categories | Use one shared taxonomy across incidents | | Single-incident bias | One failure reshapes the whole system | Aggregate recurrence by class before redesigning | | Unclassified residue | Failures that fit no class get skipped | Extend the taxonomy explicitly when a class is missing | Security and Authority Boundary Failure traces contain the data the run touched, including anything sensitive it retrieved or produced: postmortems and classification records must redact secrets at capture time, because a taxonomy entry quoting a credential is a leak with good documentation. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of fault tree analysis (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faulttreeanalysis). 2. The OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications project (https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/). body: Agentic RAG Category: Skill Level: Stability: Version: Description Agentic RAG extends a retrieval pipeline with an explicit control loop. The controller can choose a query, inspect retrieved evidence, decide whether another retrieval is justified, and stop when a bounded sufficiency condition is met. Retrieval quality and answer quality are separate concerns: the controller must not treat retrieval as proof. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Contract | |---|---|---| | | | Non-empty user question | | | callable | , each record contains and optional metadata | | | | Positive upper bound on retrieval iterations | | | callable | | | Output | Type | Contract | |---|---|---| | | | Deduplicated evidence collected in retrieval order | | | | Number of retrieval calls performed | | | | Whether the stop policy ended the loop before the hard bound | Deterministic Reference Implementation Control Protocol 1. Bound the number of retrieval rounds. 2. Keep the original question immutable; derive follow-up queries from observed evidence. 3. Deduplicate evidence by a stable identifier or canonical text. 4. Make the stop rule explicit and testable. 5. Preserve evidence provenance for every item passed to generation. 6. Generate only after the controller reaches its stop condition or hard bound. Failure Modes | Cause | Observable result | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Retrieval loop never converges | Excessive latency/cost | Enforce and a time/budget limit | | Query drift | Later searches answer a different question | Preserve the original question and constrain query rewriting | | Duplicate evidence | Context bloat | Deduplicate by stable ID or canonical text | | Low-quality retrieval | Grounded-looking but irrelevant answer | Score/re-rank and require evidence quality thresholds | | Conflicting sources | Unsupported synthesis | Preserve source provenance and surface disagreement | Safety Boundaries Retrieved documents are untrusted input and may contain prompt-injection instructions. The stop rule is not a truth detector; it only decides when the retrieval budget is exhausted or evidence is sufficient under an explicit policy. title: Approval Gates
description: Pause an agent run at defined checkpoints and route the pending action to a human decision, so consequential steps execute only after an explicit approval.
body: Approval Gates Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Autonomy is a budget, not a binary. This skill spends it deliberately: the run defines which action classes are safe to execute directly, which require a human decision before they commit, and what information the human needs to decide. A gate is a structured pause — the agent stops, presents the action and its context, and waits; the decision is recorded with the action it authorized, so the audit trail says who allowed what, not just what ran. When to Use Use for irreversible or consequential actions — payments, deletions, production changes, external commitments — and for action classes whose blast radius exceeds a configured threshold. Do not gate trivial, reversible steps; an approval process that fires a hundred times a day trains its approvers to click through without reading. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The pending action awaiting authorization | | | | Yes | Which action classes execute directly and which gate | | | | Yes | What the approver needs to decide — inputs, blast radius, reversibility | Procedure 1. Classify actions up front: which execute without a gate, which need a human, and which are refused outright regardless of approval. 2. Define the gate payload before the run starts — action, arguments, predicted effect, and rollback path — so the pause presents a decision, not a mystery. 3. Stop cleanly: the agent suspends at the gate, persists the pending action, and surfaces the decision request to the designated approver. 4. Record the verdict with its provenance — who decided, when, and on what evidence — attached to the action it authorized. 5. Execute the approved action exactly as presented; a modified action re-enters the gate rather than riding an old approval. 6. Feed rejections back into policy: repeated refusals of the same action class mean the classification, not the human, is wrong. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Approval or rejection with approver identity and timestamp | | | | Every gated action, its verdict, and its provenance | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Rubber-stamping | Approvals granted faster than they can be read | Gate only what is consequential; keep gates rare | | Gate sprawl | Everything requires approval and nothing moves | Classify most actions as auto; gate the irreversible | | Approval reuse | A modified action executed on an old approval | Changed actions re-enter the gate | | Unattributed verdicts | Nobody can say who authorized a past action | Record approver identity and timestamp with every verdict | | Silent refusal drift | Actions quietly failing as policy tightens | Feed refusal patterns back into policy review | Security and Authority Boundary The gate record is an authority artifact: approvals must bind to the exact action hash and the identity of the approver, and gate logs deserve the same integrity protection as audit logs — an attacker who can forge either owns the blast radius of the agent. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework overview (https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework). 2. The arXiv paper on human-in-the-loop agent oversight (https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657). title: Bounded Exploration
description: Spend a fixed exploration budget — trials, depth, wall time — on search and self-play style wandering, then commit to the best option found within the bound.
body: Bounded Exploration Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Exploration without a budget is wandering with good intentions. This skill makes the budget explicit: a number of trials, a depth limit, a deadline, and a stopping rule that ends the search when the bound is hit or the returns flatten. The point is not that exploration is bad — it is that unbounded exploration defers commitment forever, and the commitment is where the value is. After the budget is spent, the agent stops comparing and starts using what it found. When to Use Use when an agent must search a large option space — candidate strategies, tool combinations, plan variants — under real cost or time constraints. Do not spend exploration budget on cheap, well-understood decisions with an obvious best answer; explore where ignorance is real and the cost of being wrong is high. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The candidate space being explored | | | | Yes | Trials, depth, and wall-time limits for the run | | | | Yes | Early stop on flat returns, or spend the full budget | Procedure 1. Fix the budget before starting: trial count, depth limit, and deadline, written down so the run cannot renegotiate with itself. 2. Define the reward or quality signal before exploring; a search without a scoring function is a random walk with commentary. 3. Explore in rounds, keeping the best-so-far option at every round so the budget can end at any moment with something usable. 4. Track returns per round: when additional trials stop improving the best score, apply the stopping rule and keep the leftover budget. 5. Commit to the best option found within the bound, and record it with its score and the exploration that produced it. 6. Defer regret to calibration: revisit the budget size against outcomes over time, rather than restarting exploration on a single miss. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The highest-scoring option found within budget | | | | Trials, scores, and stopping reason per round | | | | Unspent budget returned to the caller | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Endless search | The run keeps exploring past any reasonable bound | Fix trial, depth, and wall-time budgets up front | | No scoring function | Options compared by feel rather than signal | Define the reward before the first trial | | Winner-less stops | The budget ends with nothing selected | Keep best-so-far at every round | | Budget anchoring | The bound set once and never revisited | Calibrate budget size against outcomes over time | | Regret loops | A single miss triggers a fresh unbounded search | Treat misses as calibration data, not restart triggers | Security and Authority Boundary Exploration that invokes real tools spends real authority: an exploring agent must run under the same least-privilege scope as execution, and its trial actions must be recorded like any other — a search that can execute must never leave the audit log emptier than a commit would. title: Prompt Caching
description: Order prompts so stable content forms a cacheable prefix, place cache breakpoints deliberately, and measure the achieved hit rate instead of assuming caching pays for itself.
body: Prompt Caching Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Prompt caching only pays when the stable content is ordered first and the volatile content last, and it only keeps paying while someone measures the hit rate. This skill defines the ordering contract, breakpoint placement, and the measurement loop that decides whether caching is worth its constraints for a given workload. When to Use Use when an agent workload sends a large stable prefix every turn and the provider prices cached input below fresh input. Do not use for single-shot prompts or workloads where the prefix changes every turn; caching adds constraints without return. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Stable system instructions, changed rarely | | | | Yes | Tool schemas that change on deployment boundaries | | | | Yes | Turns eligible for the cached portion | | | | Yes | The volatile per-turn suffix | | | | No | Cached and fresh per-unit prices for cost estimation | Procedure 1. Order the prompt so the stablest content comes first: system text, then tool definitions, then history. 2. Place the volatile user request strictly last; anything after it cannot be cached on the next turn. 3. Declare cache breakpoints at the boundaries between stability tiers, not at arbitrary token counts. 4. Estimate cost with the cached and fresh prices before rollout; an unmeasured saving is an assumed one. 5. Measure the achieved hit rate over real turns, not synthetic ones. 6. Re-measure whenever system text or tool definitions change; a prefix change invalidates the cache at that breakpoint. 7. Keep the prefix genuinely stable; mostly stable content pays the fresh price every turn. 8. Report cached and non-cached cost separately in the budget so the saving is auditable. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Ordered prompt parts with the cached portion marked | | | | Declared cache boundaries between stability tiers | | | | Pre-rollout cost estimate under the price table | | | | Hits divided by turns over the measured window | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Prefix churn | A timestamp or random id sits inside the prefix | Audit prefix content for volatile fields | | Misplaced suffix | The user request precedes the history | Keep the request strictly last | | Assumed savings | Rollout happens without hit-rate measurement | Measure over real turns first | | Breakpoint drift | Stability tiers change silently | Re-verify breakpoints on every content change | | Hidden coupling | System text depends on the request | Decouple the tiers or accept fresh pricing | Security and Authority Boundary Caching prompt content grants no authority to relax data handling. Cached segments may persist on the provider side beyond the request; content subject to retention or confidentiality limits must not be placed in cacheable positions without an explicit policy decision. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Anthropic’s Messages API reference covering prompt caching through the cache_control field (https://docs.anthropic.com/en/api/messages). 2. OpenAI’s prompt caching documentation (https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/prompt-caching). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation
description: Ground generation with retrieved external context by separating ingestion, retrieval, context assembly, generation, and source attribution, with explicit handling for weak or conflicting retrieval.
body: RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation Description RAG separates knowledge retrieval from language generation. The system retrieves relevant source material at query time, supplies that material to the generator, and preserves source references so the answer can be inspected. RAG is a grounding architecture, not a guarantee against hallucination. Pipeline Inputs / Outputs | Item | Type | Required | Notes | |---|---|---:|---| | Query | str | yes | User task or information need | | Corpus | documents | yes | Sources with stable identifiers | | Retriever | callable | yes | Returns ranked source chunks | | Generator | callable | yes | Produces answer from bounded context | | Answer | str | yes | Generated response | | Sources | list[str] | yes | Source IDs supplied to generator | | Retrieval scores | list[float] | recommended | Diagnostics only | Runnable Example This deterministic example uses lexical retrieval instead of pseudo-random vectors. It demonstrates the retrieval boundary without pretending to be a production embedding system. Retrieval Design - Preserve stable document IDs and source locations. - Chunk according to document structure rather than arbitrary token counts alone. - Apply authorization, tenant, language, and document-type filters where required. - Keep retrieved context bounded. - Treat lexical, dense, hybrid, and reranked retrieval as separate components with independently measurable behavior. - Do not treat a retrieval score as a probability of correctness. - When sources conflict, expose the conflict instead of selecting one silently. Generation Contract A generator should receive the query, bounded retrieved context, source identifiers, and explicit instructions for missing or conflicting evidence. Validate that every cited source identifier was actually retrieved. Citation presence alone does not prove support for the underlying claim. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Irrelevant retrieval | Weak query/index or poor chunking | Measure retrieval behavior and tune the index | | Missing evidence | Relevant source not retrieved | Broaden retrieval or report insufficient context | | Citation fabrication | Generator invents source IDs | Validate cited IDs against retrieved sources | | Context overload | Too many or oversized chunks | Bound context and rerank | | Stale knowledge | Index is not refreshed | Track source freshness and rebuild deterministically | | Conflicting sources | Incompatible corpus claims | Preserve provenance and surface the conflict | Evaluation Measure retrieval and generation separately. Retrieval can use recall@k, precision@k, or ranking metrics against a fixed evaluation set. Generation should separately assess factual support, citation correctness, refusal behavior, and completeness. Do not infer production readiness from a single benchmark. Evidence - Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401 - LangChain retrieval concepts: https://python.langchain.com/docs/concepts/retrieval/ Evidence status: references support the architecture and evaluation concepts. No performance ranking or production-readiness claim is made. title: ReAct (Reasoning + Acting)
description: Interleave Thought → Action → Observation steps in a tool-calling loop until the agent declares Final Answer. The most-used reasoning-with-tools pattern.
body: ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) Description ReAct interleaves Thought (model reasoning), Action (a tool call), and Observation (the tool's return value) inside a single loop. The model picks the next tool based on what it has learned so far and stops when it can answer. It is the simplest working architecture for tool-using agents and the foundation that more elaborate patterns (Plan-and-Execute, LATS, Tool-Use Loop) build on. When to Use - The task needs external information or actions (search, DB query, API call) — pure CoT is not enough. - You want a single tool-using loop that's easy to debug and inexpensive. - You can tolerate 5–15 model calls per task; for sub-second latency, prefer direct tool calls without the loop. title: Skill Quality Evaluation
description: Evaluate a skill or skill package against measurable quality dimensions - description fidelity, instruction actionability, runnable example validity, failure-mode coverage, and evidence strength - and produce a scored, reproducible verdict before the skill is trusted, installed, or published.
body: Skill Quality Evaluation Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Skill quality evaluation turns "is this skill good?" into a reproducible inspection with named dimensions and an explicit verdict. It scores a candidate skill against measurable quality dimensions - description fidelity, instruction actionability, runnable-example validity, failure-mode coverage, and evidence strength - and records the findings, so trusting, installing, publishing, or rejecting a skill is a documented decision instead of an impression. This skill is intended for agent runtimes, registries, and maintainers who must decide whether a skill is fit to use or publish. It does not replace security auditing, benchmark execution, or human review; it complements them. When to Use Use when a skill is about to be installed, published, promoted, or relied on, and no current quality verdict exists for its version. Do not use this as a substitute for a security audit of untrusted packages, or as proof that a skill works; a passing quality score is not evidence of runtime effectiveness. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The skill under evaluation: frontmatter, body, examples, and package files | | | | No | Quality dimensions, weights, and thresholds; defaults are used when omitted | | | | No | Available benchmark, provenance, runtime, or review evidence for the skill | | | | No | Similar existing skills used to judge duplication and novelty | | | | No | Rules mapping the weighted score to PASS, NEEDS-WORK, or FAIL | Evaluation Procedure 1. Inventory the artifact: frontmatter, body, runnable example, and any bundled package files. 2. Check description fidelity: does the declared description match what the body actually instructs? 3. Check instruction actionability: are the instructions specific and verifiable, or vague aspiration? 4. Check the runnable example: does it run, is it deterministic where determinism is claimed, and does it exercise the core contract? 5. Check failure-mode coverage: are realistic failure modes named with causes and mitigations? 6. Check evidence strength: which claims carry dated, traceable evidence, and which are unevidenced? 7. Score each dimension with the agreed weights and compute the weighted total. 8. Apply the verdict policy to produce PASS, NEEDS-WORK, or FAIL with explicit blockers. 9. Record dimension scores, findings, and the verdict as a dated review artifact. 10. Re-evaluate when the skill changes version or when new contrary evidence appears. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Per-dimension score with observed findings | | | | Weighted quality score for the evaluated version | | | | , , or | | | | Findings that must be resolved before trust or publication | | | | Dated, reproducible record of the evaluation | Decision Contract A valid evaluation must answer all of these questions: - Which dimensions were scored, with what weights and thresholds? - Does the description match the instructions? - Is the example runnable and representative? - Which failure modes are covered and which are missing? - Which claims carry dated evidence and which do not? - What findings block a PASS verdict? - What change or evidence would reopen the verdict? A skill must not be marked high-quality solely because it is popular, long, or recently updated. Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Rubric gaming | Skill text is written to satisfy the checklist without real capability | Require runnable examples and dated evidence, not keyword presence | | Description drift | Description no longer matches the body after edits | Re-evaluate on every version change | | Single-reviewer bias | One reviewer's taste dominates the verdict | Use shared dimensions, weights, and recorded findings | | Evidence theater | Old or irrelevant citations are presented as current proof | Require dated, claim-specific evidence | | Missing failure modes | Only the happy path is documented | Downgrade or fail skills without documented failure modes | | Score without action | Findings are recorded but blockers are never resolved | Tie verdicts to install and publish gates | | Tooling false confidence | Automated checks pass while runtime behavior fails | Treat automated scores as necessary, not sufficient | Security and Authority Boundary Quality evaluation grants no permissions and does not execute the skill under test beyond its own runnable example in a controlled environment. Untrusted skills must additionally pass a dedicated security audit before installation or execution. High-impact publication or installation decisions remain subject to the governing approval controls of the consuming runtime. Evidence This skill is motivated by dated public ecosystem evidence: 1. A September 2026 structured review of 26 agent skills against Anthropic skill-authoring guidance and the agentskills.io specification produced 152 concrete findings (https://github.com/fabiandistler/agents/issues/325; specification: https://agentskills.io/home). Honest boundary: these signals establish that skill quality varies measurably and that evaluation demand exists; they are not popularity or adoption data. title: Time-travel Debugging
description: Rewind an agent run to a prior checkpoint, inspect or modify state, and re-execute from that point while preserving checkpoint identity and separating diagnostic forks from production runs.
body: Time-travel Debugging Description Time-travel debugging replays a stateful agent graph from a recorded checkpoint instead of repeating earlier work. A checkpointer is required to inspect history. State edits create a diagnostic fork and should not silently mutate the original production run. The exact checkpoint API depends on the graph runtime; the example below uses the LangGraph interface already described by this skill. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Contract | |---|---|---| | | graph runtime | Compiled stateful graph with a configured checkpointer | | | | Identifier for the run history | | | | Existing checkpoint identifier | | | | Optional controlled state patch | | Output | Type | Contract | |---|---|---| | | iterable | Ordered checkpoint snapshots | | | runtime-defined | Result of execution from the selected checkpoint | | | mapping | Configuration identifying the diagnostic replay context | Reference Workflow Diagnostic Protocol 1. Capture the production and checkpoint identifier. 2. Verify that the checkpoint exists before replaying. 3. Replay the unmodified checkpoint first to establish a baseline. 4. Create a separate diagnostic thread before mutating state. 5. Record the state patch and reason for the fork. 6. Compare the forked result with the baseline. 7. Never overwrite production state merely to make a test pass. Failure Modes | Cause | Symptom | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | No checkpointer | Empty history | Configure persistent or test checkpointer before execution | | Checkpoint deleted | History unavailable | Retain checkpoints required by the operational debugging policy | | Invalid state patch | Downstream node failure | Validate state schema before | | Fork shares production identity | Production history is mutated | Use a distinct diagnostic | | Non-deterministic external tool | Replay diverges | Stub or record external effects when reproducibility matters | Reproducibility Limits Checkpoint replay restores graph state, not the external world. HTTP responses, clocks, random seeds, model outputs, databases, and tool side effects can differ unless captured or stubbed. A replay should therefore report which external inputs were restored and which were live. Validation Rules - The target checkpoint must exist before replay. - Diagnostic state changes must use a distinct run identity. - State patches must conform to the graph's state contract. - Replay results must not be presented as identical to production unless external effects were controlled. - Checkpoint identifiers and state changes should be recorded for auditability. Security Boundaries Checkpoint state can contain prompts, tool arguments, secrets, or user data. Do not expose checkpoint contents to unauthorized users, logs, or model prompts merely for debugging convenience. State patches must not be allowed to bypass authorization or approval gates. Provenance The workflow is runtime-specific at the API boundary and intentionally does not pin a LangGraph release here. The conceptual guarantees are checkpoint lookup, controlled state replay, and diagnostic isolation; verify exact runtime APIs against the deployed version. title: Tool Invention
description: Close capability gaps by designing, implementing, and validating new tools at runtime when no existing tool fits, with each invented tool reviewed, tested, and registered before reuse.
body: Tool Invention Category: Agentic Patterns | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description An agent that only uses the tools it was given stalls the first time a task needs a missing primitive. Tool invention closes that gap deliberately: confirm the gap is real, write a minimal contract, implement with tests, validate on held-out cases, and register the tool for reuse. The discipline is what separates invention from improvisation — an invented tool is a durable artifact, not a one-off hack. When to Use Use when a repeated workaround shows a missing primitive: the same task fails or degrades across sessions and no registered tool covers it. Do not invent tools to bypass an existing restriction; a guardrail that blocks a capability is a boundary, not a gap. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The recurring task that exposes the gap | | | | Yes | Existing tools with their contracts | | | | Yes | Failing runs or workarounds that show the gap | Procedure 1. Confirm the gap: search the tool registry and prove no existing tool fits, citing the failure evidence. 2. Write a minimal contract: purpose, typed inputs and outputs, failure modes, and authority requirements. 3. Implement the smallest tool that satisfies the contract; nothing speculative. 4. title: App Readiness Probing
description: Probe a launched application with an ordered, bounded check sequence and an injectable clock so downstream computer-use actions begin only once the app verifiably accepts them.
body: App Readiness Probing Category: Computer Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description An app process being alive does not mean its UI is usable: windows take time, ports open late, and services initialize in order. Readiness probing turns “it started” into evidence — an ordered list of checks re-evaluated on a fixed schedule until every check holds within a declared budget. The probe fails loudly when the budget is spent, carrying the elapsed time and the checks that still failed. When to Use Use after launching or connecting to an application — local desktop app, remote VM, or headed service — before any scripted interaction with its UI. Do not use for continuous health monitoring of long-lived services; that is infrastructure probing, which has different lifecycle rules. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Ordered readiness checks, evaluated in order each cycle | | | | Yes | Total readiness budget in seconds | | | | Yes | Delay between probe cycles | | | | No | Injectable time source for deterministic tests | Procedure 1. Define each check against an externally observable condition — listening port, window present, login prompt visible — never against process liveness alone. 2. Order checks by dependency: earlier checks must hold before later ones can be meaningful. 3. Evaluate every check each cycle in a fixed order, computing readiness as all-checks-hold. 4. Return the elapsed time at first success so startup cost is measured, not guessed. 5. On budget expiry, fail with elapsed time plus the list of still-failing checks. 6. Bind the budget to an injectable clock so probes replay identically in tests. 7. Re-measure the budget after environment changes; a budget tuned once is a stale budget. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Elapsed seconds when all checks passed, or null on timeout | | | | Checks still failing when the budget expired | | | | Number of probe cycles executed | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Premature interaction | UI driven before services finished starting | Gate all scripted actions behind the readiness probe | | Liveness confusion | Process existence treated as readiness | Probe observable capabilities, not process liveness | | Unmeasured startup | Budget guessed from one machine | Record observed elapsed times and tune on evidence | | Clock coupling | Probes read the wall clock in tests | Inject the clock for deterministic replay | | Silent timeout | Failure swallowed by the caller | Treat probe timeout as a blocking error with diagnostics | Security and Authority Boundary Probing grants no authority; it only observes. Probes must use the same authenticated session the actions will use and must not probe systems outside the automation’s declared scope. title: Desktop Notification Triage
description: Classify desktop notifications into act-now, batch, and ignore actions through explicit per-source rule tables with deduplication so an agent’s attention is allocated by policy, not reflex.
body: Desktop Notification Triage Category: Computer Use | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A notification stream is an attention budget under attack: calendars, builds, chats, and marketing all compete for the same reflex. Triage replaces reflex with a rule table — each source maps to a declared action class and deduplication key, repeated notifications collapse, and the output is an ordered action list. The rules are data, versioned with the corpus, and reviewable. When to Use Use when an agent or assistant monitors a desktop notification stream and must decide — by recorded policy — which notifications interrupt a task, which queue for later, and which are dropped. Do not use for alerting humans from your own system; that direction has its own rate and severity contracts. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Incoming notifications in arrival order | | | | Yes | Per-source action class and deduplication field | | | | Yes | Mutable deduplication state carried across calls | Procedure 1. Give every source an explicit rule row before the stream starts; unmapped sources default to ignore, never to act. 2. Compute the deduplication key from the declared field; a missing key makes a notification non-deduplicatable and it is treated as unique. 3. Drop ignored and duplicate notifications before any action; duplicates never reach the action list. 4. Emit actions in arrival order as (source, action, key) triples so the decision trail is replayable. 5. Version the rule table with the agent configuration; triage behavior must be reproducible from the recorded rules. 6. Review dropped and duplicate counts periodically; a rule that drops everything real is a misconfiguration. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Ordered action list after filtering and deduplication | | | | Notifications dropped by ignore rules | | | | Notifications collapsed by deduplication | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Attention flood | No rule table, everything acted on | Default unmapped sources to ignore and review the table | | Duplicate storms | Repeated events each treated as new | Deduplicate by the declared key before acting | | Invisible drops | Ignore rules hide real events | Count drops per source and review the counts | | Rule sprawl | Ad-hoc rules accumulated at call sites | Keep one versioned rule table with the configuration | | Order dependence | Actions replayed by internal sort | Emit in arrival order so the trail is deterministic | Security and Authority Boundary Notification contents can carry sensitive data and injected instructions. Triage classifies and filters but never executes content; instructions inside a notification are data, and acting on them requires the agent’s normal permission path. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. MDN documentation for the Notification API (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Notification). 2. Python’s queue module documentation for ordered processing (https://docs.python.org/3/library/queue.html). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. Related Skills - Accessibility Tree — a structured alternative for reading screen state without reacting to notification content. - Window Management — positions triage surfaces so interruptions land in a bounded, reviewable place. title: Idle Detection
description: Detect user idle periods from timestamped activity events against an explicit threshold so background work can schedule itself into measured quiet windows.
body: Idle Detection Category: Computer Use | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description “The user looks away” is not an observation until it is defined: idle is a gap between timestamped activity events that meets a declared threshold. This skill computes idle periods from an activity log — each gap at or above the threshold is a quiet window, including the trailing gap up to now. The threshold is a policy number, recorded with the results, not an intuition. When to Use Use when background work — indexing, syncing, heavy computation — should run in measured quiet windows on a shared machine, or when session security needs an observable inactivity signal. Do not use to infer user intent or presence for surveillance purposes; this contract measures gaps, not people. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Timestamps of user activity, sorted ascending | | | | Yes | Idle duration in seconds that defines a quiet window | | | | Yes | Current time bounding the trailing gap | Procedure 1. Require sorted activity timestamps; unsorted input is rejected before gaps are computed. 2. Compute each gap between consecutive events; a gap at or above the threshold is an idle period. 3. Include the trailing gap from the last event to now when it meets the threshold. 4. Return periods as (start, end) pairs so downstream work can schedule against real windows. 5. Record the threshold alongside the results; a bare window list is uninterpretable later. 6. Re-validate the threshold after usage changes; the right quiet window is a moving target. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Idle windows at or above the threshold | | | | Summed idle time across all windows | | | | Duration of the longest quiet window | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | False idle | Clock skew between event sources | Use one monotonic time source for events and now | | Threshold guessing | Quiet window tuned by intuition | Measure actual gap distribution and set policy from it | | Trailing gap omitted | Current quiet window never reported | Always evaluate the last event against now | | Micro-gap noise | Every small pause counted as idle | Only gaps at or above the threshold qualify | | Activity starvation | No events logged, idle undefined | Report insufficient evidence rather than inventing windows | Security and Authority Boundary Activity timestamps are behavioral data about a person. Idle detection for scheduling must respect declared consent scopes, and its logs inherit the retention rules of the activity source. title: Macro Recording
description: Record, normalize, and replay user-interface event sequences with deterministic compression of redundant input so repeated computer-use flows replay identically every time.
body: Macro Recording Category: Computer Use | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A recorded input sequence is only useful if it replays the same way twice. Raw event streams contain noise — intermediate mouse moves, doubled clicks, retraced paths — that makes replay fragile. This skill defines macro recording as a normalizing pipeline: capture typed events, compress redundant ones by explicit rules, store the script with its rules version, and replay from the normalized form only. When to Use Use when a repeated UI flow — setup, smoke checks, or form entry — should be captured once from real interaction and then replayed identically on demand. Do not use to record credentials or one-time authorization flows; those inputs belong in secret stores, not in macro scripts. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Raw input events in capture order | | | | Yes | Version of the normalization rules applied | | | | No | Time window within which repeated clicks merge | Procedure 1. Capture events as typed tuples — event type, target identifier, argument — in strict occurrence order. 2. Compress intermediate mouse-move events to the last position per continuous drag; never store every sampled point. 3. Merge rapid repeated clicks on one target into a double-click by the declared tolerance rule. 4. Keep the normalization rules versioned inside the macro; replay applies exactly the recorded version. 5. Replay strictly from the normalized script; raw captures are inputs, never the replay source. 6. Verify replay by a post-run state check, not by assuming the script worked. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The normalized, replayable event sequence | | | | Number of raw events removed by normalization | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Fragile replay | Raw capture replayed unfiltered | Normalize before storing and replay from the script | | Accidental secrets | Credentials captured into the macro | Exclude secret fields at capture time and audit scripts | | Silent merge errors | Double-click rule fires across targets | Merge only on identical targets within tolerance | | Ambiguous targets | Identifiers break after UI change | Record stable element identifiers, not coordinates alone | | Unverified replay | Success assumed from script completion | Assert post-run application state after replay | Security and Authority Boundary A macro is a recorded capability grant: it performs whatever its recording could perform. Keep macro scripts out of shared storage, exclude secrets at capture time, and scope replay to the environment it was recorded in. title: Screen Recording
description: Capture screen activity as video with deterministic region selection, frame pacing, and encoding, for task evidence and UI debugging, with explicit consent and retention handling for sensitive content.
body: Screen Recording Category: Computer Use | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A screen recording turns transient UI behavior into reviewable evidence: a bug reproduces, a procedure demonstrates itself, a session leaves an audit trail. The mechanics are region selection, steady frame pacing, and reliable encoding; the judgment is what must never be in the frame and what happens to the file afterward. When to Use Use to reproduce a UI defect with full context, record a procedure for later replay, or produce task evidence of an automated desktop session. Do not record covertly, and do not record sessions likely to contain credentials or personal input without an explicit policy permitting it. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | No | , , or explicit rectangle (default ) | | | | Yes | Maximum recording length in seconds | | | | No | Frames per second (default 15; 30 for fast motion) | Procedure 1. Determine the capture scope; map logical coordinates to the physical monitor and DPI so the region is what you think it is. 2. Check consent and policy: close or exclude windows that may contain secrets or personal data before capture starts. 3. Configure deterministic pacing and a hard frame budget derived from duration and fps. 4. Capture; if the region moves (window drag), re-anchor or fail loudly rather than silently record the wrong area. 5. Encode with a standard codec, record a checksum, and write metadata (region, fps, duration, host). 6. Verify the result covers the intended interval before reporting success. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The encoded recording | | | | Region, fps, duration, codec, capture host | | | | Integrity digest for the evidence chain | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Secrets in frame | Password field or message visible during capture | Pre-capture window exclusion; post-capture review | | Jerky replay | Variable frame pacing under load | Fixed fps with drop policy, not best-effort | | Wrong region | Multi-monitor or DPI mismatch | Map coordinates explicitly before capture | | Unbounded capture | No duration ceiling; disk fills | Hard frame budget and duration cap | | Unverifiable evidence | File mutated after the fact | Checksum at write time; store with the artifact | Security and Authority Boundary Screen recordings can contain credentials, personal data, and confidential documents. title: Screen Region Mapping
description: Map normalized screen coordinates onto integer pixel regions across logical resolutions and device pixel ratios so UI targets stay stable when displays or zoom levels change.
body: Screen Region Mapping Category: Computer Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Pixel coordinates are a fragile basis for automation: change the display scale or resolution and every stored target breaks. Normalized coordinates — 0..1 fractions of the logical screen — survive both. This skill defines the mapping contract in both directions: normalized to pixels for acting, pixels to normalized for recording, with the device pixel ratio explicit in every conversion so HiDPI displays compute correctly. When to Use Use when recorded UI targets must survive resolution, monitor, or zoom changes, or when screenshots from different device pixel ratios must be compared against one logical layout. Do not use for text-based targets; element identifiers and accessibility trees are more stable than any coordinate scheme. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Region in 0..1 fractions of the logical screen | | | | Yes | Logical resolution of the screen or window | | | | Yes | Device pixel ratio, default 1 | Procedure 1. Store automation targets in normalized units; treat pixel coordinates as derived, disposable values. 2. Carry the device pixel ratio in every conversion; omitting it silently halves or doubles regions on HiDPI displays. 3. Convert each coordinate by multiplying normalized value, logical size, and dpr, rounding half away from zero. 4. Clamp pixel results to the physical screen bounds; off-screen regions are rejected, not wrapped. 5. Round-trip check critical regions: convert to pixels and back, and reject mappings that drift beyond a declared tolerance. 6. On multi-monitor setups, anchor normalized coordinates to the specific monitor’s logical size, never to the union of screens. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Integer pixel region in physical coordinates | | | | Normalized region recovered from pixels | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | HiDPI drift | Device pixel ratio omitted from conversion | Carry dpr through every mapping explicitly | | Monitor confusion | Coordinates anchored to the union of screens | Anchor to the specific monitor’s logical size | | Rounding drift | Half-pixel rounding differs by runtime | Use one documented rounding rule and round-trip check | | Off-screen targets | Regions computed outside the bounds | Clamp and reject instead of wrapping or truncating | | Scale dependence | Targets stored in pixels | Store normalized targets and derive pixels per session | Security and Authority Boundary Screen regions describe where to act, not what may be acted on. Mapping grants no authority: every action derived from a region still passes the permission checks of the underlying automation. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. MDN documentation for window.devicePixelRatio (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/devicePixelRatio). 2. Python’s round() documentation for rounding behavior (https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#round). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: UI Element Waiting
description: Synchronize computer-use actions on observed UI state with bounded explicit-wait loops, injected clocks, and timeout budgets instead of fixed sleeps so automation is deterministic and fails fast.
body: UI Element Waiting Category: Computer Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A fixed sleep is a guess that wastes time when the app is fast and fails when it is slow. An explicit wait replaces the guess with a contract: poll a state predicate on a fixed interval until it holds or a declared budget expires. With an injected clock the loop is testable offline, and the wait either returns the observed ready time or fails with evidence of how much budget was spent. When to Use Use whenever an automation must act on an element that appears asynchronously — after launch, navigation, or a slow update — and the failure mode of a timeout should be an explicit error rather than a mistimed click. Do not use to mask an application bug; if a reasonable budget never suffices, fix the application or shorten the flow instead of raising timeouts. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | State check answering whether the element is ready | | | | Yes | Maximum wait budget in seconds | | | | Yes | Delay between predicate evaluations | | | | No | Injectable time source; wall clock when omitted | Procedure 1. Define the readiness predicate on observable state — DOM presence, pixel match, or API flag — never on elapsed time alone. 2. Declare timeout and poll interval before starting the wait; defaults must come from policy, not from the call site’s mood. 3. Compute the deadline from the injected clock so tests run deterministically offline. 4. Evaluate the predicate at least once before advancing time, so already-ready elements return immediately. 5. On timeout, fail with the budget spent and the last observed state; a silent None return hides the evidence. 6. Record observed wait times per element so budgets are tuned on measurements, not folklore. 7. Never nest waits to synthesize longer budgets; raise the declared budget instead. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Clock time when the predicate first held, or null on timeout | | | | Observed wait duration | | | | The computed deadline for audit | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Flaky timing | Fixed sleeps tuned to one machine | Replace sleeps with predicate polling and measured budgets | | Hidden timeout | Loop returns silently on expiry | Fail with the spent budget and last observed state | | Clock coupling | Tests read the wall clock directly | Inject the clock so waits replay deterministically | | Predicate drift | Ready check weaker than the real need | Test the predicate against the downstream action it guards | | Runaway wait | Deadline computed inside the loop | Compute the deadline once, before polling starts | Security and Authority Boundary Waiting on UI state grants no authority over the application. An automation observing readiness may act only within its permitted action set; polling must respect the target app’s load and authentication boundaries. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Selenium’s WebDriver waits documentation (https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/waits/). 2. Python’s time module documentation for monotonic clocks (https://docs.python.org/3/library/time.html). title: Browser Profile Management
description: Create, persist, and isolate browser profiles and contexts for automation runs, managing cookies, storage state, and settings across sessions without cross-contamination.
body: Browser Profile Management Category: Web | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A browser profile is a bag of authenticated identity and accumulated state. The skill covers defining a profile blueprint, creating isolated contexts from it rather than mutating a shared session, restoring saved storage state when persistence is required, exporting state after authenticated runs, and proving teardown left the base profile untouched. Isolation is the default because concurrent writes to one profile corrupt state and make runs order-dependent. When to Use Use when automation needs persistent login state, parallel isolated sessions, or reproducible browser environments with consistent locale, timezone, and viewport settings. Do not share a single logged-in profile across parallel runs. Concurrent sessions on one profile corrupt storage state and produce flaky, order-dependent results. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Profile definition: base settings, storage state source, isolation requirements | | | | No | Where storage state is saved to and restored from | | | | No | (default), , or | Procedure 1. Define the profile blueprint: base settings, storage state source, and the required isolation level. 2. Create a fresh context from the blueprint rather than mutating a shared browser session. 3. Restore saved storage state where persistence is required and record exactly what was restored. 4. Apply consistent locale, timezone, viewport, and permission settings for reproducibility. 5. Export storage state at the end of authenticated runs for reuse, without logging any secrets. 6. Tear down the context and confirm no state leaked into the base profile. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Identifier of the context created for this run | | | | Exported cookies and local state after the run | | | | What was shared, restored, and persisted | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Storage corruption | Parallel runs mutated one profile | Enforce context-per-run isolation | | Login state lost | Storage not exported after authentication | Export state at run end and version the exports | | Credential leakage | Secrets embedded in exported state files | Restrict permissions and never log exports | | Fingerprint drift | Device settings differ between runs | Pin viewport, locale, and timezone in the blueprint | | Cookie expiry mid-run | Restored state older than the session lifetime | Validate session age before starting | Security and Authority Boundary A profile is a credential by another name. Treat exported storage state as a secret: restrict file permissions, scope each profile to the narrowest account the task needs, and never share profiles across operators or environments. title: File Download Verification
description: Trigger downloads through an authenticated browser session, wait for completion, and verify the artifact against expected name, size, media type, and checksum before downstream use.
body: File Download Verification Category: Web | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A download is not finished when the file appears; it is finished when it is verified. The skill arms download handling before triggering the event, waits for completion with a bounded timeout, then checks size, media type, and checksum against expectations before the artifact is allowed downstream. Failures quarantine the file rather than silently passing it along. When to Use Use when automation must fetch files through an authenticated or interactive browser session and must prove the result is the expected artifact rather than a truncated or substituted payload. Do not trust the downloaded filename or extension. Verify content by checksum and media type before any downstream use, because names and extensions are attacker-controllable. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Action or URL that initiates the download | | | | No | Expected size, media type, and checksum where known | | | | No | Normalized artifact name; defaults to the observed name | Procedure 1. Arm download handling before triggering the event so the stream is captured from the start. 2. Trigger the download and capture the suggested filename and the serving URL as provenance. 3. Wait for completion with a bounded timeout; a partial file must fail, not pass. 4. Verify size, media type, and when provided checksum against the expectations. 5. Store the artifact under a collision-free normalized name with its provenance metadata. 6. Report verification results and quarantine any file that fails a check. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Stored file path and normalized name | | | | Per-check results and overall pass or quarantine verdict | | | | Serving URL, observed filename, and capture timestamp | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Partial file accepted | Connection dropped mid-transfer | Verify size and checksum; never act on partial writes | | Name spoofing | Extension suggests a benign type the content does not match | Verify media type by content, not extension | | Wrong artifact served | Redirect or session error returned an error page instead | Compare checksum against the expectation | | No expectation available | Checksum unknown before the run | Record verification limits explicitly instead of claiming pass | | Download never completes | Server trickles bytes to hold the session open | Bound the wait with a timeout and fail fast | Security and Authority Boundary Downloads cross a trust boundary into local storage. Verify the serving origin, quarantine unexpected artifacts, and never execute or open a downloaded file before verification, because the browser session may have been steered to serve attacker-controlled content. The MDN reference for the Content-Disposition header that carries download filenames (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Disposition). title: Iframe Handling
description: Locate, enter, and act inside nested iframe documents during browser automation, resolving frame identity, cross-origin limits, and stale frame references deterministically.
body: Iframe Handling Category: Web | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Iframe handling turns a flat page into a tree of documents. The skill covers enumerating frames, resolving the target frame by identity rather than by selector alone, re-scoping lookups to the frame document, and proving the current scope before and after every action. The core discipline is that a selector never identifies an element on its own in a framed page; a (frame, selector) pair does. When to Use Use when a target page embeds content in one or more iframes: embedded forms, payment widgets, media players, sandboxed previews, or third-party embeds that must be automated or audited. Do not assume a single flat DOM. The same selector can resolve in several frames, and acting inside the wrong frame produces plausible-looking but incorrect results. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Live browser page or session object | | | | Yes | Selector, frame name, or URL pattern identifying the target frame | | | | No | (default) or when nested frames must be traversed in order | Procedure 1. Enumerate all frames in the page with their name, URL, and nesting depth before any interaction. 2. Resolve the target frame by selector, name, or URL pattern; prefer URL identity when selectors collide. 3. Enter the frame and re-scope all subsequent lookups to its document root. 4. Assert a frame-specific element exists before acting; a missing anchor means the scope is wrong. 5. Perform the action inside the frame, treating every lookup as frame-relative, never global. 6. Exit to the top document explicitly and re-assert scope before continuing with other tasks. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Ordered list of frames with identity, URL, and nesting depth | | | | Outcome of the action performed inside the target frame | | | | Entered and exited frame chain recorded in order | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Wrong frame selected | Duplicate selectors across frames | Resolve by URL or nesting chain, not selector alone | | Stale frame reference | Frame reloaded after navigation | Re-resolve the frame before each action batch | | Cross-origin access blocked | Same-origin policy limits direct inspection | Drive the frame through automation APIs, not raw DOM access | | Silent frame exit | Actions continue on the parent document | Assert frame scope before every action | | Detached frame timing | Frame mounts late or asynchronously | Wait for frame availability with a bounded timeout | Security and Authority Boundary Iframes frequently embed third-party content, and entering a frame moves input across an origin boundary. Verify the frame origin before typing anything into it, never inject credentials into unverified origins, and record which origins received input as part of the audit trail. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The MDN reference for the HTML iframe element (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/iframe). 2. The Playwright frames documentation (https://playwright.dev/python/docs/frames).
