title: Infinite Scroll Handling
description: Extract complete data sets from pages that reveal content incrementally on scroll, with termination detection, batch deduplication, and bounded run budgets.
body: Infinite Scroll Handling Category: Web | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Infinite scroll pages never announce that they are finished. The skill treats scrolling as a batch protocol: extract the visible viewport, scroll one viewport height, wait for the page to settle, deduplicate against what is already collected, and terminate on a budget, a sentinel element, or a run of empty batches. Each batch is persisted as it arrives so a late failure loses only the tail. When to Use Use when a feed, gallery, or results list reveals content as the user scrolls and the full set must be collected rather than sampled. Do not scroll until the page stops by itself without a hard budget. Some feeds generate content forever and will exhaust memory, time, or rate limits before they exhaust content. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Live page containing the scrollable content region | | | | Yes | Function returning the items visible in the current viewport | | | | No | Hard bounds: max scrolls, max items, or deadline; defaults to a fixed scroll cap | Procedure 1. Extract the initial viewport before any scroll and record it as the first batch. 2. Scroll by one viewport height and wait for the network or DOM to settle before extracting. 3. Re-extract and deduplicate against already-collected batches using stable item keys. 4. Terminate when the budget is hit, the sentinel appears, or several consecutive batches yield nothing new. 5. Persist each batch before scrolling again so a late failure loses only the tail. 6. Report the collected count, batch count, and the exact termination reason. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Deduplicated items collected across all batches | | | | Per-batch counts and persistence status | | | | Stop reason, final scroll position, and budget usage | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Endless scroll loop | Feed generates content indefinitely | Enforce a hard budget on scrolls, items, and time | | Duplicate items collected | Revealed batches overlap the previous viewport | Deduplicate on stable keys before counting | | Premature stop | Slow loading read as an exhausted feed | Require consecutive empty batches, not a single one | | Dropped batches on crash | All items held in memory until the end | Persist per batch as it arrives | | Rate limited mid-run | Scroll cadence exceeds server tolerance | Back off between batches and respect limits | Security and Authority Boundary Scrolling is automated access even when it mimics a user. Respect robots directives and rate limits, collect only what the task requires, and avoid incrementally harvesting personal profiles or private content that a single page view would not expose. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The MDN reference for the Intersection Observer API used by infinite scroll implementations (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/IntersectionObserverAPI). 2. The Playwright actionability documentation for waiting on settle states (https://playwright.dev/python/docs/actionability). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Pagination Following
description: Follow paginated listings through declared next-link selectors with visited-set loop detection and a hard page cap so a crawl terminates exactly where the listing does.
body: Pagination Following Category: Web | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Paginated content hides most of the corpus behind a “next” affordance, and a naive loop either stops early or spins forever on a circular link. This skill defines pagination traversal as a bounded graph walk: each page declares how its next link is identified, a visited set rejects cycles, and a page cap bounds the walk even when the listing is generated adversarially. When to Use Use when scraping or crawling structured listings — search results, catalogs, archives — that expose next-page links or numbered pages. Do not use for infinite-scroll feeds that expose no pagination affordance; those need event-driven capture, not link following. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Observed page transitions, or a resolver producing them | | | | Yes | Hard cap on pages visited per listing | | | | Yes | Mutable cycle-detection state | Procedure 1. Declare the next-link selector convention up front — rel=next, a labeled link, or a numbered URL scheme — and use it consistently. 2. Normalize each next URL before comparison so parameter noise cannot disguise a cycle. 3. Record every visited page in the visited set; a next URL already present is a loop, and traversal stops with the loop identified. 4. Stop at the first missing next link; absence is the listing’s terminal, not an error. 5. Enforce the page cap even when the listing keeps offering links; unbounded traversal is a policy violation. 6. Emit the visited sequence plus a terminal reason — terminal, loop, or cap — so the walk is auditable. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Ordered pages actually fetched | | | | terminal, loop-detected, or page-cap reached | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Infinite loop | Next link points to an earlier page | Detect cycles with a visited set and stop with evidence | | Premature stop | Next-link selector misses the page’s convention | Declare the convention per site and test it on page one | | Silent truncation | Page cap reached but reported as done | Report the cap as its own terminal reason | | URL noise | Tracking parameters disguise repeated pages | Normalize URLs before loop detection | | Off-list drift | Next selector matches unrelated links | Constrain following to the listing container | Security and Authority Boundary Pagination traversal is still fetching; robots rules, rate limits, and terms of service apply to every page visited. The page cap is a politeness bound as much as a correctness one. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. MDN documentation for link type rel attributes including next (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Attributes/rel). 2. The WHATWG HTML specification section on link types (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/links.html). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. body: Robots.txt Parsing Category: Web | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Politeness on the web starts with a parsed contract, not string matching. robots.txt groups directives by user-agent, allows and disallows paths, requests a crawl delay, and points to sitemaps. This skill defines a minimal deterministic parser — grouping, per-agent rule lists, sitemap collection — and a query interface so “may this agent fetch this path” is a testable function of recorded rules. When to Use Use before any crawl or scrape touches a new host, and as the standing policy engine that answers per-path fetch questions during crawling. Do not use robots.txt parsing as a legal position; it encodes machine etiquette, and separate permission, terms, and law still apply. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Raw robots.txt body fetched from the host | | | | Yes | The requesting agent’s product token | | | | No | Target path evaluated against the parsed rules | Procedure 1. Strip comments and blank lines before directive parsing; directives survive, decoration does not. 2. Group rules by user-agent block: directives following a User-agent line belong to that agent until the next one. 3. Collect Sitemap lines globally; they are host-level, not per-agent. 4. Store Allow, Disallow, and Crawl-delay as ordered per-agent rule lists. 5. Answer path queries by longest-prefix match, with Allow and Disallow resolved by rule specificity. 6. Treat parse failure or absence of robots.txt under the declared fallback policy — ask-permissive or ask-conservative — chosen once and recorded. 7. Re-fetch robots.txt at a bounded interval during long crawls; a cached policy outlives its welcome. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Parsed per-agent directive lists | | | | Host-declared sitemap URLs | | | | Path decision, or null when no rule applies | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Misgrouped rules | Directives attached to the wrong agent | Reset the current agent on every User-agent line | | Prefix mismatch | Rule scope guessed instead of matched | Resolve queries by longest-prefix specificity | | Stale policy | robots.txt cached for the crawl’s life | Re-fetch at a bounded interval and after fetcher errors | | Comment noise | Directive values read with trailing comments | Strip comments before parsing values | | Untracked fallback | Missing robots.txt handled by mood | Choose one fallback policy up front and record it | Security and Authority Boundary Respecting robots.txt is a floor, not a license. Parsing grants no authority to fetch; authentication, terms of service, and rate limits still bind, and crawl behavior must stay within the host’s declared delay. body: Shadow DOM Interaction Category: Web | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Shadow DOM hides component internals behind a boundary that ordinary selectors cannot cross. The skill covers probing for shadow roots, composing locator chains across each boundary, asserting that a composed chain resolves to exactly one element, and respecting closed roots by interacting only through the interfaces a component exposes. Every boundary crossed is recorded so a failure can be traced to the correct layer. When to Use Use when component libraries or web components encapsulate markup in shadow roots and standard selectors cannot reach the interactive elements inside them. Do not force open closed shadow roots through internal framework APIs. A closed root is a component contract; interact through its exposed methods and attributes only. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Selector for the host element whose shadow root is targeted | | | | Yes | Selector for the element inside the shadow root | | | | No | (default) or for engines without shadow-piercing locators | Procedure 1. Choose piercing mode when the automation engine supports it; otherwise walk each shadow boundary explicitly. 3. Compose a locator chain across the boundaries and record the full path from the page root to the target. 4. Assert the composed chain resolves to exactly one element; zero or many results both mean the chain is wrong. 5. Interact through exposed methods or attributes when the root is closed instead of bypassing the boundary. 6. Record every boundary crossed so failures can be attributed to the correct layer of the component tree. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Hosts and shadow boundaries traversed, in order | | | | Elements resolved inside the shadow root | | | | Outcome of the action performed on the target element | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Selector misses the target | Element lives behind a shadow boundary | Probe hosts and compose chains across each boundary | | Closed root blocks access | Component refuses internal inspection | Use exposed interfaces; do not bypass the boundary | | Nested depth exceeded | Chain stops one boundary short | Record and follow the full host path | | Slot content mislocated | Projected content resolves in a different root | Resolve through the slot, not the light DOM | | Stale host after re-render | Component re-created the shadow tree | Re-probe and recompose the chain before acting | Security and Authority Boundary Shadow DOM is an encapsulation boundary that some components rely on for security assumptions. title: URL Normalization
description: Normalize URLs by lowercasing scheme and host, removing default ports and fragments, sorting query parameters, and collapsing path noise so identical resources compare equal.
body: URL Normalization Category: Web | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Two strings that differ can still name the same page: mixed case, an explicit :443, a stray fragment, unsorted parameters. Naive deduplication misses them all. Normalization applies a declared, ordered set of transformations — scheme and host lowercased, default ports removed, empty fragments dropped, parameters sorted — producing one canonical form per resource so equality checks mean something. When to Use Use before storing, deduplicating, or comparing URLs from crawls, logs, or user input, and as the canonicalization step of any fetch cache key. Do not normalize URLs whose case-sensitive path is part of an API contract; preserve those verbatim and exclude them from normalization by policy. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The URL to canonicalize | | | | No | Whether query parameters are sorted; default true | | | | No | Whether to drop the fragment; default true | Procedure 1. Split the URL into scheme, host, port, path, query, and fragment before any transformation. 2. Lowercase scheme and host; they are case-insensitive by URL grammar. 3. Drop ports that are the scheme default (443 for https, 80 for http); keep non-default ports. 4. Collapse an empty fragment; when stripping is on, drop any fragment per policy. 5. Sort query parameters by name then value so parameter order stops producing duplicates. 6. Normalize the path — collapse duplicate slashes, resolve dot segments — without changing case. 7. Return the canonical string and use it, not the input, as every comparison and cache key. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The normalized URL | | | | Whether normalization altered the input | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Case-sensitive paths | Host rules applied to the path | Lowercase scheme and host only; paths stay as-is | | Parameter-order duplicates | Same resource stored twice | Sort query parameters before comparison | | Port mishandling | Non-default ports stripped | Strip only scheme-default ports | | Cache fragmentation | Raw keys used in the fetch cache | Key every cache on the canonical form | | Over-normalization | API URLs altered under contract | Exempt case-sensitive paths by explicit policy | Security and Authority Boundary Normalization rewrites identifiers; it must never rewrite authority. Credentials embedded in URLs are a separate defect to flag and strip deliberately, not silently, and canonical forms inherit the trust level of their source. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. RFC 3986 defining URI syntax and normalization (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986). 2. This skill defines that bucket — capacity and refill rate per host, an injectable clock for deterministic tests, and an allow/deny answer per request — so a crawl’s politeness is a recorded contract that can be measured, tuned, and logged. When to Use Use whenever an agent fetches from hosts it does not own, when a host declares a crawl delay, or before any parallel fetch loop could otherwise stampede a single origin. Do not use to throttle your own outbound API quota when the platform enforces it already; double throttling wastes time without adding politeness. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Sustained refill rate of the bucket | | | | Yes | Burst size: tokens available at once | | | | Yes | Per-host bucket key; budgets never share | | | | No | Injectable time source for deterministic tests | Procedure 1. Create one bucket per host; a shared bucket lets one fast host starve every other. 2. Refill tokens by elapsed time multiplied by the declared rate, capped at the burst capacity. 3. Admit a request only when a full token is available; deny without consuming. 4. Honour host-declared crawl delays by treating them as a lower bound on the rate. 5. Log allow and deny decisions with timestamps so backpressure is measured, not inferred. 6. Never bypass the bucket on error paths; retries consume tokens like any other request. 7. Inject the clock in tests so refill arithmetic replays deterministically. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Whether the request may proceed now | | | | Remaining tokens after the decision | | | | Cumulative denials for observability | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Stampede | Parallel fetches share no throttle | Route every fetch through one per-host bucket | | Refill drift | Tokens computed from wall clock in tests | Inject the clock so refill arithmetic is deterministic | | Burst abuse | Capacity larger than the host tolerates | Set burst from the host’s crawl delay and measured limits | | Retry bypass | Error-retry paths skip the bucket | Charge retries the same tokens as first attempts | | Invisible pressure | Denials never logged | Count denials per host and surface the metric | Security and Authority Boundary Rate limiting is a politeness boundary, not an authorization one. Passing the bucket grants no right to fetch; robots rules, terms of service, and authentication still apply, and denial must degrade gracefully rather than escalate. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia’s overview of the token bucket algorithm (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Token_bucket). 2. MDN documentation for the Retry-After response header (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Retry-After). title: URL Redirect Tracing
description: Trace redirect chains hop by hop with loop detection and a hard hop cap so agents know the final canonical target of a URL before trusting or storing it.
body: URL Redirect Tracing Category: Web | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A URL that redirects is a claim about where content really lives, and the chain matters: shorteners launder destinations, loops waste budgets, and mixed http-to-https hops change the security posture mid-chain. This skill records every hop as (from, to, status-class), detects cycles, and refuses to follow past a declared hop cap. When to Use Use when resolving shortened or syndicated links into their final targets, when auditing where a stored URL actually lands, or before treating a fetched origin as trustworthy. Do not use to bypass a site’s redirect intent; if a host routes you to a consent or login page, that response is the answer, not an obstacle. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Observed redirect transitions with terminal markers | | | | Yes | Hard cap on followed redirects per trace | | | | Yes | Mutable loop-detection state | Procedure 1. Record each hop as it happens — from URL, to URL, status class — never reconstruct the chain from memory after the fact. 2. Normalize URLs before cycle comparison; a loop hidden by a trailing slash is still a loop. 3. Treat a repeated URL as a cycle and stop immediately, reporting the loop entry point. 4. Stop at the hop cap and report it distinctly from a terminal resolution. 5. Preserve the full chain in the result; a bare final URL without its chain is unauditable. 6. Flag scheme downgrades (https to http) in the chain as a security-relevant event. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The full recorded redirect chain | | | | Terminal target, or null when unresolved | | | | terminal, loop-detected, or hop-cap reached | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Redirect loops | Two URLs redirect to each other | Detect cycles with a visited set and stop | | Unbounded chains | Adversarial chains exhaust the budget | Enforce a hard hop cap per trace | | Memory-reconstructed chains | Hops inferred after fetching completes | Record every hop as it happens | | Scheme downgrade missed | https-to-http hop treated as neutral | Flag downgrades in the chain report | | Noise loops | Trailing-slash variants seen as cycles | Normalize URLs before comparison | Security and Authority Boundary Redirect chains cross trust boundaries: a chain that ends off-origin changes what credentials and cookies are safe to send. Trace before trusting, and never forward authentication material to a target the chain has not resolved. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. MDN documentation for HTTP 301 permanent redirect (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/301). 2. Wikipedia’s overview of URL redirection (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/URL_redirection). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Web Archive Lookup
description: Query archived web snapshots through timestamped request construction and nearest-snapshot selection so historical page state is retrieved explicitly and reproducibly.
body: Web Archive Lookup Category: Web | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Pages change and disappear, and an agent that cited one yesterday may need the bytes it saw, not today’s revision. Web archives answer with timestamped snapshots, but only if requests are built correctly: a canonical URL form, a timestamp in the archive’s format, and an explicit rule for choosing among nearby snapshots. This skill defines that lookup as a deterministic computation. When to Use Use when verifying a citation against a prior page state, recovering deleted content for evidence, or comparing a page across time. Do not use archived copies as a substitute for fetching the live page when current information is the requirement; archives lag and the present is authoritative. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The page URL whose history is needed | | | | Yes | Requested capture time in the archive’s compact format | | | | Yes | Available capture timestamps for the URL | Procedure 1. Normalize the URL before requesting archives; equivalent spellings fragment the snapshot history. 2. Construct the archive request with the normalized URL and the requested timestamp in the documented format. 3. When the exact timestamp is absent, select the nearest earlier snapshot under a declared rule and record both requested and selected times. 4. Report when no snapshot precedes the request; an empty history is an answer, not an error to retry. 5. Record the archive’s identifier for the chosen snapshot so the same evidence can be retrieved again. 6. Treat archived content as historical evidence with its capture date attached; undated citation of an archive is a defect. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The archive lookup URL built from the inputs | | | | The selected capture timestamp, or null when none precedes the request | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Fragmented history | URL variants each archive separately | Normalize the URL before any archive request | | Nearest-after bias | Later snapshot silently substituted | Select nearest-earlier by rule and record both times | | Undated citations | Archive content cited without capture date | Attach the snapshot timestamp to every retrieval | | Empty history retried | Missing snapshots treated as fetch errors | Report an empty history explicitly | | Live/archived confusion | Historical copy cited as current fact | Label archived content with its capture date | Security and Authority Boundary Archived pages are third-party records, not the original source’s word; they can be incomplete or manipulated upstream. Archive lookups grant no authority over the original site and inherit the archive’s own terms of use. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia’s overview of the Wayback Machine (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayback_Machine). 2. The Internet Archive’s developer documentation (https://archive.org/developers/). title: Web Scraping

body: Web Scraping Description Web scraping pulls a URL and returns its main readable content as clean text or Markdown — stripped of nav, ads, footer, JS warnings, cookie banners. It's the second half of agentic browsing: web search picks the URL, scrape gets the actual answer. Naive floods the LLM with chrome and JavaScript stubs. title: Web Search
description: Query a search API (Tavily, Serper, Bing, Brave, Exa) and return ranked URLs + snippets. The agent's bridge to fresh, open-web information when its training cutoff or private corpus isn't enough.
body: Web Search Description Web search is the agent's escape hatch from the training cutoff: when it doesn't know, it searches. The contract is simple — query string in, ranked list of out — but the choice of provider, query rewriting, and result re-ranking dictate whether the agent finds the answer or makes one up. This skill wraps a single provider (Tavily by default — small, agent-tuned, returns clean snippets) behind a stable interface, then adds query rewriting, caching, and a host-allowlist guard. You can swap providers without touching the consumer. When to Use - The question is about fresh events, prices, releases, news, or anything past the model's cutoff. - The corpus is the open web, not a private collection (use RAG for the latter). - You need citations with publication dates — search APIs return both. - Don't use when the question is purely conceptual (the model already knows), or when the answer must come from your own data. title: Cohort Analysis
description: Segment records into cohorts by a shared anchor event, measure retention and behavior across periods, and compare cohort trajectories with explicit handling of censoring and cohort size.
body: Cohort Analysis Category: Data | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Cohort analysis compares groups defined by when they started, not by who they are. The skill covers assigning entities to cohorts by their first anchor event, binning cohorts by the calendar rule, computing period-by-period retention relative to cohort size, and censoring the trailing periods where not enough time has elapsed to observe the window. Comparisons are always normalized rates with cohort sizes attached, never raw counts. When to Use Use when behavior must be compared across groups defined by a starting event: signup month, first purchase, activation week, or onboarding batch. Do not compare raw counts across cohorts of different sizes. Normalize to rates and report cohort sizes alongside every comparison. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Timestamped records with an entity key and an event type | | | | Yes | The anchor event and the binning rule defining cohort membership | | | | No | Number of periods after the anchor to measure; bounded by default | Procedure 1. Assign each entity to a cohort by its first occurrence of the anchor event. 2. Bin cohorts by the rule in the definition: calendar month, week, or event index. 3. For each cohort, compute the size at the anchor and the survivors in each later period. 4. Convert counts to rates relative to cohort size; never report raw counts alone. 5. Flag censored trailing periods where not enough time has elapsed to observe the window. 6. Compare trajectories across cohorts and annotate every difference with cohort sizes. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Cohorts by period with sizes and survivor counts | | | | Per-cohort retention rates over the measured periods | | | | Periods excluded from comparison for insufficient elapsed time | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Survivorship bias | Only fully observed histories compared | Include censored periods and mark them in every chart | | Small-cohort volatility | Tiny cohorts read as dramatic trends | Report sizes and aggregate tiny cohorts before comparing | | Anchor event misdefined | Cohorts assigned by first record instead of the anchor | Validate the anchor against a hand-checked sample | | Period edge effects | Partial trailing period treated as complete | Mark incomplete windows as censored, not as zero | | Timezone drift | Cohort bins shift at month boundaries | Fix a timezone before binning and keep it fixed | Security and Authority Boundary Cohort tables aggregate personal behavior. Use the minimum viable entity key, avoid rejoining identifiers after aggregation, and publish rates rather than raw per-entity histories wherever the decision allows. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. title: Data Anonymization
description: Transform data sets to reduce re-identification risk using suppression, generalization, and pseudonymization, with k-anonymity checks and honest reporting of residual risk.
body: Data Anonymization Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Anonymization is measured, not declared. The skill covers classifying fields into direct identifiers, quasi-identifiers, and sensitive attributes, applying the policy of transforms, then measuring what remains: equivalence-class sizes over quasi-identifier combinations, records below threshold, and utility lost to generalization. Output that cannot meet the threshold is suppressed or further generalized rather than passed through with a false label. When to Use Use when data containing personal or identifying elements must be shared, published, or analyzed outside its origin context. Do not treat column deletion as anonymization. Remaining quasi-identifiers such as postcode, timestamps, and rare value combinations re-identify most individuals when combined. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Records containing direct or quasi-identifying fields | | | | Yes | Field-level transforms and the risk threshold the output must meet | | | | No | Re-identification checks to run; defaults to k-anonymity over quasi-identifiers | Procedure 1. Classify every field as direct identifier, quasi-identifier, sensitive, or neutral before transforming. 2. Apply the policy: suppress or tokenize direct identifiers and generalize quasi-identifiers. 3. Measure residual risk, including k-anonymity over every quasi-identifier combination. 4. Report the equivalence-class distribution and the records that fall below the threshold. 5. Suppress or further generalize below-threshold records instead of passing them through. 6. Document the transforms applied so the output can never be presented as raw source data. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Transformed records meeting the stated threshold | | | | Equivalence-class distribution and residual risk figures | | | | Per-field transforms applied, for reproducibility and auditing | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Re-identification through combination | Quasi-identifiers generalized too coarsely | Measure k over combinations, not per field | | Over-generalization | Utility destroyed to satisfy the threshold | Tune per-field granularity and report the loss | | Pseudonyms reversed | Mapping table shipped with the output | Keep the mapping separate and access-controlled | | Linkage across releases | Same generalization used in two published sets | Vary bins across releases or use privacy-preserving models | | Free-text leakage | Names remain inside narrative fields | Scan and redact unstructured text, not just columns | Security and Authority Boundary Anonymization failures cause irreversible privacy harm. Never claim the output is anonymous without measuring residual risk, keep re-identification mappings under separate access control, and stop and escalate when the threshold cannot be met instead of shipping weakly protected data. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The NIST guide to de-identifying government data sets (https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/188/final). 2. The NIST Privacy Framework (https://www.nist.gov/privacy-framework). title: Data Contract Enforcement
description: Define and enforce machine-readable data contracts covering schema, types, ranges, and freshness, failing production pipelines loudly when producers drift from the agreed shape.
body: Data Contract Enforcement Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A data contract is an executable agreement between a producer and a consumer. The skill covers expressing the contract as code: field names, types, ranges, nullability, and freshness expectations, then enforcing it at handoff boundaries so that a producer change surfaces as a loud, attributable failure in the producer pipeline rather than silent corruption downstream. Failures are reported with the violated clause, not a generic schema error. When to Use Use when a data set crosses a team or system boundary and downstream consumers must be protected from silent schema and quality drift. Do not enforce contracts only in tests. Without enforcement at the production handoff, producers can ship breaking changes at any time and consumers absorb them silently. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Machine-readable schema, types, ranges, and freshness rules | | | | Yes | The batch or stream being validated at the boundary | | | | No | (default) or for low-trust transitions | Procedure 1. Express the contract in code: fields, types, ranges, nullability, and freshness windows. 2. Version the contract and record which version each producer declares. 3. Validate the incoming data set at the handoff boundary, collecting every violation. 4. Fail or quarantine the batch on violation; never pass degraded data through as if clean. 5. Report violations by clause with producer, contract version, and offending records. 6. Negotiate contract changes as versioned migrations with consumer sign-off before rollout. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Pass or fail verdict with the clause-level evidence | | | | Each violated rule with sample offending records | | | | The contract version the data was validated against | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Silent schema drift | Contract not enforced at the boundary | Validate at handoff, not only in tests | | Generic failure reports | Violations collapsed into one schema error | Report per clause with sample records | | Contract and code diverge | Contract edited without producer sign-off | Version contracts and review migrations | | Freshness never checked | Only structure enforced | Include freshness windows in the contract | | Quarantine fills up | Failing batches parked without owners | Alert on quarantine depth and assign triage | Security and Authority Boundary Contracts describe data an organization may be legally accountable for. Keep contract definitions in version control with review, log validation outcomes for audit, and never relax a contract to let a failing producer through without a recorded decision. title: Data Lineage
description: Record where each dataset came from and what it fed — inputs, transformations, outputs — so any result can be traced to its sources and any change traced forward.
body: Data Lineage Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A number without ancestry is a rumor with formatting. This skill records ancestry as a first-class artifact: every dataset declares its inputs, the transformation and code version that produced it, and the outputs that depend on it. Lineage answers two questions the moment they are asked — where did this come from, and what breaks if this changes — and a lineage graph that cannot answer both is decoration, not documentation. When to Use Use for datasets that feed decisions, reports, or models — anywhere a wrong number needs to be traced to its source or an upstream change needs its blast radius known. Do not hand-maintain lineage for throwaway exploratory scratch data; capture it where outputs persist and matter, and let the pipeline write the graph. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The dataset whose ancestry is being recorded | | | | Yes | Upstream datasets and their versions | | | | Yes | The code, version, and parameters that produced the dataset | Procedure 1. Record inputs precisely: which upstream datasets, at which versions or snapshots, fed the transformation. 2. Record the transformation itself — code version, parameters, and environment — enough to reproduce the output. 3. Write lineage at run time from the pipeline itself, not by hand afterward; hand-maintained lineage is yesterday's graph. 4. Register outputs symmetrically: a dataset knows what it fed, so impact analysis can walk forward as easily as backward. 5. Attach the lineage record to the data — a table property, a manifest, a catalog entry — not to a wiki page. 6. On any upstream change, consult the forward graph before it merges: blast radius is a lineage query, not a guess. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Inputs, transform, and outputs for the dataset | | | | Downstream datasets affected by a change to this one | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Hand-drawn graphs | Lineage edited by hand and drifting from reality | Capture lineage at run time from the pipeline | | Version-blind inputs | Upstream named but not pinned to a snapshot | Record input versions or snapshots, not just names | | Half-lineage | Origins recorded but dependents unknown | Register outputs symmetrically for forward walks | | Orphan manifests | Lineage stored far from the data it describes | Attach lineage to the dataset, not the wiki | | Unqueried impact | Upstream changes merged without blast-radius checks | Make forward impact a pre-merge step | Security and Authority Boundary Lineage is a map of how sensitive data moves: a complete graph shows exactly where restricted columns flow, so lineage stores must enforce the same access scope as the data they describe, and impact queries must not leak the existence or shape of restricted datasets to callers who cannot read them. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The OpenLineage open standard for lineage (https://openlineage.io/). 2. Wikipedia's overview of data lineage (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_lineage). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Data Profiling
description: Measure a dataset before using it — row counts, distributions, null rates, cardinalities — so assumptions about the data are recorded facts instead of hopes.
body: Data Profiling Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Every analysis rests on beliefs about its data: that ids are unique, that the date column is a date, that the two category columns relate the way they did last quarter. Profiling replaces those beliefs with measurements: counts, distinct values, null rates, ranges, and distribution shapes, recorded per column and compared over time. The profile is not the analysis — it is the ground the analysis stands on, and a profile that changed since last week is often the whole explanation for a number that stopped making sense. When to Use Use when a dataset is new to you, before publication or reporting on it, and periodically on datasets assumed stable. Do not profile a known-stable, schema-verified table on every read; repeated profiling of unchanged data is cost without information. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The data being profiled | | | | Yes | Counts, null rates, distinct values, ranges to measure | | | | No | A prior profile to diff against | Procedure 1. Profile structure first: column names, types, row count, and how those differ from any recorded schema. 2. Measure completeness per column — null rates and default values — and distinctness: cardinality and top values. 3. Profile ranges and distributions for numeric and temporal columns, recording min, max, and shape, not just the mean. 4. Diff against the baseline profile and flag every metric that moved beyond its historical band. 5. Record the profile with the dataset version and date, so future comparisons have something concrete to diff. 6. Turn anomalies into constraints: a property that surprised you is a rule for the validation boundary. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Per-column measurements with dataset version and date | | | | Movements against the prior profile, empty when none | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Assumed schemas | Analysis built on a shape nobody verified | Profile structure before any measurement | | Mean-blindness | Averages hiding bimodal or skewed reality | Record distribution shape, not just the mean | | Unrecorded profiles | Measurements made once and lost | Persist profiles with dataset version and date | | Unbounded profiling | Whole-table scans repeated on every read | Profile new or changed data; sample what is stable | | Anomaly blindness | A moved metric nobody diffs against history | Always diff against the prior profile | Security and Authority Boundary Profiles are exfiltration-shaped: cardinalities, top values, and ranges of sensitive columns can disclose individual records, so profiling outputs on restricted data inherit its access scope and profiling jobs must not write measurements to stores more public than the data itself could reach. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of data profiling (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dataprofiling). 2. Wikipedia's overview of descriptive statistics (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Descriptivestatistics). title: Data Validation
description: Check datasets against declared constraints — schema, types, ranges, and cross-field rules — before they enter analysis or models, failing loudly at the boundary.
body: Data Validation Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Data arrives wrong more often than it arrives late: nulls where keys live, strings where numbers were promised, duplicate rows quietly doubling a metric. This skill moves checking to the boundary: constraints are declared alongside the pipeline, every batch is validated on arrival, and a violation stops the data instead of following it downstream. The essential move is declaring expectations explicitly — an undeclared constraint cannot be checked, and an unchecked constraint eventually becomes a wrong number someone acted on. When to Use Use at every ingestion boundary — files, API feeds, database extracts — and before anything feeds reporting, training, or user-visible output. Do not validate beyond what consumers depend on; a constraint nobody relies on still costs every batch and fails runs for no operational reason. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The batch or table arriving at the boundary | | | | Yes | Declared types, required fields, and nullability | | | | Yes | Value rules — ranges, enums, uniqueness, cross-field logic | Procedure 1. Declare the schema first — column names, types, nullability — and version it beside the pipeline that enforces it. 2. Add value constraints that consumers actually rely on: ranges, enum membership, uniqueness of keys, referential joins. 3. Run validation on arrival, per batch, and collect all violations rather than stopping at the first. 4. Route failures by severity: hard violations quarantine the batch, soft ones are logged with counts and rates. 5. Report violation statistics as data — failure rates by rule over time — so drift is visible before it becomes an outage. 6. Change the schema deliberately: a constraint change ships as a reviewed edit with a migration, not as a hotfix to silence a failing rule. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The batch that passed, cleared for downstream use | | | | Per-record rule failures with the offending values | | | | Rule-level pass and failure counts for the batch | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Silent coercion | A wrong-typed column parsed into plausible nonsense | Type-check at the boundary; never rely on parse leniency | | Null smuggling | Missing keys flow into aggregates as zeros or blanks | Declare nullability; fail on missing required fields | | Duplicate keys | The same record counted twice in a metric | Uniqueness-check primary keys per batch | | Rule sprawl | Constraints accumulated that nobody depends on | Retire constraints no consumer relies on | | Failure fatigue | Frequent red pipelines ignored as background noise | Severity-route; only hard violations block | Security and Authority Boundary Validation reports quote offending values: constraint failures on sensitive columns must surface the shape of the violation without reproducing the raw value in logs, and validation stages should inherit the access scope of the data they check. title: Embedding Generation
description: Turn text (or images, audio) into dense unit-normalised vectors with a hosted embedding model. Batch the API calls, cache by content hash, and handle the per-token / per-input limits explicitly.
body: Embedding Generation Description Embedding generation converts arbitrary inputs (most commonly text) into fixed-dimensional dense vectors that encode semantic similarity: similar inputs land near each other in vector space. The vectors are produced by a frozen pre-trained model and consumed by retrieval, clustering, classification, and recommendation systems. This skill covers the production-grade contract: deterministic batching to maximise throughput, content-hash caching so you don't re-embed unchanged inputs, dimension reduction (via Matryoshka truncation when supported), and the silent-failure modes — wrong tokenizer, mixing dimensions, missing normalisation — that bite teams six months in. When to Use - You need a vector representation that downstream code (vector store, classifier, ranker) can consume. - The input is text (most common), or images/audio with a multimodal embedding model. - You're embedding once and querying many times → cache by content hash; embeddings are deterministic for fixed model+content. - Don't use when a sparse keyword index (BM25, tf-idf) is sufficient or when you need a probability distribution rather than a similarity vector. Inputs / Outputs | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Up to 2048 inputs per request (OpenAI limit) | | | | Embedding model name | | | | Truncate output (Matryoshka); requires supporting model | | | | Inputs per HTTP call (default 100) | | | | L2-normalise so dot product equals cosine (default ) | | → | | One vector per input | | → | | Total tokens billed | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Inputs silently truncated | Single text exceeds model's max-tokens (8192 for ) | Pre-chunk; reject or split with overlap | | Re-billed for unchanged docs | No caching | Hash by and persist (Redis, disk) | | Dimension mismatch with index | Embedded with (3072) but index expects 1536 | Pin the ( , ) pair in your index metadata | | Cosine drift over time | Switched model without re-embedding the corpus | Embedding-model version is part of the index identity; rebuild on switch | | Slow throughput | Sequential single-input calls | Batch up to ; the API charges per token, not per call | | Non-deterministic results | Random seed in some open-source models | Pin model+version; cache by content hash | | Multilingual queries miss | Used a monolingual English model | Use a multilingual model ( is) or per-language indexes | Variants | Variant | When | |---|---| | Hosted text (above) | Default for production; pay-per-token, low ops | | Local sentence-transformers | Offline / sensitive data; CPU-OK for <100 dims | | Matryoshka truncation | Cut dimensions (e.g. 3072 → 512) for cheap storage at small quality cost | | Image embeddings (CLIP) | Cross-modal search (text ↔ image) | | Late-interaction (ColBERT) | Per-token vectors, much higher recall, much higher index cost | Frameworks & Models | Provider / Model | Dim | Notes | |---|---|---| | OpenAI | 1536 (truncatable) | Default; title: Feature Engineering
description: Design and derive model-ready features from raw tables and text, applying scaling, encoding, and windowed aggregation while preventing target leakage and train-serve skew.
body: Feature Engineering Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Feature engineering is where most modeling failures are manufactured. The skill covers profiling raw fields, fitting transforms such as scaling and encoding on the training scope only, deriving past-only windowed aggregates for time-ordered data, encoding categoricals with a fixed vocabulary and an explicit unknown bucket, and validating the resulting matrix for leakage markers and drift. The fitted transform is persisted so inference reproduces training features exactly. When to Use Use when raw data must be transformed into numeric features for statistical or machine-learned models, including encodings, interactions, and time-window aggregates. Do not compute features from information unavailable at prediction time. Target-derived aggregates and post-outcome fields leak, and they inflate evaluation scores that collapse in production. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Source records in their raw, typed form | | | | Yes | Feature definitions with transforms, encodings, and windows | | | | No | (default) or ; controls which statistics are learned | Procedure 1. Profile each raw field for type, missingness, cardinality, and range before transforming. 2. Fit transforms such as scaling and encoding on the training scope only, then apply elsewhere. 3. Derive windowed aggregates with strictly past-only windows for time-ordered data. 4. Encode categoricals with a fixed vocabulary; unseen levels map to an explicit unknown bucket. 5. Validate the output matrix for leakage markers, missing values, and feature drift. 6. Persist the fitted transform so inference reproduces the training features exactly. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Model-ready features with stable column order | | | | Fitted statistics needed to reproduce the features | | | | Leakage checks, missingness, and drift findings | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Target leakage | Feature derived from the label or post-outcome data | Audit every feature for prediction-time availability | | Train-serve skew | Statistics fit on the full data set | Fit on the training scope only and persist the transform | | Unknown category crash | New levels appear at inference | Map unseen levels to an explicit unknown bucket | | Window leakage | Aggregates include the current outcome | Enforce past-only windows with an explicit lag | | Missing value explosion | Naive handling of absent fields | Encode missingness as an explicit signal | Security and Authority Boundary Feature pipelines can encode protected attributes and leak them through proxies. When to Use Use when records carry locations that must be mapped, joined by proximity or containment, aggregated by region, or measured for distance and area. Do not compute distances in unprojected degrees. Reproject to a planar system first, or the numbers will be silently wrong. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Geometries or coordinates with their source coordinate reference system | | | | No | Projection for measurement; required for distance or area computation | | | | No | Boundary polygons for spatial joins and regional aggregation | Procedure 1. Parse geometries and record the coordinate reference system declared for each source. 2. Validate geometry topology; repair or drop self-intersecting and invalid shapes. 3. Reproject to the target CRS before any distance, area, or density computation. 4. Perform spatial joins by predicate, with within, intersects, or nearest stated explicitly. 5. Aggregate attributes by region and report unmatched features separately. 6. Write outputs with the CRS recorded so downstream consumers cannot misread them. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Geometries in the target CRS with validation status | | | | Match counts per region and unmatched features | | | | Per-region attribute summaries | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Degrees treated as distance | Planar math on unprojected coordinates | Reproject first, or use great-circle formulas | | CRS mismatch join | Layers in different projections overlaid silently | Reproject all layers to one CRS before joining | | Invalid geometries | Self-intersections break spatial predicates | Validate and repair topology before joining | | Point-in-polygon edge cases | Boundary points counted inconsistently | Define an explicit boundary policy and apply it | | Unmatched features hidden | Points outside all regions dropped | Report unmatched features separately from matches | Security and Authority Boundary Precise location data re-identifies individuals and reveals sensitive movement patterns. Aggregate or fuzz coordinates to the resolution the task needs, restrict access to raw tracks, and never publish joins that attach identities to sensitive locations. title: Incremental Processing
description: Process new data as it arrives instead of reprocessing the whole corpus — checkpoints, watermarks, and late-arrival handling — so cost stays flat as history grows.
body: Incremental Processing Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A pipeline that recomputes everything on every run is a pipeline with a half-life: the corpus grows, the run lengthens, and the day arrives where the run no longer fits between the arrivals. This skill switches the unit of work from the dataset to the delta: the process tracks what it has already consumed, takes only the new records past that mark, and handles the stragglers — late, out-of-order, or corrected records — by explicit rule rather than by accident. When to Use Use when data arrives continuously or the corpus is large enough that full recomputation no longer fits its window — event streams, append-only logs, growing tables. Do not add incremental machinery to small, fully recomputable datasets; a full pass over a small table is simpler, idempotent by construction, and easier to reason about. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The arriving data with an ordering or event time | | | | Yes | The consumed position the run resumes from | | | | Yes | Window wait, watermark, or drop for late arrivals | Procedure 1. Pick the position marker — an offset, a timestamp, or a sequence column — that strictly advances as new data arrives. 2. Persist a checkpoint after each processed unit, and make downstream updates idempotent so a replay from the checkpoint is safe. 3. Process only records past the checkpoint, committing the new checkpoint only after the unit is durably processed. 4. Handle late arrivals by rule: bounded wait behind a watermark, correction events, or explicit drop — never by silent overwrite. 5. Measure lag — arrival time to processed time — and alarm when the checkpoint stops advancing, because a stalled marker is the failure mode. 6. Periodically reconcile the incremental result against a full recomputation, so drift between the two is caught at a known cost. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Records consumed since the previous checkpoint | | | | The new resume position, durable after commit | | | | Arrival-to-processed delay and stall detection | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Checkpoint stalls | The marker stops advancing and data piles up | Alarm on lag and on checkpoint age | | Replay damage | Reprocessing a unit double-counts downstream | Make downstream updates idempotent per event | | Late-arrival chaos | Out-of-order records dropped or duplicated silently | Apply an explicit watermark and late policy | | Full-scan relapse | The incremental path quietly recomputing everything | Track processed volume per run | | Unverified drift | Incremental result slowly diverges from truth | Reconcile periodically against a full recomputation | Security and Authority Boundary Incremental state is attack surface: checkpoints record positions and the process holds partial aggregates, so both must inherit the access scope of the source data, and late-arrival or correction paths — which can rewrite aggregates — deserve the same authorization checks as the primary path. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Apache Kafka documentation (https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/). 2. Wikipedia's overview of stream processing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stream_processing). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Missing Data Imputation
description: Profile per-column missingness, choose an explicit imputation strategy per column, fit fill values on training rows only, and record an imputation mask so later analyses can audit the change.
body: Missing Data Imputation Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description How values are missing carries as much signal as the values themselves, and a single global fill rule such as zero-for-everything destroys that signal. This skill defines the disciplined loop: profile per-column missingness, pick a strategy per column, fit fill values on training rows only, and record an imputation mask so every filled cell stays identifiable for later audit. When to Use Use when training or reporting data has missing cells and the fill rule affects the result. Do not use for already-masked experimental data where missingness is part of the design; that case is analysis configuration, not imputation. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Records with absent cells represented as null | | | | Yes | Columns to profile and fill | | | | Yes | Per-column strategy such as median, mode, constant, or none | | | | No | Row subset used to fit fill values, defaulting to training rows | Procedure 1. Profile every column: missing count, missing rate, and the pattern of co-missingness across rows. 2. Classify each column’s missingness mechanism before choosing a strategy; uniform filling across mechanisms is a smell. 3. Choose a strategy per column and record why it was chosen. 4. Fit fill values on the declared fit scope only; never let test or future rows influence a fill value. 5. Apply fills to a copy; the original rows stay untouched for audit. 6. Record an imputation mask alongside the filled data so every filled cell is identifiable later. 7. Re-profile after filling and compare distributions; a fill that moves a distribution needs a second look. 8. Document the mask’s retention period; the mask is analytical metadata, not a permanent record. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Copies with missing cells filled per strategy | | | | Row-column positions that were filled | | | | Per-column missingness before and after filling | | | | Fitted fill values with their fit scope | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Global fill | One rule is applied to every column | Choose a strategy per column and record why | | Test leakage | Fill values are fitted on all rows | Fit on training rows only | | Mask loss | Filled data ships without its mask | Ship the mask beside the filled data | | Distribution shift | The fill moves the column’s shape | Re-profile after filling and compare | | In-place overwrite | Original rows are mutated | Fill copies and keep the originals untouched | Security and Authority Boundary Imputing values grants no authority to invent records. Filled cells are estimates and must remain identifiable as such through the mask. Data subject to privacy or retention limits keeps those limits through the whole loop: profiling, filling, and the mask inherit them. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The pandas user guide on missing data (https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/userguide/missingdata.html). 2. Wikipedia’s article on missing data (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missing_data). title: Stream Processing
description: Process unbounded event streams with windowed aggregation, watermarking, and exactly-once handling, keeping results correct under late arrival, replay, and backpressure.
body: Stream Processing Category: Data | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Stream processing computes over data that never stops arriving. The skill covers partitioning by key, defining windows with explicit late-arrival policy, advancing watermarks to bound results, emitting windowed aggregates, and handling replay and failure through idempotent sinks. Correctness comes from declared semantics: at-least-once delivery with idempotent writes, or exactly-once where the engine supports transactional state. When to Use Use when events must be aggregated, joined, or alerted on as they arrive rather than in batch: telemetry, click streams, sensor feeds, or transaction flows. Do not treat an unbounded stream as if it were a growing table. Without windows and watermarks, results never finalize and memory grows without bound. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Partitioned, append-only event source with per-key ordering | | | | Yes | Window type, size, allowed lateness, and watermark policy | | | | Yes | Idempotent or transactional output destination | Procedure 1. Declare delivery semantics first: at-least-once with idempotent sinks, or exactly-once with transactional state. 2. Partition by key so per-key ordering holds; record the partitioner choice. 3. Define windows with an explicit type, size, and allowed lateness; never use defaults silently. 4. Advance watermarks from event time and emit window results when the watermark closes the window. 5. Handle late events per policy: update the result if the sink allows, or route them to a side output. 6. On failure, restore state from the checkpoint and replay from the committed offset, proving no double emission. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Closed-window aggregates with event-time bounds | | | | Events that missed their window, routed to a side output | | | | Watermark progression used to close each window | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Window never closes | Watermark stalls on sparse partitions | Idle-source watermarks or wall-clock fallback | | Late events lost or double-counted | Replay without idempotent sink | Idempotent writes keyed by window and offset | | Unbounded state growth | Keys accumulate without retention | Set state TTL sized to the window policy | | Skew stalls the pipeline | One hot key dominates a partition | Key salting or pre-aggregation before partitioning | | Event-time vs processing-time confusion | Late data read as anomalies | Carry event time end to end and watermark on it | Security and Authority Boundary Streams often carry personal or operational data at high velocity. Scope access at the topic or partition level, avoid enriching events with unrelated lookups mid-stream, and make sinks tamper-evident because stream outputs frequently drive automated decisions. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Apache Kafka documentation covering consumer semantics and delivery guarantees (https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/). 2. The Apache Flink documentation on event time and watermarks (https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/). The skill covers choosing a generation strategy: fully synthetic from declared distributions, or fitted to a source with constraints that prevent memorization, then validating the output for statistical fidelity, referential integrity, and leakage of real records. The output is labeled synthetic, with its provenance recorded so it can never be mistaken for production data. When to Use Use when development, testing, or demonstrations need realistic data volumes and shapes without access to real personal or proprietary records. Do not present synthetic data as a privacy solution by default. Naive fitting can memorize rare records; privacy claims require measurement, not generation method labels. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Declared distributions and constraints, or a fitted model spec | | | | Yes | Number of records to generate | | | | No | Referential, range, and consistency rules the output must satisfy | Procedure 1. Declare the schema and per-field distributions, or fit distributions to a source sample. 2. State the fidelity target: which statistics and correlations the output must preserve. 3. Generate records with a fixed seed for reproducibility, applying constraints during generation. 4. Validate the output for schema conformance, statistical fidelity, and referential integrity. 5. Check for leakage: nearest-neighbor overlap with any real source records must be explained. 6. Label the data set synthetic with provenance, seed, and generator version. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Generated records satisfying the specification and constraints | | | | Distance between source and synthetic statistics | | | | Seed, generator version, and specification used | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Memorized rare records | Generator overfits outliers from a real source | Constrain fitting and run overlap checks | | Broken referential integrity | Child keys generated without parents | Generate hierarchies in dependency order | | Implausible combinations | Independent per-field fitting destroys correlations | Model joint structure or post-filter | | No reproducibility | Unseeded generation cannot regenerate a bug | Fix and record the seed | | Synthetic data in production | Generated records mixed into real tables | Label provenance and keep stores separate | Security and Authority Boundary Synthetic data lowers exposure but is not automatically safe: a poorly fitted generator can reproduce real individuals. Measure overlap against source data, never mix synthetic and production stores, and label outputs so downstream consumers cannot mistake them for real records. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Synthetic Data Vault project for fitted synthetic tabular data (https://github.com/sdv-dev/SDV). 2. The Faker library for specification-driven synthetic records (https://github.com/joke2k/faker). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Brand Voice Development
description: Define a reusable brand voice from values and audience, specifying tone dimensions, vocabulary rules, and example rewrites so all writers sound like one consistent speaker.
body: Brand Voice Development Category: Creative | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A brand voice is a small set of decisions applied consistently, not a mood board. The skill covers extracting voice traits from brand values, defining each trait as a position on a tone axis with do-and-never examples, writing vocabulary and punctuation rules, and validating drafts by rewriting the same sample in the defined voice. A voice is done when an unfamiliar writer can apply the spec and pass a blind consistency check. When to Use Use when an organization needs its writing to sound consistent across channels, writers, and formats, from support replies to marketing copy. Do not describe the voice only with adjectives such as friendly and bold. Without axis positions, vocabulary rules, and contrast examples, every writer interpolates differently. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Brand values, positioning, and audience definition | | | | No | Existing writing the voice should preserve or correct | | | | No | Channel-specific tone adjustments, keyed by channel | Procedure 1. Extract candidate voice traits from brand values and the audience relationship. 2. Reduce the traits to three to five axes and pick a position on each, with rationale. 3. Write do-and-never examples per trait so contrast is explicit, not implied. 4. Define vocabulary rules: preferred terms, banned terms, and grammar choices. 5. Rewrite one canonical sample passage in the new voice and annotate every change. 6. Run a blind consistency check with an unfamiliar writer before publishing the spec. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Trait axes, positions, and rules, machine-referenced per piece | | | | Before-and-after pairs demonstrating each trait | | | | Per-channel tone adjustments that preserve the traits | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Trait soup | Too many traits for writers to hold in mind | Cut to three to five axes | | Inconsistent across channels | One static tone applied everywhere | Define channel overrides that preserve traits | | Drift over time | No validation loop after the spec ships | Re-run consistency checks on live copy periodically | | Adjectives only | No axis positions or contrast examples | Require do-and-never pairs per trait | | Voice copies a competitor | Samples over-weighted toward external material | Anchor in the brand brief, not imitation | Security and Authority Boundary A voice spec encodes how an organization speaks and is a reputational asset. Keep positioning and unreleased campaign strategy confidential, and ensure the voice never overrides accuracy or legal disclosure requirements in regulated content. The Google developer documentation style guide (https://developers.google.com/style). title: Character Design
description: Build fictional characters as explicit profiles — voice, motivation, capability, limits — with mechanically checkable arc beats so characters stay consistent and their growth is deliberate.
body: Character Design Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A character is a contract with the reader: the way they speak, what they want, what they cannot do. Breaking that contract by convenience is how stories lose trust. This skill defines a character as a structured profile — identity, motivation, capabilities with explicit limits, and voice rules — plus a beat sheet for their arc, so consistency is checkable against a record instead of remembered vibes. When to Use Use when introducing a recurring character into any narrative work — prose, games, scripts — whose behavior must stay consistent across scenes and writers. Do not use for background figures who appear once; a full profile for a walk-on role is overhead. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Identity, motivation, capabilities, and limits | | | | Yes | Planned arc beats in story order | | | | No | Beat types the arc must contain | Procedure 1. Write the profile before the character acts: motivation, capability set with explicit limits, and voice rules with examples. 2. State what the character cannot do; limits are what make capability meaningful. 3. Plan the arc as an ordered beat list and check it contains the required beat types before writing. 4. Check every written scene against the profile; out-of-character action requires either a new beat that earns it or a profile revision. 5. Keep the profile versioned with the work so any scene can be traced to the character state it assumed. 6. Give each distinct character a distinguishable voice rule set; interchangeable voices are a design failure. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The recorded character profile | | | | Required arc beats not yet planned | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Out-of-character action | Scene convenience overrides the profile | Check scenes against the profile or revise it deliberately | | Missing arc stages | Key beats skipped in planning | Check required beats before writing the arc | | Interchangeable voices | All characters speak alike | Write and test a distinct voice rule per character | | Capability inflation | Limits quietly dropped under plot pressure | Restate limits in the profile and enforce them | | Stale profiles | Character grows but the record does not | Version the profile with each earned change | Security and Authority Boundary Characters borrowed from real people or cultures carry real obligations. Design with researched respect, avoid caricature, and keep provenance notes so borrowed elements are used with attribution and consent where applicable. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia’s overview of characterization (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characterization). 2. Wikipedia’s overview of the character arc (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_arc). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Color Palette Generation
description: Generate color palettes with grounded color theory, checking contrast ratios, accessibility thresholds, and perceptual harmony so palettes work for real interfaces, not just swatches.
body: Color Palette Generation Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A palette is a system of roles with constraints, not a set of attractive colors. The skill covers deriving palettes from a base hue using declared harmony strategies, assigning roles such as background, surface, text, accent, and state, then verifying the assignments against WCAG contrast thresholds and the expected display contexts. A palette ships only with its measured contrast table, because the ratios are the part that makes it usable. When to Use Use when an interface, brand, or document needs a coherent set of colors with known contrast behavior across text, states, and backgrounds. Do not judge a palette by its swatches alone. Colors that look harmonious side by side can fail legibility the moment one becomes text on another. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Anchor color as a hex value or named reference | | | | No | Harmony rule: (default), , , or | | | | No | Required palette roles; defaults to interface roles | Procedure 1. Convert the base color to a working space such as HSL or OKLCH and derive candidate steps. 2. Generate harmony candidates per the chosen strategy, keeping lightness and saturation controlled. 3. Assign roles: background, surface, text, accent, and state colors. 4. Compute contrast ratios for every text-on-background pairing the design needs. 5. Adjust lightness until all required pairings pass WCAG AA, or better where the brief demands. 6. Emit the palette with hex values, roles, and the measured contrast table. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Colors with hex values and assigned roles | | | | Measured ratio for each required pairing | | | | Pass or fail per pairing against the stated threshold | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Illegible text pairs | Palette judged visually without measurement | Compute and enforce WCAG ratios for all pairs | | Vibrancy-only harmony | All steps share similar lightness | Spread lightness across roles deliberately | | Context-blind colors | Palette tuned for one background only | Verify pairings on every expected background | | State colors ambiguous | Error, warning, and success hues too close | Separate state hues and test with color-vision simulation | | Swatch-to-system mismatch | Colors unassigned to roles | Always emit roles with values | Security and Authority Boundary Palettes carry accessibility obligations in many products. Do not soften measured thresholds to save an aesthetic, and test with color-vision deficiency simulation before shipping state colors that users must distinguish to operate safely. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Adobe Color harmony and accessibility tool (https://color.adobe.com/). 2. The Wikipedia article on color theory (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_theory). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it.
