title: Dialogue Writing
description: Write character dialogue with explicit speaker turns, subtext layers, and mechanical exchange checks so conversations stay consistent, purposeful, and attributable line by line.
body: Dialogue Writing Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Dialogue has mechanics and meaning: every line belongs to a speaker, turns should not blur into monologue by accident, and what a character says should rarely be exactly what they mean. This skill treats dialogue as structured data — (speaker, text) turns with optional subtext — plus checks for alternation, tagging, and emptiness, so the craft decisions sit on a verifiable exchange structure. When to Use Use when writing scenes of two or more voices where speaker attribution and turn structure must stay clean — prose, scripts, or interactive fiction. Do not use for interior monologue; unattributed thought is not dialogue and follows different rules. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Dialogue turns in order with explicit speakers | | | | No | Intended unstated meaning per line | | | | No | Per-speaker voice constraints | Procedure 1. Write every line as an explicit (speaker, text) turn; unattributed lines are a structural defect, not a style. 2. Run the exchange checks before polishing prose: same-speaker runs must be intentional, empty lines removed. 3. Give each line a purpose — information, pressure, or relationship change — and cut lines with none. 4. Set the subtext deliberately; when text equals meaning, that sameness should be the decision, not the default. 5. Read voices against their speaker rules; a line that fits no voice is a draft error. 6. Keep the exchange table with the draft so revisions do not silently drop speakers or turns. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The checked, ordered exchange | | | | Structural problems found by the checks | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Speaker blur | Turns run together without clear attribution | Tag every line and run the alternation check | | Talking heads | Exchange carries no scene purpose | Give each line information, pressure, or change | | Flat text | Characters say exactly what they mean | Set subtext deliberately per line | | Voice bleed | All characters speak with one voice | Write per-speaker voice rules and check against them | | Unversioned drafts | Revisions drop turns silently | Keep the exchange table with the draft | Security and Authority Boundary Dialogue written in real people’s voices — impressions of living individuals — carries defamation and dignity risks. Fictional voices should stay fictional, and borrowed real-world dialect deserves researched respect. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. title: Game Mechanic Design
description: Design and tune game mechanics as rule systems with resources, loops, and failure states, documenting economy balance and player choice structure before implementation.
body: Game Mechanic Design Category: Creative | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A mechanic is a rule system, not a feature name. The skill covers expressing mechanics as resources, actions, and loops; defining the core loop and its failure and mastery states; tuning numbers against an economy model so strategies stay diverse; and documenting the system precisely enough to prototype and critique before any art exists. Designs are tested on paper against degenerate strategies first. When to Use Use when a new game, mode, or system needs its rules designed and balanced before implementation, or when an existing mechanic needs retuning. Do not balance with intuition alone. Without an economy model, dominant strategies and dead mechanics ship and are expensive to fix after players learn them. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Intended player experience, session length, and challenge curve | | | | Yes | The rule idea: resources, actions, and win or loss conditions | | | | No | Numeric starting points for tuning | Procedure 1. Express the mechanic as resources, actions, and a loop that connects them. 2. Define the failure states and the mastery curve, including how each failure teaches. 3. Model the economy: sources, sinks, and exchange rates between resources. 4. Simulate representative strategies on paper and identify dominant or dead options. 5. Tune numbers until distinct strategies stay viable within the target session length. 6. Document the system with the loop diagram, the economy table, and open risks. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Rules, resources, actions, and loop definition | | | | Sources, sinks, rates, and tuned parameters | | | | Viable strategies found and degenerate cases fixed | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Dominant strategy | One option strictly beats the others | Simulate strategies before implementation and retune | | Dead resources | A resource has no sink or use | Add exchanges or remove the resource | | Runaway economy | Compound growth breaks the difficulty curve | Cap accumulation or add scaling sinks | | Failure that teaches nothing | Loss states give no signal about why | Attach feedback to every failure state | | Unreadable rules | Spec too vague to prototype | Formalize resources, actions, and loops first | Security and Authority Boundary Mechanic designs include monetization structures that can be manipulative. Model the economy honestly, disclose odds where randomized purchases exist, and avoid dark patterns that exploit loss aversion or sunk cost in players. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Wikipedia article on game mechanics (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_mechanics). 2. The Machinations tool for modeling and simulating game economies (https://machinations.io/). title: Name Generation
description: Generate candidate names systematically from declared inventories with pattern, collision, and exclusion checks so naming is explored deliberately and recorded reproducibly.
body: Name Generation Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Naming by staring at a blank page produces the first defensible option; naming by generation produces the space of options and then chooses. This skill defines name generation as a constrained search: a morpheme inventory, a construction pattern, a banned list, and collision checks against existing names — producing a reproducible candidate set instead of a lucky guess. When to Use Use when a product, character, place, or brand needs a name and the process should explore the option space deliberately rather than seize the first idea. Do not use where naming is externally fixed by standards, clients, or convention; constrained search cannot substitute for a mandated name. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Declared morpheme inventories for construction | | | | Yes | Shape rule a candidate must satisfy | | | | Yes | Substrings and collisions excluded from results | Procedure 1. Declare the inventories and construction rules before generating; free-form generation cannot be reproduced or audited. 2. Generate the full candidate set from the inventories under the construction rules. 3. Filter by the declared pattern so shape violations never reach review. 4. Apply the banned list and collision checks against existing names before presenting candidates. 5. Present candidates with their construction provenance — which morphemes and rules produced them. 6. Record the chosen name with the generator settings so the decision is reproducible later. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Filtered, ordered candidate names | | | | Candidates removed by pattern or exclusion rules | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | First-idea capture | The first plausible name ends the search | Generate the candidate space before choosing | | Unrecorded settings | The choice cannot be reproduced later | Keep inventories, patterns, and rules with the decision | | Silent collisions | Existing names never checked | Screen candidates against known names before review | | Unvetted meaning | Morphemes carry unintended readings | Check candidates for unfortunate meanings across audiences | | Pattern drift | Construction rules loosened to force a favorite | Keep the pattern fixed and let candidates compete | Security and Authority Boundary Generated names can collide with trademarks and communities. Generation produces candidates, not clearances; legal and cultural vetting remains a required step before any public use. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia’s overview of onomastics, the study of names (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onomastics). 2. Wikipedia’s overview of naming conventions (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_convention). title: Plot Structure
description: Organize a story into declared structural acts with positioned beats so pacing, reversals, and climaxes land where the chosen form requires and deviations are deliberate.
body: Plot Structure Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Structure is the load-bearing frame a story hangs from: acts, beats, and their positions. Without declared positions, a “slow second act” is a feeling; with them, it is a measurable gap between the inciting event and the midpoint. This skill defines plot structure as a table — beats named, positioned on a 0–100 scale, and assigned to declared acts — so the shape is visible and every deviation is a decision. When to Use Use when planning or diagnosing a story’s shape — novels, screenplays, episodes — before or during drafting, or when a draft feels structurally off. Do not use to impose structure on completed work by force; if a story resists the chosen form, change forms deliberately rather than mangle the story. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Story beats with positions on a 0–100 scale | | | | Yes | Declared act boundaries on the same scale | | | | No | Beats the chosen form mandates | Procedure 1. Choose the structural form first and declare its act boundaries on a normalized 0–100 scale. 2. Position each beat on the same scale; relative position is the contract, not chapter count. 3. Check that every beat falls inside exactly one act; boundary orphans indicate scale drift. 4. Check the form’s required beats are present and positioned within their expected ranges. 5. Report structural gaps — long stretches with no beat — as measurable intervals, not impressions. 6. Revise positions on evidence when pacing is off; the table is the plan of record. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Beats mapped to their acts | | | | Beats outside every declared act | | | | Unusually long beat-free intervals | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Act drift | Beats straddle declared boundaries | Normalize positions to one scale and reassign | | Missing mandatory beats | The chosen form’s obligations unmet | Check required beats against the declared form | | Unmeasured pacing | “Slow” sections felt but not located | Report beat-free intervals as numbers | | Form mismatch | Story forced into an unsuitable structure | Choose the form from the story, not habit | | Stale plan | Draft diverges from the structural table | Keep the table current or admit it is abandoned | Security and Authority Boundary Structure tools shape creative output but claim no ownership; a structural template is scaffolding, and the finished work inherits only the licenses of its actual sources. Wikipedia’s overview of dramatic structure (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dramaticstructure). title: Podcast Script Writing
description: Write podcast scripts and episode outlines with cold opens, segments, host cues, and ad placements, tuned to time targets and speaker-friendly rhythm.
body: Podcast Script Writing Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A podcast script must sound spoken, not read. The skill covers structuring an episode as a cold open, segments with time boxes, and an outro; writing for the ear with short sentences and explicit host cues; placing transitions and ad reads at natural seams; and marking every line with a time estimate so the episode hits its target duration. Speaker difficulty is checked by reading cadence, not word count alone. When to Use Use when an audio episode needs a script or a tight outline: narrative shows, interview prep, news digests, or branded series with required segments. Do not deliver a text meant for silent reading. If a sentence cannot be spoken in one breath or loses meaning when heard once, rewrite it. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Topic, audience, target duration, and required segments | | | | Yes | Source material and facts the episode must present | | | | No | Target length in minutes; drives the time budget per segment | Procedure 1. Break the brief into a cold open, ordered segments, and an outro with a time budget each. 2. Verify every factual claim in the research material and mark attributed claims. 3. Write spoken-style lines: short sentences, contractions, and explicit host cues. 4. Insert transitions and ad placements at segment seams only, never mid-argument. 5. Estimate speaking time per block at a fixed words-per-minute rate and rebalance the budget. 6. Read-check the script for breath length, tongue twisters, and lines that only work on paper. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Full spoken script with host cues and timing marks | | | | Segments with time budgets and transition types | | | | Claims with their source status for verification | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Reads as written prose | Long sentences and subordination built for the eye | Apply breath-length checks and rewrite | | Overtime or underfilled | No time budget per segment | Budget words per segment at a fixed rate | | Ad breaks mid-argument | Placement not at a seam | Allow transitions only at segment boundaries | | Unsupported claims aired | Research not verified before scripting | Fact-log every claim with source status | | Flat segment pacing | Uniform rhythm across the whole episode | Vary energy: open high, breathe mid, land the outro | Security and Authority Boundary Podcast scripts carry legal exposure: defamation risk from unverified claims, and licensing risk from quoted material. Attribute contested claims, keep the fact log with the script, and do not read sponsor copy beyond the approved disclosure. title: Poetry Forms
description: Write within fixed poetic forms by checking their mechanical constraints — syllable counts, line counts, rhyme schemes — so form compliance is verified rather than asserted.
body: Poetry Forms Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A fixed form is a contract in counts: five and seven for the haiku, fourteen lines with a rhyme scheme for the sonnet. Meeting the contract by assertion is how “approximate haiku” happens. This skill treats form compliance as checkable arithmetic — per-line syllable counts against declared targets, line count against the form, rhyme pattern against the scheme — with the checks running before the poem is presented as done. When to Use Use when writing in a fixed form, when an exercise or publication requires exact form compliance, or when teaching forms where the mechanics matter. Do not use for free verse; imposing fixed-form checks on open forms misreads the contract. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The poem’s lines in order | | | | Yes | Declared constraints: syllables, line count, rhyme scheme | Procedure 1. Declare the form’s numeric contract up front — syllable targets per line, line count, rhyme scheme. 2. Count syllables per line with a stated counting convention, and record the count next to each line. 3. Check line count against the form before deeper checks; wrong length is the first failure. 4. Map rhyme classes per line and compare the resulting pattern against the declared scheme. 5. Report every deviation with the offending line rather than a bare failure flag. 6. Revise the line, not the check; weakening the contract to pass is self-deception. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Syllable count per line, in order | | | | Lines violating the declared form | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Approximate form | Counts asserted without checking | Run the arithmetic and record per-line counts | | Heuristic overtrust | Vowel-run counter treated as ground truth | Flag heuristic counts for human review on hard cases | | Contract weakening | Targets edited to fit the draft | Revise the line, not the declared form | | Scheme drift | Rhyme pattern left unchecked | Map the realized scheme against the declared one | | Form confusion | Free verse judged by fixed-form rules | Match the checks to the declared form | Security and Authority Boundary Form constraints govern counts and sound, not appropriation. Diction borrowed from living traditions carries the same research and respect obligations as any cultural material, regardless of syllable totals. title: Slogan and Tagline Creation
description: Create and evaluate slogans and taglines against brand positioning, memorability, and trademark and clarity constraints, presenting candidates with the reasoning that produced them.
body: Slogan and Tagline Creation Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A tagline compresses positioning into a line people can repeat. The skill covers extracting the single claim a tagline must carry from the brand brief, generating candidates through distinct compression strategies, then filtering them: against the positioning, against clarity when read once, against cultural and legal risk, and against distinctiveness from competitors. Output is a shortlist with rationale, not a popularity list. When to Use Use when a product, campaign, or organization needs a short verbal identity line, or an existing one must be refreshed. Do not pick a winner by taste alone. Without written criteria, the selection measures the room, not the brand. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Positioning, audience, and the single claim to compress | | | | No | Length, language, tone, and legal screening limits | | | | No | Number of candidates to shortlist; defaults to a small set | Procedure 1. Extract the one claim the tagline must carry and the audience language for it. 2. Generate candidates through distinct strategies: compression, contrast, and rhythm variants. 3. Filter for clarity: each candidate must be understood correctly on a single hearing. 4. Screen for risk: unintended meanings in other languages and marketplace confusion. 5. Score the survivors against memorability heuristics: brevity, rhythm, and claim fit. 6. Shortlist with rationale attached per candidate and record why the others were cut. body: Storyboard Generation Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A storyboard is the contract between a script and a shoot. Break the script into shots; each shot gets one panel with a unique number. 2. For each panel, specify framing, camera movement, subject blocking, and screen direction. 3. Write a one-to-two sentence panel description that a reviewer can verify against the script. 4. Check continuity across panels: position, time of day, costume, and screen direction. 5. title: Worldbuilding
description: Construct fictional settings as an explicit fact ledger with category constraints and mechanical consistency checks so a story world stays coherent as it grows.
body: Worldbuilding Category: Creative | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A fictional world breaks the moment its facts disagree: the bridge was built two centuries after the plague it preceded. This skill treats worldbuilding as a ledger — every established fact recorded once, with dates, places, and in-world sources — plus mechanical checks that new material does not contradict the record. The ledger is the artifact; prose merely cites it. When to Use Use when creating or extending a fictional setting — for novels, games, or campaigns — that will outlive a single writing session and must remain internally consistent. Do not use for improvisational settings that exist for one scene; a ledger for throwaway fiction is overhead, not value. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The established fact ledger with dates and sources | | | | Yes | New material proposed for the ledger | | | | No | Category rules, e.g. event ordering or population bounds | Procedure 1. Record every accepted fact exactly once with its in-world date, location, and the source that established it. 2. Check every draft fact against the ledger before it is accepted; contradictions are reported with both records. 3. Encode ordering constraints between dated events so chronology is checked mechanically, not by memory. 4. Prefer reconciling a contradiction over retconning silently; when a retcon is chosen, record it as a new ledger entry. 5. Keep the ledger versioned with the work so any chapter can be traced to the world state it was written against. 6. Leave gaps explicitly marked as unknown; unrecorded is not the same as unrestricted. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The updated fact ledger | | | | Draft facts that conflict with the ledger | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Chronology drift | Dates held in memory across chapters | Record every dated fact in the ledger and check drafts | | Silent retcons | Old facts rewritten without a record | Log every retcon as its own ledger entry | | Fact duplication | One event recorded with two dates | Key facts by a single canonical name | | Unbounded invention | New material contradicts category rules | Check drafts against recorded constraints | | False gaps | Unknown mistaken for unrecorded | Mark unknowns explicitly in the ledger | Security and Authority Boundary Fictional worlds can contain real patterns worth protecting: place names, cultures, and communities borrowed from reality deserve respectful, researched use, and the ledger documents provenance so inherited material is cited, not erased. title: Agent Skill Security Audit
description: Audit an agent skill and its bundled resources before installation or execution, checking declared behavior, permissions, credential access, network egress, obfuscation, and sandbox requirements.
body: Agent Skill Security Audit Description An agent skill is executable trust-boundary content when it contains instructions, scripts, hooks, references, or tool permissions. Audit the complete skill package before installation or execution rather than trusting its description or publisher metadata. The audit is primarily static and compares declared behavior with the actual SKILL.md instructions and every bundled executable/resource file. Check for unexpected permission grants, credential reads, network egress, obfuscated content, hidden behavior, unsafe hooks, and mismatch between advertised and observable behavior. Dynamic analysis is optional and must run only in an isolated sandbox with synthetic or no credentials, bounded resources, controlled network access, and explicit teardown. An audit result is evidence for a trust decision; it is not a guarantee that a skill is benign. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | skillroot | path | yes | Root directory containing the skill manifest and bundled resources | | declaredpermissions | list | no | Permissions/tools explicitly declared by the skill or host metadata | | runtimepolicy | object | no | Sandbox, filesystem, network, credential, and execution constraints | | auditmode | enum | yes | static or sandboxed | Output is a structured audit record containing findings, evidence locations, severity, confidence, declared-vs-observed deltas, sandbox requirements, and a disposition such as allow, review, or deny. Audit Procedure 1. Parse frontmatter and record declared name, purpose, permissions, compatibility, and provenance. 2. Inventory SKILL.md, scripts, hooks, binaries, configuration, references, and generated files under the skill root. 3. Compare advertised behavior with actual instructions and executable content. 4. Identify credential and sensitive-file access, including environment variables, SSH material, cloud credentials, token stores, and unrelated user data. 5. Identify network destinations and egress mechanisms. Treat undeclared network access as a finding requiring review. 6. Inspect for shell/process execution, package installation, dynamic code loading, obfuscation, encoded payloads, persistence, or attempts to hide behavior from the user. 7. Compare declared tool permissions with the minimum permissions required by observed behavior. 8. Record exact evidence locations and never treat absence of a detected pattern as proof of safety. 9. If dynamic analysis is required, run only in an isolated sandbox with synthetic credentials, bounded resources, controlled egress, and no access to the auditor real environment. 10. Produce a fail-closed disposition when high-confidence critical behavior is incompatible with the declared purpose or execution policy. Runnable Example This example is a bounded static signal detector, not a malware detector. Production audits need language-aware analysis, archive/binary handling, symlink controls, policy evaluation, and reproducible evidence capture. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Trusting metadata | Description differs from bundled behavior | Audit executable/resource contents and record declared-vs-observed deltas | | Credential exposure | Skill reads real secrets or credential stores | Deny or isolate access; use synthetic credentials for dynamic testing | | Hidden egress | Network access is not declared or constrained | Default to no network and allow only policy-approved destinations | | Permission overreach | Skill requests tools broader than its purpose | Apply least privilege and require explicit review for elevated permissions | | Obfuscation | Encoded/dynamic content hides behavior | Flag for manual/static analysis and preserve exact evidence location | | Sandbox escape | Dynamic test reaches the host | Use a maintained isolated runtime with resource, filesystem, and network controls | | False negative | Static checks miss behavior | Treat audit output as evidence, not a safety guarantee; use layered controls | | False positive | Benign implementation matches a heuristic | Record confidence and require contextual review rather than automatic condemnation | Design Rules 1. Treat every third-party skill package as untrusted input until its behavior is reviewed. 2. Audit the complete package, not only SKILL.md frontmatter. 3. Preserve provenance and exact evidence locations for every finding. 4. Compare declared permissions and behavior against the least-privilege execution policy. 5. Default dynamic analysis to synthetic/no credentials, bounded resources, and restricted network access. 6. Never claim that a static scan proves a skill is safe. 7. Keep audit evidence separate from authorization; a passing audit does not itself grant permission to execute a skill. 8. Prefer deterministic checks for path, permission, secret, network, and package-integrity findings where practical. References - OWASP Secure Agent Playbook issue #21: https://github.com/OWASP/secure-agent-playbook/issues/21 - 2026 research on detecting malicious agent skills: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06547 - Skills Tree Sandboxed Execution: sandboxed-execution.md - Skills Tree Secret Scanning: secret-scanning.md Evidence Evidence status: the cited sources support the audit problem and defensive methodology. This skill does not claim complete malware detection, compliance certification, or universal safety. Related Skills - Sandboxed Execution - Secret Scanning - Permission Checking - Input Sanitization - Audit Logging Changelog | Date | Version | Change | |---|---|---| | 2026-10 | v1 | Added demand-driven contract for pre-installation and pre-execution agent-skill security auditing |

title: Approval Before Destructive Tools
description: Require explicit human or automated approval before any agent executes an irreversible tool action.
body: Approval Before Destructive Tools Category: security | Level: intermediate | Stability: stable | Version: v2 Description Destructive tools — database deletes, file overwrites, API calls that send emails or charge customers, infrastructure changes — must never execute based solely on LLM intent. An approval gate enforces a mandatory review step: the agent proposes the action, execution is interrupted, a human or automated policy approves or rejects, and only then does the tool run. This prevents hallucination-driven data loss. title: Audit Logging
description: Record security-relevant agent actions in a structured, tamper-evident audit trail without logging secrets or unnecessary personal data.
body: Audit Logging Description Audit logging gives an agent system an attributable record of security-relevant actions: tool calls, resource access, authorization decisions, approvals, failures, and externally visible side effects. The log should support investigation and accountability without becoming a second data-leak channel. Use structured events with stable event types, actor identity, correlation IDs, timestamps, outcome, and a minimal resource reference. Do not record API keys, passwords, session cookies, full prompts containing sensitive data, or raw tool responses by default. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | yes | Agent, service, or human identity responsible for the event | | | string | yes | Stable action name such as or | | | string | yes | Minimal resource identifier; avoid embedding sensitive payloads | | | string | yes | , , , or | | | string | no | Identifier linking related events across a workflow | | | dict | no | Non-sensitive structured context | Output is a structured audit event containing timestamp, identity, action, resource reference, outcome, and an integrity field. Runnable Example The example demonstrates an append-only hash chain primitive. A production implementation also needs protected storage, clock handling, access controls, retention policy, and key management where stronger authenticity guarantees are required. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Secret leakage | Raw tool input/output is logged | Allowlist fields and redact secrets before serialization | | Unattributed action | Shared or missing actor identity | Require authenticated actor/service identity | | Broken correlation | Each component invents unrelated IDs | Propagate a workflow correlation ID | | Log tampering | Logs are writable by the workload being audited | Separate writer and reader permissions and use append-only storage | | Excessive retention | Logs become a privacy/security liability | Define retention by purpose and data class | | Clock ambiguity | Host clocks differ | Store UTC timestamps and use a trusted event ordering strategy | | High-cardinality noise | Every internal operation becomes an event | Log security-relevant state transitions, not arbitrary debug output | Design Rules 1. Treat logs as sensitive data. 2. Log decisions and outcomes rather than secrets or complete payloads. 3. Make actor and correlation identity explicit. 4. Separate operational debugging from compliance/security audit records. 5. Define retention and deletion rules before deployment. 6. Test that denied actions generate auditable events. 7. Never treat a hash chain alone as proof of external authenticity. title: Container Escape Detection
description: Detect container breakout attempts by monitoring privileged operations, namespace and capability anomalies, and kernel interface abuse from inside and around the container runtime.
body: Container Escape Detection Category: Security | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Container isolation is a soft boundary that attackers probe before they break it. The skill covers baseline of legitimate container behavior, then watching for the escape signatures: unexpected capability use, namespace and cgroup tampering, host filesystem mounts, kernel module loading, and device node access. Detections carry the workload identity so an event can be tied to a specific deployment, not just a host. When to Use Use when containerized workloads, especially those running untrusted or third-party code, must be monitored for breakout attempts toward the host. Do not assume the container image is trusted because it passed admission control. Escapes frequently come from exploited application code inside an approved image. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Syscall, capability, and namespace events from the container runtime | | | | Yes | Normal behavior profile per workload: allowed syscalls and mounts | | | | No | (default) or for cross-node correlation | Procedure 1. Establish the per-workload baseline: syscalls, capabilities, mounts, and device access in normal operation. 2. Stream runtime events and attribute each to a workload identity and node. 3. Flag privileged deviations: capability escalation, namespace switching, and host path mounts. 4. Correlate across nodes for lateral signatures when fleet scope is enabled. 5. Score detections by proximity to the host boundary: what a successful escape would reach. 6. Emit detections with the event chain, workload identity, and containment recommendation. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Escape attempts with event chains and proximity scoring | | | | Per-workload deviations from normal behavior | | | | Suggested node and workload isolation steps | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Privileged-legitimate confusion | Sidecar containers legally use high capabilities | Baseline per workload, not per node | | Kernel-level events missed | Runtime instrumentation too shallow | Instrument at the syscall or eBPF layer | | Escape already complete | Detection tuned only for attempts | Watch for post-escape signatures such as host process spawning | | Fleet-wide blind spot | Per-node alerts miss lateral movement | Correlate at fleet scope for shared tactics | | Alert fatigue | No scoring, every anomaly equal | Score by proximity to the host boundary | Security and Authority Boundary Escape detections imply compromised workloads. Treat them as live incidents: preserve forensic evidence, isolate nodes before investigation, and do not trust container-local logs after an escape is confirmed, because the attacker controls that plane. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Falco runtime security project for container and syscall monitoring (https://github.com/falcosecurity/falco). 2. The Trivy vulnerability and misconfiguration scanner for containers (https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy). title: Dependency Integrity Verification
description: Verify third-party package artifacts against pinned digests, signatures, and provenance attestations before installation so the build consumes exactly the artifacts that were reviewed.
body: Dependency Integrity Verification Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A dependency declaration names what you want; the artifact that arrives is what you run. Integrity verification closes that gap: versions pinned to exact hashes, digests recomputed at install time, signatures checked against a known identity, and provenance attestations matched to the build that produced the artifact. Anything that cannot be verified is rejected rather than installed and inspected later. When to Use Use before installing any third-party package in build, CI, or runtime environments — especially in automated pipelines that install without a human reading the output. Do not treat integrity verification as vulnerability scanning: a verified artifact is exactly the reviewed bytes, which can still contain a reviewed vulnerability. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The dependency to install | | | | Yes | The pinned hash from the reviewed lockfile | | | | No | Detached signature over the artifact | | | | No | Build provenance statement for the artifact | Procedure 1. Pin exact versions with hashes in the lockfile; floating ranges bypass review by construction. 2. Fetch the artifact and recompute its digest locally; never trust the registry's advertised hash alone. 3. When a signature is available, verify it against a pinned signing identity, not a key fetched at verify time. 4. When provenance is available, check that the attestation's build matches the expected source and workflow. 5. Reject on any mismatch — digest, signature, or provenance — and fail the install. 6. Record the verification result (package, digest, verdict) so the decision is auditable later. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Whether the artifact matched its pinned integrity data | | | | First failed check when rejected | | | | Package, version, digest, and verdict for the audit trail | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Floating versions | ranges install whatever resolves today | Pin exact versions with hashes in the lockfile | | Registry substitution | Artifact swapped between resolve and install | Recompute the digest at install time | | Keys fetched at verify time | Signing key taken from the channel it vouches for | Pin the signing identity independently | | CI cache poisoning | Cached artifacts skip verification | Verify after cache restore, not only on download | | Mirror drift | Internal mirror serving different bytes | Verify digests from mirrors exactly like upstream | Security and Authority Boundary Integrity verification proves the artifact is the one that was attested; it says nothing about the safety or quality of the code inside. Vulnerability scanning, license review, and human review remain separate, mandatory steps. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of supply chain attacks on software distribution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supplychainattack). 2. The Sigstore documentation on artifact signing and verification (https://docs.sigstore.dev/). title: Forensic Log Reconstruction
description: Rebuild a coherent incident timeline from partial, overlapping, and clock-skewed logs, producing an evidence-backed sequence with provenance and stated confidence per event.
body: Forensic Log Reconstruction Category: Security | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Incident logs never line up: clocks drift, sources overlap or gap, and formats disagree. The skill covers collecting logs from all relevant sources into an immutable evidence store, normalizing timestamps against a common clock with skew estimates, ordering events with uncertainty bounds rather than false precision, and attributing each reconstructed event to its source lines. The timeline is the deliverable, and every entry carries its evidence. When to Use Use when an incident must be understood from heterogeneous logs: what happened, in what order, and with what evidence supporting each claim. Do not merge logs by raw timestamp. Clock skew between sources routinely reorders cause and effect, and a wrong order is worse than an honest uncertainty range. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Logs with source, format, and observed or assumed clock offset | | | | Yes | Time range and assets in scope | | | | No | The reference clock events are normalized against | Procedure 1. Collect all in-scope logs into an append-only evidence store with source provenance. 2. Parse each source into a common event record: time, actor, action, and target. 3. Estimate per-source clock skew using handshake artifacts or known anchor events. 4. Normalize timestamps against the clock authority, carrying skew bounds as uncertainty. 5. Order events into a timeline, marking where uncertainty leaves the order ambiguous. 6. Attribute every timeline entry to its source lines so any claim can be re-verified. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Ordered incident events with uncertainty bounds and provenance | | | | Orderings that cannot be resolved within skew bounds | | | | Map from timeline entries to source log lines | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | False chronological precision | Skewed clocks treated as truth | Carry skew bounds and mark ambiguous order | | Missing middle | A source gap read as attacker dwell time | Mark gaps explicitly with their cause | | Log tampering undetected | No integrity check before analysis | Hash sources on collection and verify before use | | Timezone chaos | Sources mix local and UTC stamps | Normalize to a single clock authority first | | Unattributed conclusions | Timeline claims with no source lines | Require provenance per entry before publishing | Security and Authority Boundary Forensic timelines are legal-grade evidence in many incidents. Preserve originals immutably, document the chain of custody for every source, and never publish an incident timeline that attributes actions to individuals without direct evidence. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The NIST guide to integrating forensic techniques into incident response (https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/86/final). 2. The Wikipedia article on computer forensics (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_forensics). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Harm Detection
description: Triage potentially harmful agent inputs and outputs with explicit categories, thresholds, and escalation paths before high-impact actions.
body: Harm Detection Description Harm detection is a safety gate that classifies content or planned actions against an explicitly defined risk policy before an agent acts or responds. It should identify relevant categories, preserve uncertainty, and escalate ambiguous or high-impact cases instead of silently converting a classifier result into authorization. The detector can combine deterministic rules, specialist classifiers, and human review. It is a risk-control layer, not a universal guarantee that content is safe. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | yes | Content to classify | | | string | no | Intended agent action if action-aware screening is used | | | dict | yes | Categories, thresholds, and escalation behavior | | | dict | no | Minimal context required for classification | | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | string | , , or | | | list[str] | Policy categories triggered | | | float | Classifier confidence when available | | | string | Safe explanation of the decision | Runnable Example This deterministic example is intentionally conservative and incomplete. Production classifiers require a documented taxonomy, evaluation set, threshold policy, false-positive/false-negative analysis, and an escalation path. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | False negative | Classifier misses harmful content | Use layered controls and action-specific authorization | | False positive | Benign content matches a category | Provide review/escalation rather than silent rejection when appropriate | | Context loss | Classification sees too little context | Pass only the minimum context required for the policy decision | | Classifier prompt injection | User content manipulates a classifier | Treat classifier input as untrusted and constrain its output schema | | Policy drift | Categories or thresholds become outdated | Version the policy and evaluate changes before rollout | | Over-trust | A classifier result is treated as authorization | Keep safety screening separate from identity/permission checks | Design Rules - Define categories and actions before implementing the classifier. - Keep and semantics explicit. - Do not expose hidden classifier prompts or sensitive evidence in user-facing messages. - Log policy decisions without storing unnecessary harmful content. - Re-test thresholds when models or policies change. - Use human review for ambiguous high-impact cases. title: Human In Loop
description: Pause high-risk agent actions for explicit human approval with deny-by-default timeouts, auditable decisions, and safe resume or abort behavior.
body: Human In Loop Description Human-in-the-loop control inserts an explicit approval boundary before actions whose risk, authority, cost, or irreversibility exceeds an established threshold. The agent should prepare the proposed action and evidence, then wait for a decision from an authorized reviewer. Approval must be bound to the exact action being approved. A generic approval such as "yes, continue" should not authorize a different action later in the workflow. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | yes | Canonical action identifier | | | string | yes | Resource or target affected | | | string | yes | Policy risk classification | | | dict | no | Facts needed by the reviewer | | | int | no | Maximum approval wait | | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | bool | Explicit approval result | | | string | Audit correlation identifier | | | string | Reviewer decision reason when supplied | Runnable Example The demo deliberately denies by default. A production implementation should use an authenticated, durable approval channel and bind the reviewer decision to an immutable action summary. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Approval replay | Old approval reused for a new action | Bind approval to action, target, parameters, and expiry | | Wrong reviewer | Reviewer lacks authority | Check reviewer identity and required scope | | Timeout bypass | Agent continues after timeout | Timeout must produce a deny/escalate state | | Approval fatigue | Too many low-risk approvals | Use explicit risk thresholds and batch only equivalent safe actions | | Missing evidence | Reviewer cannot understand the action | Present concise, relevant evidence and expected effects | | Race condition | Target changes after approval | Revalidate target state immediately before execution | Design Rules - Deny by default on timeout or unavailable approval service. - Never interpret silence as approval. - Make approvals single-purpose and time-bounded. - Re-check permissions and target state after approval. - Record who approved what, when, and under which policy version. - Provide an explicit abort path. title: Input Sanitization
description: Validate and clean every untrusted string before it reaches an LLM, a tool call, or a filesystem/SQL/HTTP boundary. Layered defense against prompt injection, SQL injection, path traversal, command injection, and PII leakage.
body: Input Sanitization Description Every string that enters your agent is untrusted: user messages, tool outputs, retrieved documents, file contents, web fetches. Each one is a candidate vector for prompt injection ("ignore previous instructions"), SQL injection ( ), path traversal ( ), command injection, and data exfiltration. This skill is the layered defense: (1) structural validation (Pydantic / JSON schema) for shape, (2) boundary-specific escaping (parameterised SQL, , ), (3) content-level analysis (PII detection, classifier, allowlist), and (4) isolation (separate LLM call to triage suspicious input). Defense is layered because any single check is bypassable. When to Use - Any time untrusted text is going to be: (a) concatenated into a prompt, (b) passed to a tool, (c) used as a path/filename, (d) interpolated into SQL/shell. - Even when the input "comes from your database" — if it was originally typed by a user, it's untrusted. - Don't skip for "internal" tools — most prompt-injection attacks today come via retrieved documents, not the user message. Inputs / Outputs | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The untrusted input (str, dict, list, …) | | | | What's allowed (max length, charset, allowed paths, …) | | → | | Passed every layer | | → | | Cleaned version safe to forward | | → | | Specific rules tripped (for audit logs) | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Layer 1 passes; layer 2 still vulnerable | Defence-in-depth bypass at the SQL/path/shell boundary | All four layers must run; never skip the boundary-specific layer | | Allowlist too loose | Charset allows control chars, RTL overrides ( ) | Pin to printable ASCII + curated Unicode ranges | | Allowlist too strict | Drops legitimate non-English | Test on real i18n samples; whitelist ranges | | PII regex misses unusual formats | International phones, IBAN | Add a classifier (e.g. Microsoft Presidio) for tail PII | | Unicode normalisation differs | vs (combining) bypasses match | NFC-normalise before any regex check | | Indirect prompt injection via tool output | Trusted tool returned attacker-controlled text | Re-run sanitization on EVERY message into the LLM, not just the user's | | Sanitization log itself leaks PII | includes the matched span | Keep counts, not values | Variants | Variant | When | |---|---| | Allow-list (above) | Default for structured inputs; title: JWT Validation
description: Validate JSON Web Tokens by verifying the declared algorithm, signature, and claims in a fixed order so access decisions rest on cryptographic evidence instead of unverified payload strings.
body: JWT Validation Category: Security | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A JWT is three base64url parts and a lot of trust. Skipping the verification order — algorithm, signature, then claims — is how alg=none and algorithm-confusion attacks happen. This skill defines validation as a fail-closed sequence: pin the expected algorithm, verify the signature with a constant-time comparison, then evaluate claims (expiry, audience, issuer) with an injectable clock. When to Use Use whenever an agent or service accepts a JWT as evidence of identity or authorization, before any decision is made on its contents. Do not use JWTs as long-term session storage; validation is per-request evidence, and revocation needs server-side state. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The compact serialized JWT | | | | Yes | The verification key for the pinned algorithm | | | | Yes | The single algorithm accepted; anything else is rejected | | | | No | Injectable clock for expiry claim evaluation | Procedure 1. Pin the expected algorithm in configuration; accept only that value from the token header. 2. Reject tokens whose header declares a different algorithm, a missing algorithm, or none — before any signature math runs. 3. Verify the signature over the exact signing input (header.payload) with a constant-time comparison. 4. Only after the signature holds, parse the payload and evaluate claims: expiry against the injected clock, audience, issuer. 5. Fail closed on every check; a token that fails any step is rejected without partial trust. 6. Log the validation outcome — verified or rejected with reason — without logging the token itself. 7. Never decode the payload for authorization before the signature check passes; unsigned payload is attacker input. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The verified payload claims | | | | Whether the token passed the full sequence | | | | First failed check when rejected | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Algorithm confusion | Attacker-chosen alg trusted from the header | Pin one expected algorithm in configuration | | alg=none acceptance | Unsigned tokens treated as valid | Reject missing or none algorithms before signature math | | Claim skipping | Payload trusted without signature verification | Verify the signature before parsing any claims | | Expiry clock skew | Wall clock read during validation | Inject the clock and evaluate exp deterministically | | Token leakage in logs | Rejected tokens logged verbatim | Log outcomes and reasons, never the token string | Security and Authority Boundary Token validation is the enforcement point, not the policy. A cryptographically valid token still bounds only what its claims assert: authority comes from the issuer’s policy, and every downstream action must pass its own permission checks. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. RFC 7519 defining JSON Web Tokens (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519). 2. The jwt.io introduction to JWT structure and signature verification (https://jwt.io/introduction). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Key Rotation Automation
description: Automate cryptographic key and credential rotation across services with dual-key overlap, staged rollout, and telemetry-verified revocation, eliminating long-lived shared secrets.
body: Key Rotation Automation Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Rotation fails when it breaks production or when the old key survives. The skill covers inventorying keys and their dependents, rotating with dual-key overlap so consumers migrate without downtime, staging rollout by dependency order, then revoking the old key only after verifying zero usage. Every step is driven by measured telemetry, not calendar optimism. When to Use Use when long-lived keys and credentials must be replaced on a schedule or after exposure, across services that cannot all be updated atomically. Do not rotate by deleting the old key and hoping. Without usage telemetry and overlap, rotation becomes an outage with a security rationale. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Keys with type, scope, age, and dependent services | | | | Yes | Per-key usage counts over a recent window | | | | No | Rotation interval, overlap period, and staging order | Procedure 1. Inventory every key with its scope, dependents, and last-rotation date. 2. Generate the replacement and publish it alongside the old key as dual-active. 3. Migrate dependents in dependency order, verifying each accepts the new key. 4. Watch usage telemetry until the old key shows zero uses over the overlap window. 5. Revoke the old key and record the revocation evidence. 6. Alert on any key that exceeds its rotation interval or shows anomalous usage. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Per-key rotation history with overlap and revocation evidence | | | | Keys past their rotation interval or unused and revocable | | | | How to restore the previous key if a consumer breaks | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Rotation outage | Old key revoked before consumers migrated | Dual-active overlap gated by usage telemetry | | Zombie keys | Revoked key still cached by a service | Verify zero usage over the window before revoking | | Inventory gaps | Key unknown to the inventory never rotates | Discover keys by scanning config and secrets stores | | New key weaker | Generated with deprecated parameters | Generate to current policy and verify before publishing | | Emergency break-glass confusion | Rotation lands during an incident | Freeze rotations during active incidents | Security and Authority Boundary Rotation automation holds privileged access. title: Least-Privilege Scoping
description: Scope every agent action to the minimum permission set the current step needs, with deny-by-default grants, explicit expiry, and per-action audit records so lateral movement stays contained.
body: Least-Privilege Scoping Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A credential that can do everything will eventually do something you did not intend. Least-privilege scoping treats authorization as a narrow, expiring grant instead of ambient power: each step names the capability and resources it needs, receives exactly that, and loses it on completion. Deny-by-default evaluation, per-grant expiry, and revocation mean a compromised step can only reach what that step was already allowed to touch. When to Use Use when an agent or automation holds credentials that can read, write, or delete beyond the single action it is performing — tool tokens, cloud roles, or API scopes. Do not use as a substitute for permission checks at the point of use; scoping narrows what a grant covers, and each call still needs its own decision. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The capability the step wants to invoke | | | | Yes | The specific objects the action targets | | | | Yes | The standing policy grants are checked against | | | | No | Lifetime of the grant; defaults to the step boundary | Procedure 1. Start from deny-by-default: an unlisted action is rejected before any tool call is attempted. 2. Enumerate the exact capability and resource IDs the step needs; wildcard scopes require explicit justification. 3. Check the request against the standing policy, then issue a grant scoped to those resources with an expiry. 4. Evaluate each subsequent tool call against the active grant — resource by resource, not by coarse role. 5. Revoke the grant at step completion, and treat any post-revocation call as a policy violation to log. 6. Record issued grants and their use in an audit trail that answers: who, what scope, which resources, how long. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The issued grant, or null when denied | | | | Allow or deny with the policy rule that decided it | | | | Issuer, scope, resources, expiry, and usage count | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Standing admin token | One long-lived credential reused across steps | Issue per-step grants with expiry | | Wildcard scope | Convenience grants like resource | Require explicit justification and review | | Scope creep | Step reuses a grant for adjacent resources | Evaluate each call against the grant, not the role | | Orphaned grants | Completion paths that skip revocation | Revoke in a cleanup path and audit usage after expiry | | Silent denies | Denials logged nowhere | Record every decision with the deciding rule | Security and Authority Boundary Scoping limits what a compromised step can reach; it does not decide whether an action is correct. A perfectly scoped grant can still perform a wrong action — purpose review and destructive-action approval remain separate, human-owned checks. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. RFC 6749 defining scoped OAuth 2.0 access (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749). 2. Wikipedia's overview of the principle of least privilege (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principleofleast_privilege). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. description: Authenticate remote MCP and agent tools with OAuth while keeping credentials outside skill definitions and enforcing explicit authorization boundaries.
body: MCP OAuth Authentication Description Authenticate a remote MCP server or agent-facing service through OAuth without embedding credentials in a skill, tool schema, repository, or generated artifact. Treat authentication and authorization as separate contracts: OAuth establishes identity/session state; authorization determines which tools and operations the agent may invoke. When to Use - A remote MCP server requires OAuth/OIDC authentication. - Tokens rotate or expire during long-running agent sessions. - A skill must describe authentication requirements without carrying secrets. - Tool availability depends on the authenticated principal. Inputs / Outputs | Area | Contract | |---|---| | Inputs | Authorization-server metadata, client configuration, redirect policy, requested scopes, runtime identity, and protected-resource metadata when available. | | Outputs | Authenticated session state, token metadata needed for runtime use, granted scopes, and explicit authorization status. | | Never output | Client secrets, refresh tokens, access tokens, or other credentials in skill text, logs, prompts, or generated indexes. | Procedure 1. Discover protected-resource and authorization-server metadata from authoritative configuration. 2. Validate redirect URI, issuer, audience/resource, PKCE requirements, and requested scopes. 3. Complete authorization using the approved client and user interaction boundary. 4. Store tokens only in the runtime credential store; never in skill files or prompts. 5. Before each privileged tool call, verify that the identity and granted scope authorize the operation. 6. On expiry or invalidation, fail closed and require the defined re-authentication path. 7. Record non-secret authentication evidence sufficient to diagnose failures. Runnable Example Failure Modes - OAuth succeeds but the MCP session exposes no authorized tools. - Stale or revoked refresh token. - Redirect URI mismatch. - Wrong audience/resource or scope. - Authentication succeeds but authorization is insufficient. - Tokens or authorization codes leak into logs or model context. Security Boundary OAuth does not grant permission to perform arbitrary tool actions. Tool authorization remains authoritative and must be evaluated independently. title: Password Hashing
description: Store passwords as salted, iterated hashes with a declared cost parameter and constant-time verification so credential material is never stored in recoverable form.
body: Password Hashing Category: Security | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A password stored in plaintext is a breach waiting for a date; a password hashed once without salt is a rainbow-table lookup. This skill defines credential storage as a contract: a per-user random salt, a slow memory-hard or iterated hash function, a declared cost parameter, and constant-time comparison on verification. The stored record keeps the algorithm and cost with the digest so migration to stronger parameters is possible. When to Use Use whenever a system stores a user-provided secret for later verification — passwords, PINs, API secrets — and must never recover the plaintext. Do not use for non-recoverable-but-high-entropy tokens like OAuth client secrets; those can be stored as plain fast hashes since entropy does the work. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The secret being stored or verified | | | | Yes | Per-user random salt, generated at first store | | | | Yes | Iteration count or hardness parameter, declared in policy | | | | Yes | The existing record for verification | Procedure 1. Generate a fresh random salt per credential at first store; reuse of salts across users is a defect. 2. Derive the digest with a salted slow hash and a cost parameter declared in policy, never chosen per call. 3. Store the salt, cost, and algorithm identifier alongside the digest so verification and migration are unambiguous. 4. Verify by re-deriving with the stored parameters and comparing in constant time; early-exit comparison leaks timing. 5. Reject passwords below the declared minimum entropy policy before hashing; the hash cannot repair a weak secret. 6. Rehash transparently on next successful login when the policy cost rises, and record the migration. 7. Never log the password, its digest, or the comparison result beyond pass/fail. title: Permission Checking
description: Authorize agent actions against explicit identities, capabilities, resource scopes, and policy constraints before executing tools or accessing data.
body: Permission Checking Description Permission checking is the authorization boundary between an agent's intent and an executable action. Evaluate the authenticated actor, requested action, target resource, granted scope, and policy constraints before invoking a tool or mutating state. Prefer deny-by-default authorization with narrowly scoped capabilities. Authentication identifies the actor; authorization decides what that actor may do. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | yes | Authenticated agent/service identity | | | string | yes | Requested operation | | | string | yes | Target resource | | | set[str] | yes | Granted capabilities/scopes | | | dict | yes | Resource and action constraints | | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | bool | Whether the action may proceed | | | string | Safe decision explanation | | | string | Policy version used for the decision | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Privilege escalation | Broad wildcard permissions | Use least-privilege scopes and resource constraints | | Confused deputy | Agent uses a privileged service on behalf of an untrusted caller | Propagate caller identity and intent | | TOCTOU | Resource changes between check and use | Revalidate immediately before sensitive operations | | Stale grants | Long-lived cached authorization | Bound cache lifetime and invalidate on policy changes | | Missing tenant boundary | Resource ID alone does not encode ownership | Include tenant/owner scope in authorization | | Fail-open behavior | Authorization service unavailable | Default to deny for sensitive actions | Design Rules 1. title: Privilege Escalation Detection
description: Detect privilege escalation attempts from authentication, authorization, and system logs by modeling normal permission change paths and flagging deviations in near real time.
body: Privilege Escalation Detection Category: Security | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Privilege escalation rarely breaks in one step; it chains small permission wins. The skill covers modeling the legitimate paths by which accounts and processes gain privilege in an environment, then watching for events that fall outside those paths: unexpected group membership changes, service account logins on new hosts, elevation anomalies, and token manipulation. Detections are chains, so the output correlates events rather than raising single-line alerts. When to Use Use when authorization-relevant logs must be monitored for accounts or processes obtaining more privilege than their documented paths allow. Do not alert on every permission change. Without a model of legitimate paths, the detection floods operators and real escalations hide in the noise. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Authentication and authorization events with timestamps and principals | | | | Yes | Documented legitimate privilege change paths per role and host | | | | No | Correlation window in minutes for chaining related events | Procedure 1. Ingest authentication and authorization logs and normalize principals, actions, and targets. 2. Load the permission baseline: who may grant what, through which documented paths. 3. Match each event against the baseline; unmatched events are candidate deviations. 4. Correlate candidates within the window into chains: grant, use, and persist sequences. 5. Score chains by blast radius: what the gained privilege reaches. 6. Emit detections with the full chain, the baseline clause violated, and recommended response. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Escalation chains with events, violated baseline clause, and score | | | | Legitimate-but-unmodeled paths that need baseline updates | | | | Suggested containment per detection | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Alert flooding | No baseline, so every change is suspicious | Model legitimate paths first, then deviate | | Missed slow chains | Events days apart never correlated | Add long-window correlation for persistence stages | | Service account blind spots | Shared accounts break principal identity | Attribute actions to workload identity where possible | | Baseline staleness | New admin processes unmodeled | Review baseline gaps emitted by the detection loop | | Single-event alerts | Chains scored as isolated lines | Score and raise chains, not isolated events | Security and Authority Boundary Escalation detections name accounts and hosts that may already be compromised. Treat detection output as need-to-know, deliver response actions through the incident process, and never auto-revoke broadly without a human confirming the chain is not a legitimate change. title: Rate Limiting
description: Bound agent and tool request frequency to control abuse, runaway loops, concurrency spikes, and resource cost.
body: Rate Limiting Description Rate limiting constrains how frequently an agent, user, tool, or endpoint may perform an operation during a defined interval. In agent systems it is also a control against runaway tool loops and unbounded external API cost. Choose a limiter according to the failure mode: token bucket for bursts, sliding windows for straightforward request counts, or provider-side quotas when the external service is authoritative. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | yes | Identity/resource bucket | | | int | yes | Maximum allowed rate | | | float | yes | Time window or refill interval | | | int | no | Weighted request cost | | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---:| | | bool | Whether the request may proceed | | | float | Approximate delay when blocked | Runnable Example For distributed systems, use an atomic shared store or the upstream provider's quota mechanism; an in-memory limiter is process-local. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Bypass | Key can be changed by the caller | Derive identity from authenticated context | | Burst overload | Fixed window allows boundary bursts | Use sliding window or token bucket | | Distributed race | Multiple workers update counters independently | Use atomic centralized state | | Retry storm | Clients retry immediately after denial | Return bounded retry information and use backoff | | Starvation | One tenant consumes the whole quota | Partition limits by tenant/agent/resource | | Clock issues | Wall-clock adjustments | Use monotonic time for local windows | Design Rules - Apply limits at the earliest authoritative boundary. - Rate-limit expensive tools separately from cheap operations. - Combine request limits with concurrency and budget limits. - Make blocked requests observable without logging sensitive payloads. - Use provider-specific quotas when they are stricter than local limits. title: Rollback / Undo
description: Make high-impact agent mutations reversible with explicit snapshots, transaction boundaries, postcondition checks, and safe rollback semantics.
body: Rollback / Undo Description Rollback protects against failed or undesired agent actions by preserving enough state to restore a known-good condition. It is appropriate for multi-step mutations where partial completion could leave inconsistent state. Rollback is not equivalent to deletion or backup. A rollback design must define what state is captured, when it is captured, which operations are reversible, and how concurrent changes are handled. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | callable/object | yes | Reversible mutation | | | object | yes | State required to restore the prior state | | | object | no | Preconditions/postconditions | | | dict | no | Retry, timeout, and recovery rules | | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | or | | | string | Failure reason when recovery occurs | | | string | Correlation identifier | Runnable Example The example is in-memory and does not address concurrent writers. Production systems need transactional storage, version checks, or compensating operations appropriate to the target system. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Partial rollback | Not all side effects are reversible | Use transactions or explicit compensating actions | | Stale snapshot | Another actor changed state after snapshot | Use version/ETag checks and conflict detection | | Rollback failure | Recovery path has its own failure | Make recovery observable and escalate to an operator | | Irreversible side effect | Email/payment/external call cannot be undone | Require approval before execution and use compensating actions | | Lost snapshot | Snapshot stored in same failure domain | Store recovery state separately with controlled access | | Silent divergence | State restores but external side effects remain | Verify postconditions and record residual effects | Design Rules - Capture state immediately before mutation. - Bind rollback to the exact action/version being reverted. - Prefer native transactions when available. - Use compensating actions for irreversible external effects. - Never claim successful rollback without a postcondition check. - Audit both commit and rollback outcomes. References - OWASP Transaction Authorization guidance: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/TransactionAuthorizationCheat_Sheet.html - Python context manager protocol: https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#context-managers Evidence Evidence status: guidance is grounded in transaction and recovery principles; rollback completeness is system-specific. title: Sandboxed Execution
description: Execute untrusted agent-generated code inside a separately enforced isolation boundary with resource, filesystem, network, and timeout controls.
body: Sandboxed Execution Description Sandboxed execution separates untrusted code from the agent host and limits what the code can read, write, execute, and connect to. A timeout alone is not a sandbox. Production isolation should be enforced by an operating-system, container, VM, or dedicated execution service boundary. Treat the sandbox policy as part of the security contract: filesystem visibility, network egress, CPU/memory limits, process privileges, runtime image, and cleanup must all be explicit. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | yes | Untrusted program | | | int | yes | Maximum execution duration | | | string | yes | Explicit network policy such as | | | path | no | Isolated working directory | | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---:| | | string | Captured standard output | | | string | Captured standard error | | | int | Process result | | | bool | Whether the execution exceeded the limit | Runnable Example This example demonstrates timeout-bounded subprocess execution only. It is not a security sandbox and must not be used as isolation for hostile code without an additional OS/container/VM boundary. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Host escape | Weak isolation boundary | Use a maintained container/VM runtime and least privilege | | Network exfiltration | Unrestricted egress | Default to no network; allow only required destinations | | Resource exhaustion | CPU/memory/process abuse | Enforce hard resource quotas outside the guest process | | Filesystem exposure | Host paths mounted into the sandbox | Use an isolated workspace and read-only mounts where possible | | Dependency attack | Untrusted packages installed at runtime | Use pinned images/packages and controlled registries | | Cleanup failure | Processes survive after timeout | Kill the process tree and verify cleanup | Design Rules - Do not call or on untrusted input in the agent process. - Do not treat a Python timeout as a security boundary. - Default network access to disabled. - Use non-root execution and a minimal runtime image. - Apply resource limits outside the untrusted process. - Delete temporary state after execution and verify cleanup. - Keep sandbox credentials separate from host credentials. References - Python subprocess documentation: https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html - OWASP Server-Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/ServerSideRequestForgeryPreventionCheatSheet.html Evidence Evidence status: the cited Python documentation supports process execution semantics; isolation guarantees depend on the external sandbox technology and configuration. body: Secret Scanning Description Secret scanning detects API keys, access tokens, private keys, passwords, and other credential material before it propagates through an agent system. Never store a real secret in a skill example or test fixture. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | yes | Content to scan | | | mapping | no | Custom patterns in addition to provider detectors | | | dict | no | File/source metadata used for policy | | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | list | Secret type and location metadata without exposing the secret | | | bool | Whether policy requires stopping the operation | | | list[str] | Actions such as revoke, rotate, or remove | Runnable Example The patterns are illustrative and intentionally incomplete.
