Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | False negative | New or provider-specific token format | Keep detectors updated and use provider validation | | False positive | Random high-entropy text matches | Use contextual validation and allowlisted test fixtures | | Secret exposure in findings | Scanner stores the matched value | Store type/location/hash, not the credential | | Already leaked secret | Detection occurs after publication | Revoke/rotate immediately and remove from affected history | | Bypass abuse | Developer bypasses push protection | Require documented reason and review for exceptions | | Secret in generated artifacts | CI only scans source files | Scan generated files and release artifacts too | Design Rules - Scan before commit and again in CI. - Prefer provider-aware detectors and push protection. - Never print the matched secret in logs. - Treat detection as an incident trigger, not proof that the credential is harmless. - Rotate/revoke exposed credentials before cleanup work. - Keep test fixtures obviously synthetic. title: Session Management
description: Create, rotate, and expire agent sessions with server-side state, opaque identifiers, and re-authentication on privilege change so identity evidence stays fresh instead of indefinitely trusted.
body: Session Management Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A session is a server-side record plus a token that points at it; the token is evidence, not the identity itself. Session management keeps the record authoritative: opaque identifiers, rotation on login and privilege change, idle plus absolute expiry, and invalidation that actually invalidates. A leaked old token stops working because the record moved on — not because someone hoped it would. When to Use Use when an agent or service maintains state across requests on behalf of an identity — web sessions, agent run sessions, or API tokens issued per engagement. Do not use sessions as long-term authorization storage; a session says who someone was recently, and privilege should be re-established when the risk window grows. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Authenticated identity the session represents | | | | Yes | Max gap between requests before expiry | | | | Yes | Max total lifetime regardless of activity | | | | Yes | Server-side session state | Procedure 1. Store session state server-side; issue only an opaque, high-entropy identifier to the client. 2. Set both idle and absolute expiry; whichever fires first ends the session. 3. Rotate the identifier on login, on privilege change, and on any suspected disclosure. 4. Invalidate the server record on logout; a client-side cookie clear is not invalidation. 5. Require re-authentication for sensitive operations even inside a valid session. 6. Record creation, rotation, and expiry events in the audit log with actor and time. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Opaque identifier for the active session | | | | active, expiredidle, expiredabsolute, or revoked | | | | Session lifecycle events for auditing | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Client-side session trust | State stored where the client can edit it | Keep the record server-side; issue opaque IDs | | Eternal sessions | Only idle expiry configured | Enforce absolute TTL on top of idle timeout | | Missing rotation | Same identifier across privilege changes | Rotate on login and privilege change | | Predictable identifiers | Sequential or low-entropy session IDs | Use high-entropy random identifiers | | Logout theater | Cookie cleared client-side, record alive | Invalidate the server record on logout | Security and Authority Boundary A session carries recent identity evidence; it is not proof of continued presence or intent. Re-authentication, step-up verification, and the decision to trust a session at all remain with the identity provider and the calling service. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SessionManagementCheat_Sheet.html). 2. MDN's reference on the Set-Cookie header and session attributes (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie). title: Social Engineering Detection
description: Detect social engineering attempts across messages and support channels by recognizing pretexting, urgency, authority impersonation, and credential harvesting patterns.
body: Social Engineering Detection Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Social engineering attacks people, not code, so detection works on message patterns and process anomalies. The skill covers screening inbound communications for the classic patterns: manufactured urgency, unverifiable authority, pretext setup, and redirection to off-channel or credential capture. It flags for review rather than silently blocking, because false positives on legitimate urgent mail are costly, and it never auto-responds to a suspected attacker. When to Use Use when inbound email, chat, or support requests must be screened for phishing, pretexting, executive impersonation, and credential or payment redirection. Do not auto-reply to suspected attacks or reveal the detection. Acknowledgment teaches the attacker what worked and marks the target as monitored. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Inbound communications with headers, sender, and content | | | | Yes | Known internal identities and their verified channels | | | | No | Scores that route to review, warn, or block | Procedure 1. Inspect links and attachments for credential capture and off-channel redirection. 4. Score the message from matched patterns and route by threshold: review, warn, or block. 5. Escalate with the evidence: matched patterns, sender analysis, and links. 6. Never auto-respond; suspected messages are silently routed to review. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Per-message classification with matched patterns and score | | | | Messages routed to security review with evidence attached | | | | Grouped view when several messages share a sender or template | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | False confidence in blocking | Novel pretexts evade keyword patterns | Route on pattern plus identity anomalies, and staff a review path | | Legitimate urgent mail flagged | Real urgency reads as manufactured | Warn rather than block borderline messages | | Display-name spoof missed | Only reply-to checked | Compare full sender identity, not display names | | Attacker tipped off | Auto-replies reveal the detection | Silently route; never acknowledge | | Isolated alerts | Campaign messages triaged one by one | Group by sender and template to see campaigns | Security and Authority Boundary This skill processes private communications. title: Threat Intelligence Enrichment
description: Enrich security events and observables with structured threat intelligence, mapping indicators to tactics and campaigns while resisting feed poisoning and stale data.
body: Threat Intelligence Enrichment Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Enrichment turns an IP or hash into context only when the source is trustworthy and current. The skill covers normalizing observables, matching them against structured feeds, attaching tactic and campaign context with source attribution, and scoring confidence with feed age and source reputation included. When to Use Use when alerts, logs, or user reports must be prioritized with external threat context: known actors, campaign affiliation, and observed infrastructure. Attach available context: tactics, campaign names, and related infrastructure. 4. Score confidence combining source reputation, record age, and corroboration across feeds. 5. Age out stale indicators so old intelligence cannot keep driving verdicts. 6. Emit enrichment with provenance so any verdict can be traced to its records. title: Threat Modeling
description: Model a system’s components against a structured threat taxonomy with per-interaction mitigations so security work is driven by an enumerated, reviewable threat list instead of ad-hoc paranoia.
body: Threat Modeling Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Security without enumeration becomes either paralysis or theater. Threat modeling imposes order: decompose the system into components and interactions, walk a fixed taxonomy — spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege — per component, and record a mitigation or an explicit acceptance for every threat found. The model is the artifact; fixes are tracked against it. When to Use Use when designing or changing a system that handles untrusted input, credentials, or privileged operations, and when the security posture must be explainable to a reviewer. Do not use as a substitute for testing; a model guides where to test and review, and unverified mitigations are intentions, not protections. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | System decomposition under review | | | | Yes | Recorded threats and their handling per component | | | | Yes | The threat classes walked per component | Procedure 1. Decompose the system into components and their interactions before naming a single threat. 2. Walk the declared taxonomy for every component, in a fixed order, so classes are never skipped silently. 3. Record each threat with its entry point and a mitigation, or an explicit accepted-risk note — never an empty cell. 4. Treat missing mitigations as findings with owners and deadlines, not as future hopes. 5. Update the model whenever the decomposition changes; a model of the old system protects nothing. 6. Re-test mitigations that the model claims; an untested mitigation is a documented guess. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Enumerated threats and their handling status | | | | Taxonomy classes with no recorded interaction | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Taxonomy skipping | Only familiar threat classes examined | Walk the full taxonomy per component in fixed order | | Empty-cell acceptance | Threats noted without mitigation or decision | Require a mitigation or an explicit accepted-risk note | | Stale model | System changed, model unchanged | Re-model on every decomposition change | | Untested mitigations | Controls recorded but never verified | Track mitigations as testable findings with owners | | Paralysis inversion | Enumeration replaces remediation | Every finding needs an owner and a deadline | Security and Authority Boundary The model itself is sensitive: it enumerates exactly where the system is soft. Treat threat models as need-to-know artifacts and protect them with the same care as the codebase. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. title: Backpressure Handling
description: Detect and shed or buffer load when downstream consumers fall behind, using explicit queue limits, load-shedding policies, and honest propagation instead of unbounded queues.
body: Backpressure Handling Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Backpressure is the system admitting it is saturated instead of hiding the lag in a growing queue. The skill covers measuring consumer lag against explicit thresholds, choosing the response per queue type: bounded buffers for bursty-but-must-complete work, immediate shedding for latency-sensitive work, and degradation for work that has cheaper fallbacks. Pressure is propagated to callers honestly, because a lie here becomes a timeout there. When to Use Use when producers can outrun consumers: agent fleets, ingestion pipelines, or request handlers where queue growth is worse than refusal. Do not respond to saturation with an unbounded queue. It converts a visible overload into an invisible one that eventually fails bigger and later. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Depth, arrival rate, and consumption rate per queue | | | | Yes | Thresholds and the response per queue type: buffer, shed, or degrade | | | | No | Degraded-mode responses available when shedding is undesirable | Procedure 1. Instrument every queue with depth and arrival and consumption rates before tuning anything. 2. Classify each queue: must-complete, latency-sensitive, or degradable. 3. Set explicit thresholds for each queue marking normal, pressured, and saturated states. 4. Respond by class: bounded buffer, immediate shed with a clear refusal, or degraded fallback. 5. Propagate pressure upstream honestly so callers can slow down instead of guessing. 6. Alert on sustained pressure, not transient bursts, and record shed decisions for review. title: Capability-Based Skill Selection
description: Select and sequence canonical skills for a task by matching required capabilities, discriminating competing candidates, checking eligibility and dependencies, and using execution evidence to choose the next skill.
body: Capability-Based Skill Selection Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Capability-based skill selection turns a task into an explicit skill decision rather than treating retrieval as selection. It identifies the capabilities required by the current task, compares competing canonical skills, checks evidence, compatibility, authority, and prerequisites, then selects an executable skill and determines what should happen next from the observed result. This skill is intended for agent runtimes and orchestrators that consume a canonical skill registry. It does not replace search, the registry, dependency graph, or execution runtime. When to Use Use when an agent must decide which skill to invoke for a concrete task and more than one plausible skill may match. Do not use this as a substitute for simple deterministic lookup when the canonical skill ID is already known. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | / | Yes | Current task, objective, or unresolved subtask | | | | Yes | Project state, constraints, environment, prior results, and available tools | | | | Yes | Candidate canonical skills discovered from the registry/search boundary | | | | No | Required capabilities already inferred by an upstream goal/capability resolver | | | | No | Skills already executed successfully for the current task | | | | No | Available benchmark, provenance, freshness, compatibility, or runtime evidence | Selection Procedure 1. Normalize the task into the capabilities required to make progress. 2. Resolve candidate skills through the canonical registry and reject unknown or non-canonical IDs. 3. Separate direct matches from merely related skills. 4. Compare competing candidates using task fit, required capability coverage, eligibility, compatibility, evidence quality, freshness, and known limitations. 5. Resolve mandatory prerequisites before selecting a dependent skill. 6. Prefer the smallest sufficient skill set; do not select skills merely because they are related. 7. Produce an explicit selection rationale and rejected-candidate reasons. 8. Invoke the selected executable skill only when its prerequisites and authority conditions are satisfied. 9. Verify the result against the task acceptance criteria. 10. If verification fails, classify the failure and select the next justified skill or recovery action rather than blindly repeating the same invocation. 11. Stop when the task is verified complete, blocked by an external condition, or requires escalation. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Canonical skill ID/version selected for the current step | | | | Dependencies that must be satisfied before invocation | | | | Plausible candidates rejected with explicit reasons | | | | Next invocation, verification, recovery, escalation, or terminal decision | | | | Evidence needed to verify the selected action | | | | , , or | Decision Contract A valid selection must answer all of these questions: - What capability is required now? - Which canonical skill satisfies it? - Why is it better than the competing candidates? - Which prerequisites must run first? - Is the skill eligible in the current context? - What evidence will verify the invocation? - What result causes the agent to invoke the next skill? - What result causes recovery, substitution, escalation, or termination? A skill must not be selected solely because it contains matching keywords. Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Retrieval mistaken for selection | Top search result is treated as authoritative | Evaluate competing candidates against task requirements | | Ambiguous candidates | Several skills satisfy overlapping capabilities | Require explicit discrimination reasons and tie-break evidence | | Hidden prerequisite | Dependent skill selected before required capability exists | Resolve prerequisite/dependency graph before invocation | | Stale or weak evidence | Candidate has outdated or insufficient proof | Prefer fresher, provenance-backed evidence and surface the gap | | Ineligible candidate | Compatibility, authority, or runtime constraints are unmet | Reject candidate and continue with an eligible alternative | | Repeated failed invocation | Same action is retried without new evidence | Classify failure and choose recovery, substitution, or escalation | | Premature completion | Selection succeeds but task outcome is unverified | Require outcome evidence before | | Over-selection | Agent invokes related skills without causal need | Select the smallest sufficient skill set | Security and Authority Boundary Skill selection does not grant permissions. The selected skill must execute only within its declared authority, security boundary, compatibility constraints, and available runtime permissions. High-impact or irreversible actions must remain subject to the governing approval and policy controls of the consuming agent runtime. Evidence This skill is motivated by two complementary evidence classes: 1. Public demand signals around automated task breakdown, agent orchestration, and assignment based on skills/performance. 2. Skills Tree's current behavioral evaluation gap: retrieval quality is now measured, but task-specific skill discrimination, dependency-aware selection, invocation, and next-skill decisions are not yet comprehensively benchmarked. The demand evidence is recorded in ; it is not treated as popularity or adoption data. title: Circuit Breaking
description: Stop calling a failing dependency after a threshold, fail fast while the circuit is open, and probe with trial calls before closing so one slow or broken service cannot take the caller down with it.
body: Circuit Breaking Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Retries have a limit beyond which they become part of the outage. A circuit breaker converts persistent failure into a fast, local decision: after a threshold of consecutive failures the circuit opens and calls short-circuit immediately; after a reset window a limited probe tests the water; only a successful probe closes the circuit again. The caller sheds load and stays responsive while the dependency recovers. When to Use Use around any remote dependency whose failure or latency can exhaust the caller — model APIs, databases, downstream services called on a request path. Do not wrap workloads where every call must succeed; a breaker that skips required work turns degraded mode into silent data loss. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The dependency the breaker guards | | | | Yes | Consecutive failures that open the circuit | | | | Yes | Open period before a probe is allowed | | | | Yes | The single trial call used in half-open state | Procedure 1. Track consecutive failures per dependency, not globally; one bad endpoint should not open every circuit. 2. When the count reaches the threshold, open the circuit and fail fast — no call, no queue, no waiting. 3. While open, answer immediately with a defined degradation result, never with an exception shape callers have not agreed to. 4. After the reset timeout, move to half-open and allow exactly one probe call; the rest still fail fast. 5. Close on a successful probe and reset the counter; re-open and restart the timer on a failed probe. 6. Export circuit state as a metric; state transitions are the outage narrative. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Current circuit state | | | | What the breaker did with this call | | | | Consecutive failures at decision time | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Flapping | Threshold or timeout tuned to noise | Calibrate to the dependency's real error profile | | No half-open state | Open circuits close on faith after the timer | Require one successful probe before closing | | Shared breakers | One circuit for heterogeneous calls | Track per dependency and per call class | | State lost on restart | Counters held in process memory only | Persist or re-warm counters; treat restart as probe | | Silent degradation | Short-circuits invisible to callers and operators | Export state metrics and log every transition | Security and Authority Boundary The breaker protects the caller's time and threads; it does not repair the dependency or verify its recovery. Post-incident validation of the dependency stays with its owner, and an open circuit is a degraded state, never a healthy one. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Circuit Breaker pattern on microservices.io (https://microservices.io/patterns/reliability/circuit-breaker.html). 2. Wikipedia's overview of fault tolerance (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fault_tolerance). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Cross-Agent Locking
description: Coordinate exclusive access to shared resources across distributed agents using leases with fencing tokens, preventing deadlocks and torn writes from concurrent mutation.
body: Cross-Agent Locking Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description When two agents can mutate the same resource, correctness needs a lock, and distributed locks need more than mutual exclusion. The skill covers choosing lock granularity, issuing time-bounded leases with fencing tokens so a stalled holder cannot corrupt later writers, ordering acquisition to prevent deadlock, and handling the crash case: leases expire, the next holder proceeds, and the fencing token rejects the zombie. Lock state lives in a coordinator both sides can see, never in agent memory. When to Use Use when multiple agents operate on shared state or resources that must not be mutated concurrently: shared files, external accounts, or single-instance workflows. Do not treat advisory flags in a shared document as locks. Without a coordinator, expiry, and fencing, two agents will both believe they hold the resource. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Identifier of the shared resource to protect | | | | Yes | Maximum lease duration before forced expiry | | | | Yes | Shared lease store both acquiring agents can observe | Procedure 1. Choose lock granularity: the smallest scope that prevents the conflict, not the whole task. 2. Acquire a lease from the coordinator with a bounded TTL and a fencing token number. 3. Record the token with every mutation so stale writes can be rejected downstream. 4. Acquire multiple locks in a fixed global order to prevent deadlock cycles. 5. Release the lease immediately after the critical section; never hold across waits. 6. Handle expiry: renew in-flight if needed, and accept rejection when a higher token exists. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Holder identity, token, TTL, and expiry time | | | | Ordered acquisition and release events | | | | Contested acquisitions and fencing rejections | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Split-brain hold | Lease expiry unobserved by a stalled holder | Fencing tokens rejected at the resource | | Deadlock | Locks acquired in different orders | Fixed global acquisition order | | Lock leak | Crashed agent never released | Bounded TTL with automatic expiry | | Over-broad locking | Whole-task locks serialize everything | Lock the smallest conflicting scope | | Advisory lock ignored | A rogue agent bypasses the coordinator | Enforce at the resource with token checks, not trust | Security and Authority Boundary Lock coordinators become shared infrastructure with availability impact. Authenticate lease acquisition, scope tokens to the resource, and audit the acquisition log, because the log is the evidence in any post-incident dispute over who held what. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The etcd distributed key-value store used for leases and coordination (https://etcd.io/). 2. The Apache ZooKeeper coordination service (https://zookeeper.apache.org/). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Dead-Letter Queuing
description: Route repeatedly failing messages to a dedicated dead-letter queue with full failure metadata so poison payloads are quarantined for inspection instead of blocking the pipeline or vanishing.
body: Dead-Letter Queuing Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Some messages cannot be processed, and retrying them forever converts one bad payload into a stuck pipeline. Dead-letter queuing draws the line: after a bounded number of attempts, the message moves to a dedicated dead-letter queue carrying its attempts, errors, and original payload. The main queue keeps flowing, the failure stays inspectable, and a replay path exists for after the cause is fixed. When to Use Use with any task queue or event pipeline where a malformed or failing message must not block subsequent messages. Do not use a dead-letter queue as a trash bin: entries are quarantined pending diagnosis, and unbounded growth without review hides an outage in plain sight. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The message being processed | | | | Yes | Processing attempts before dead-lettering | | | | Yes | Prior failures for this message id | | | | Yes | The dead-letter destination with its metadata schema | Procedure 1. Track attempts per message id; the count travels with the message, not with worker memory. 2. On each failure, record the error and timestamp; retry only while under the attempt bound. 3. At the bound, move the message to the dead-letter queue with its payload, attempts, and error history attached. 4. Surface dead-letter depth and entry age as operational alarms; a growing dead-letter queue is a failing pipeline. 5. Diagnose entries before replay: fix the consumer or correct the payload, then replay deliberately. 6. Re-run replayed messages through the same accounting so a still-failing replay dead-letters again, visibly. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Disposition of the message | | | | The quarantined message with metadata when dead-lettered | | | | Attempts made before the disposition | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Infinite retry | No attempt bound on failing messages | Count attempts per id and enforce the bound | | Silent drop | Failures discarded without a dead-letter queue | Every non-processed message lands somewhere inspectable | | Unreviewed backlog | The dead-letter queue grows with no alarm watching it | Alarm on depth and oldest entry age | | Blind replay | Messages replayed before the cause is fixed | Fix first, replay deliberately, re-account on failure | | Metadata loss | Entry stored without errors or attempt count | Attach payload, attempts, and error history to the entry | Security and Authority Boundary The dead-letter queue quarantines and preserves; it does not diagnose. Root-cause analysis, payload correction, and the decision to replay remain operator work, with the quarantine treated as evidence, not as a fix. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of dead-letter queues (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadletterqueue). 2. title: Deadline Propagation
description: Carry one absolute end-time deadline through every orchestration hop so each step budgets its remaining time, children inherit a tightened deadline, and late results are discarded rather than delivered.
body: Deadline Propagation Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Relative timeouts do not compose: three sequential steps with a 5-second timeout each can stall a caller for 15 seconds. Deadline propagation fixes the arithmetic by carrying one absolute end time: each hop computes remaining time against the same clock, children receive the tighter of their own budget and the parent's remaining time, and results that arrive after the deadline are discarded instead of patched into the run late. When to Use Use in any multi-hop orchestration — service calls, subagent trees, pipelines — where a caller's total wait must stay bounded. Do not substitute per-hop timeouts without checking the sum; a chain of local limits is not a global one. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The absolute end time for the whole run | | | | Yes | Injectable current time for deterministic decisions | | | | No | The step's own preferred local budget | | | | No | Downstream hops inheriting the deadline | Procedure 1. Set one absolute deadline at run start, from the caller's wall-clock budget; it is a timestamp, not a duration. 2. At each hop, compute remaining time as deadline minus now; a hop with no remaining time fails fast without starting. 3. Give each child the tighter of its own budget and the parent's remaining time minus the parent's reserve. 4. Reject late results even if they eventually complete; a result after the deadline is not a result for this run. 5. Record per-step time consumption so postmortems can show where the budget went. 6. Reserve a margin for serialization and cleanup; a deadline with no reserve fails at the packaging step. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Time left at the decision point | | | | The tightened deadline handed to a child | | | | Whether the step or result is usable | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Relative-only budgets | Per-step timeouts whose sum exceeds the caller's budget | Propagate one absolute deadline | | Deadline-blind queues | Enqueued work starts without checking the clock | Check remaining time at dequeue, not just enqueue | | Children outliving parents | Children keep their local budget after the parent expired | Hand children the tighter of own budget and parent remaining | | Late results accepted | Stragglers patched in after expiry | Classify post-deadline results as late and discard | | No time accounting | Postmortems cannot say where time went | Record per-step consumption against budget | Security and Authority Boundary Deadline propagation bounds wall-clock time; it does not certify the quality of what was rushed to fit. Quality gates, evaluation, and review apply the same standards regardless of how much budget a step had. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The gRPC core concepts documentation on deadlines and cancellation (https://grpc.io/docs/what-is-grpc/core-concepts/). 2. Wikipedia's overview of timeouts in computing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeout_%28computing%29). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Distributed State Replication
description: Replicate shared workflow and memory state across agent workers with a consistency model, quorum acknowledgment, and deterministic merge so any worker can resume after failure.
body: Distributed State Replication Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Replication turns local state into a survivable one. The skill covers choosing a consistency model appropriate to the workload, serializing state with deterministic ordering, replicating with quorum acknowledgment before declaring a write durable, and merging concurrent updates with a deterministic rule so all replicas converge without a human referee. The test of the design is whether a fresh worker can resume the workflow from replicated state alone. When to Use Use when multi-agent or multi-node execution must survive worker failure without losing workflow progress, or when several workers need a consistent view of shared state. Do not replicate state with wall-clock timestamps as the ordering key. Clock skew across workers produces last-write-wins on the wrong write. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The workflow or shared state to replicate | | | | Yes | (default) or as the ordering authority | | | | No | Replica count; defaults to a majority-of-workers quorum | Procedure 1. Define the state object and its write paths before choosing replication mechanics. 2. Choose the consistency model and the ordering authority: a leader or a quorum rule. 3. Serialize updates with a deterministic order: sequence numbers or version vectors, never wall clocks. 4. Replicate each update and declare durability only after quorum acknowledgment. 5. Merge concurrent updates with a deterministic conflict rule so replicas converge. 6. Recover failed workers by rebuilding their state from the acknowledged replica log. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | State as acknowledged by a quorum of replicas | | | | Ordered updates with sequence numbers and acknowledgments | | | | How a failed worker rebuilds from the replica set | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Split-brain state | Two authorities accepted conflicting writes | Single leader or quorum rule with fencing | | Clock-skew corruption | Wall-clock ordering across workers | Sequence numbers or version vectors for ordering | | False durability | Write acknowledged locally only | Quorum acknowledgment before declaring durable | | Non-deterministic merge | Conflicts resolved differently per replica | One deterministic merge rule applied everywhere | | Unbounded log | Replica history grows without compaction | Snapshot and compact behind acknowledged progress | Security and Authority Boundary Replicated state widens exposure: every replica holds the full state, including anything sensitive the workflow carries. Encrypt replication traffic, scope replica membership through authenticated membership, and compact secrets out of snapshots where the workflow no longer needs them. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Raft consensus algorithm reference (https://raft.github.io/). 2. The etcd distributed key-value store implementing Raft replication (https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Dynamic Team Formation
description: Assemble and disband multi-agent teams at run time by matching task requirements against agent capabilities, with explicit role contracts and budget-aware sizing.
body: Dynamic Team Formation Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Not every task deserves a team. The skill covers deciding when a single agent suffices, deriving required roles from the task decomposition, selecting agents by declared capability rather than identity, writing per-role contracts with inputs, outputs, and authority limits, and sizing the team against a budget. Teams disband on completion with artifacts returned, because lingering agents are cost and confusion. When to Use Use when a task decomposes into heterogeneous subtasks that benefit from specialists working in parallel or in sequence within one run. Do not spawn a full team for every task. Larger teams pay communication overhead that simple tasks cannot amortize, and unnecessary agents multiply cost and failure surface. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Subtasks with required capabilities and dependencies | | | | Yes | Available agents with declared capabilities and cost model | | | | No | Cost, concurrency, and time bounds for the whole team | Procedure 1. Decide whether the task needs a team at all: single-agent unless decomposition shows real heterogeneity. 2. Derive required roles from the subtasks, one role per distinct capability cluster. 3. Select agents by declared capability fit, recording the second choice for each role. 4. Write per-role contracts: inputs, outputs, authority limits, and escalation path. 5. Size the team against the budget, trading concurrency against cost per unit of work. 6. Disband on completion, returning artifacts and freeing capacity explicitly. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Roles, assigned agents, and the capability evidence for each match | | | | Per-role input, output, authority, and escalation terms | | | | Sizing rationale, budget usage, and disband event | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Team bloat | Agents added for symmetry rather than need | Size from the decomposition, not a fixed template | | Capability mismatch | Agents selected by name or affinity | Select on declared capabilities and record evidence | | Orphaned subtasks | No agent holds a required capability | Fail formation or split the subtask; never silently drop | | Lingering agents | Team never disbanded after completion | Make disband an explicit step with artifact handoff | | Contract ambiguity | Roles overlap or authority undefined | Per-role contracts before any work starts | Security and Authority Boundary Dynamically formed teams can expand the blast radius of a compromised member. Scope each agent to the minimum authorities its role contract needs, audit capability declarations in the registry, and never allow formation logic to grant authority it cannot revoke. title: Evidence Verification
description: Verify meaningful repository changes with direct implementation, test, CI, and documentation evidence.
body: Evidence Verification Description Verify completion claims against direct repository, test, CI, security, and documentation evidence. Separate verified facts from assumptions and unresolved risks. 1. Identify the claim being verified and its strongest evidence source. 2. Inspect the actual changed implementation. 3. Execute or inspect required validation gates. 4. Verify the resulting main commit and relevant CI runs. 5. Check security implications and documentation synchronization. 6. Report verified facts separately from unresolved risks and assumptions. 7. Use the precise completion states defined by AGENTS.md. Runnable example Inputs / outputs / failure modes | Input | Output | Failure mode | |---|---|---| | Changed files | Scope evidence | Claimed change is not present | | Tests | Behavioral evidence | Tests are missing or failing | | CI checks | Repository-level evidence | Required check is pending/failing | | Security scans | Risk evidence | Security result is absent | | Documentation | State continuity | Docs still describe old behavior | Failure Modes - Evidence substitution: accepting an adjacent artifact (a passing CI run for a different commit, a related document) as proof of the actual claim; match evidence to the exact claim, commit, and artifact. - Assumption laundering: classifying inferred or reported facts as "verified" without a direct artifact; keep verified, assumed, and unresolved strictly separated. - Incomplete evidence matrix: verifying positive claims but not absence claims (no regression, no unresolved risk); negative claims need named evidence too. - Stale evidence: reusing evidence collected before a change that could invalidate it; timestamp and re-check evidence at verification time. title: Execution Handoff
description: Execute repository work under the established governance model and leave a complete continuation packet.
body: Execution Handoff Description Carry work from verified intake through bounded execution, validation, documentation synchronization, and a continuation-ready handoff. A handoff must preserve enough evidence for another agent to continue without reconstructing hidden context. 1. Load authoritative state before execution. 2. Convert the objective into a bounded execution plan. 3. Inspect before changing and preserve existing functionality. 4. Escalate strategic, destructive, breaking, or high-impact decisions. 5. Execute specialist work within scope. 6. Validate implementation, security, CI, and documentation. 7. Synchronize current state and decisions when material state changes. 8. Before closing, preserve objective, decision source, files, tests, evidence, risks, remaining work, documentation updates, and next action. Runnable example Inputs / outputs / failure modes | Input | Output | Failure mode | |---|---|---| | Objective and constraints | Bounded work plan | Scope expands without authority | | Repository state | Safe execution context | Baseline is stale | | Implementation changes | Verified result | Existing behavior is unintentionally broken | | CI/security evidence | Completion state | Gates remain unresolved | | Current state and decisions | Continuation packet | Handoff omits material context | Failure Modes - Handoff information loss: omitting live decision state (why, what was ruled out, what remains) so the next agent must reconstruct work from scratch. - Unverified-state handoff: passing along work whose verification step never actually ran, presenting assumptions as completed facts. - Unbounded continuation: a handoff implying authority or scope the original work never had; state explicit boundaries and blockers. - Documentation drift: the handoff record describing intent rather than the actual end state; the record must reflect the verified end state, not the plan. title: Idempotency Keys
description: Assign client-generated idempotency keys to state-changing requests so retries and at-least-once delivery produce one effect, with duplicate calls returning the recorded first result.
body: Idempotency Keys Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description At-least-once delivery means the same request will sometimes arrive twice; idempotency keys turn that from a bug into a non-event. The client attaches a unique key to each operation intent, the server checks the key before executing, and a replayed key returns the stored first response instead of executing again. The stored response plus a payload fingerprint closes the gap between "same key" and "same request". When to Use Use for any state-changing request that may be retried — payment calls, task creation, webhook handlers, queue consumers under at-least-once semantics. Do not bother for pure reads or naturally idempotent operations; the machinery earns its cost only where duplicates have effects. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Client-generated unique key for this operation intent | | | | Yes | Digest of the payload the key refers to | | | | Yes | Server-side record of executed keys | | | | Yes | How long replayed keys resolve to stored results | Procedure 1. Generate the key client-side, unique per operation intent — not per session, not per process. 2. Before executing, look the key up: a hit with a matching fingerprint returns the stored response; a hit with a mismatching fingerprint is an error. 3. On a miss, execute once, then store the response keyed by the key and fingerprint. 4. Keep the TTL at least as long as the client's longest retry window; shorter expiry quietly reintroduces duplicates. 5. Keep keys out of URLs and logs; they identify operations and may correlate to sensitive intents. 6. Treat in-flight keys as locked: concurrent duplicate calls wait for the first execution rather than racing it. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The first execution's response, returned on every replay | | | | Whether this call returned a stored result | | | | When the key record expires | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Key reuse across payloads | Same key sent with different request bodies | Store and compare a payload fingerprint | | Server-generated keys | Key minted per attempt, not per intent | Generate the key client-side per operation intent | | No stored response | Key existence recorded, result discarded | Store the response, not just the key | | TTL shorter than retries | Key expires while the client is still retrying | Keep the TTL above the retry window | | Keys in URLs | Idempotency keys landing in access logs | Send keys in headers or bodies, never the path | Security and Authority Boundary Idempotency protects the server's effect from duplication; it does not order distinct operations. Sequencing two different calls — even related ones — needs explicit ordering, which this skill does not provide. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Stripe's API documentation on idempotent requests (https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests). 2. Wikipedia's overview of idempotence (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idempotence). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Kanban Task Management
description: Maintain a persistent, file-backed Kanban board as the shared source of task truth between a coding agent, its orchestrator, and a human reviewer: an explicit task lifecycle with receipted transitions, a blocked-by dependency DAG with a derived ready set, and a per-task merge gate whose completion evidence is verified before a task may be marked done.
body: Category: Orchestration Skill Level: Intermediate Stability: experimental Version: v1 Added: 2026-10 Last Updated: 2026-10 Description Kanban task management gives an agent a durable board it can read and mutate between sessions instead of holding the plan in context. The board is plain files under version control in the repository being worked, so task state survives crashes, context resets, and handoffs between agents and humans. This page defines a portable contract for lifecycle, dependencies, concurrency, and completion evidence; concrete implementations are references, not requirements. The Portable Contract Any conforming implementation must provide: - Board store: task records stored as files inside the repository (or a directory the repository's review surface can see). Never a side-channel database a code review cannot diff. - Task record: stable ID, status, summary, tags, edges (referencing other task IDs), an append-only list of transition receipts, and evidence references (commit SHAs, merge receipts). - Transition receipts: every status change must append a receipt (timestamp, old→new status, human-readable response message, optional evidence). Receipts are never rewritten or deleted. - Controller CLI: the only writer. Mutations happen through controller commands; direct hand-edits of board files are out-of-contract (see Concurrency Model). - Derived ready set: a query that returns, without mutating anything, the tasks an agent may legally pick up next (status eligible and all targets satisfied per the semantics below). Task Lifecycle: Legal and Illegal Transitions States: , plus (soft, orthogonal) and (a flag on , not a fifth state). | Transition | Legal? | Rule | |---|---|---| | | ✅ | Planning step; receipt required | | | ✅ | Fast-track pick; receipt required | | | ✅ | Only from the ready set (all blockers satisfied); receipt required | | | ✅ | Only if the task's merge gate is satisfied (see Completion Evidence); receipt + evidence | | | ✅ | Return: work stopped; receipt must say why | | | ✅ | Re-plan; receipt required | | | ✅ | Reopen: new receipt citing the defect/omission; prior receipts retained; task re-enters ready computation | | , | ❌ | Reopen must pass through so an owner takes the task again | | | ❌ | Skips execution evidence and the gate | | any → | ✅ | Soft archive: history and receipts stay queryable; never a delete | | | ✅ | Restore: new receipt; dependency edges re-validated against current IDs | | | ❌ | Restore first, then execute the normal gate | | any transition | ❌ | Without a response receipt, or via a hand-edit instead of the controller | Setting/clearing the flag on is always legal with a receipt; a blocked task leaves the ready set until cleared. Blocked-By Dependency Semantics Edges are validated at write time and re-validated by every ready-set computation: | Blocker state | Semantics | |---|---| | (completed) | Satisfied — does not gate the dependent task | | | Does not gate, but the controller emits a warning receipt | | Missing ID | Rejected at edge-creation time. If discovered later, the edge is unresolved: the dependent task is not ready and a validation error is surfaced | | Cyclic | Rejected at creation by cycle check over the DAG; late-discovered cycles make all members not-ready | | / / | Gates normally until the blocker reaches or | The ready set is always recomputed from the live DAG — cached orderings are never trusted. Concurrency Model Read-before-mutate is not concurrency control: two agents can both read the same state and then both write, losing one transition. The contract prescribes exactly one of: 1. Single controller: one controller process owns the board and serializes mutations, or 2. Optimistic CAS: every mutation carries the content hash of the board state it was computed against; on mismatch the controller aborts and the agent re-reads. Hand-edited board files are detected as drift and must be reconciled through the controller. Completion Evidence Implementations may declare a completion gate per task: | Level | requires | |---|---| | | Response receipt only | | | Receipt + at least one commit SHA on the task's work branch; the controller verifies the SHA exists | | | Receipt plus independently verified evidence that the relevant change reached the target branch, recorded with the resulting merge/target commit SHA | A gate must verify the repository's actual merge state. Reopening a completed task creates a new evidence cycle and never rewrites Git history. Example The following commands illustrate the contract using the YYLO Ledger, a git-native reference implementation. The dependency edge is added with the documented dependency command rather than as an option to task creation: The exact task ID returned by must be used when adding the dependency; do not assume a preselected ID. Third-Party Implementation Boundary YYLO Ledger and its related skills are external implementations of the pattern, not dependencies of this skill. References are not trusted repository policy. If adopting an external implementation, review its source and permissions independently and pin a known release or commit where reproducibility matters. Provenance and Contributor Attribution The original Kanban skill contribution was submitted by InsightFactoryAPP as PR #266, originating from the contributor fork . The original contribution commit was and is retained as provenance evidence. The Skills Tree maintainer subsequently refiled and normalized that contribution in PR #267 rather than merging the external fork directly. The resulting canonical skill is therefore maintainer-integrated work with InsightFactoryAPP credited as the original contributor. This attribution does not imply that every subsequent revision was authored by the original contributor. Implementations | Implementation | Form | Notes | |---|---|---| | YYLO Ledger | Git-native task CLI ( ) | Receipts, dependency DAG, ready set; reference implementation of this contract | | ledger-tasks-yylo | Portable for agents | Teaches board operations and source-of-truth boundaries to any skill-capable agent | | YYLO CLI | Orchestrator ( ) | Delegates ; adds worktree-per-task and merge-queue gating on top | When to Use vs Alternatives | Approach | Persistence | Dependency-aware ordering | Best for | |---|---|---|---| | In-process task queue | None (process lifetime) | Priority only | Single-session fan-out | | Database-backed tracker | External server | Usually yes | Team SaaS workflows | | File-backed Kanban board (this skill) | Git/repository | DAG + ready set | Coding agents sharing one repo with humans | Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Lost update | Two writers mutate from the same read state | Single controller or CAS; never hand-edit | | Lifecycle bypass | Direct edits skip validation | Controller refuses on drift | | Stale dependency edges | Blocker archived, renumbered, or removed | Ready set recomputed from the live DAG | | False completion | without verified evidence | Completion gate enforced at transition time | | Silent task loss | Archive treated as delete | Archive is soft and history remains queryable | | Cycle deadlock | Circular discovered late | All members not-ready + validation error | Prompt Patterns Notes - The board is local-first: no server, and the store lives in the repository, so reviews and merges see task state as first-class content. - The required response message on every transition is the audit trail humans review. - Cross-project routing should be opt-in and explicitly allow-listed. - This skill describes a capability contract; it does not prescribe a particular CLI, database, agent framework, or hosting service. title: LangGraph Checkpointing
description: Persist agent graph state at every step using LangGraph checkpointers for fault tolerance and resumability.
body: LangGraph Checkpointing Category: orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: stable | Version: v2 Description LangGraph checkpointers save a snapshot of the graph state after every node execution into a persistent store (in-memory, SQLite, PostgreSQL, or Redis). Each snapshot is associated with a , enabling the graph to resume from any prior checkpoint. This powers fault tolerance, human-in-the-loop interruption, and time-travel debugging. Without a checkpointer, graph state is ephemeral and lost on crash. title: Result Aggregation
description: Collect parallel task results into one ordered report with per-task status, explicit handling of failures and stragglers, and deterministic merge order so the combined output stays reproducible.
body: Result Aggregation Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Parallel execution multiplies results and failure shapes at the same time. Aggregation turns a cloud of futures into one report: each task contributes a (id, status, output) tuple, missing tasks appear as missing instead of vanishing, and the merge order is deterministic. The aggregate carries per-task provenance, so any claim in the combined output can be traced back to the task that produced it. When to Use Use whenever work is split across parallel subagents or workers and the caller needs one combined, trustworthy answer. Do not use unordered ad-hoc merging; a merge that depends on arrival order produces a different output on every run. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Every task the plan dispatched | | | | Yes | Completed results, keyed by task id | | | | Yes | How completed, failed, and missing tasks are merged | | | | Yes | How long the aggregate waits for stragglers | Procedure 1. Register the full expected task id set at dispatch time; the plan, not the arrival count, defines completeness. 2. Collect results as (id, status, output) tuples; failures are results, not exceptions to swallow. 3. On aggregation, subtract completed ids from expected ids; anything unaccounted is missing — with the timeout recorded. 4. Apply the merge policy per status: include completed, record failed, mark missing; the policy decides what missing means for the whole. 5. Merge in task id order, never arrival order, so identical inputs produce identical output. 6. Emit the aggregate with per-task provenance: which task produced which part of the combined result. title: Runbook-Driven Orchestration
description: Execute operational workflows as versioned, machine-readable runbooks with declared steps, verification gates, and escalation paths, so automation follows the reviewed procedure exactly.
body: Runbook-Driven Orchestration Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A runbook-driven run follows the document, not the model’s improvisation. The skill covers expressing an operational procedure as a versioned runbook with explicit steps, preconditions, verification commands, and escalation paths; validating the runbook before use; executing steps with state recorded at each gate; and stopping on any failed verification instead of continuing creatively. The run remains auditable because the automation’s actions map one-to-one onto reviewed instructions. When to Use Use for operational procedures that must be executed consistently across shifts and operators: deployments, incident mitigation, and routine maintenance with failure risk. Do not let the executor improvise around a failed step. A failed verification stops the run and escalates; creative continuation defeats the point of a reviewed procedure. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Versioned, machine-readable procedure with steps and gates | | | | Yes | Environment parameters the runbook references | | | | No | (default) or for rehearsal | Procedure 1. Load the runbook version under approval and verify its signature or review status. 2. Validate the runbook: every step has a command, expected outcome, and failure action. 3. Execute steps in order, recording state and output at every gate. 4. Run each verification gate before advancing; a failed gate stops the run. 5. Escalate through the declared path with the recorded state attached, never past it. 6. Archive the run record: runbook version, context, outputs, and every gate result. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Steps executed with outputs and gate results | | | | The verification that stopped the run, with evidence | | | | Where the run was handed off and with what state | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Improvised continuation | Executor worked around a failed gate | Hard stop on any failed verification | | Runbook drift | Documented procedure diverged from reality | Dry-run validation on schedule and before use | | Missing failure actions | A step fails with no declared response | Require a failure action per step at validation | | Ambiguous context | Parameters resolved by guesswork mid-run | Bind all context before step one | | Unreviewed edits | Runbook changed without approval | Version, review, and refuse unapproved versions | Security and Authority Boundary Runbooks encode privileged operations. Sign and review runbook versions, execute with the least privilege the steps require, and record every gate result immutably, because the run record is the audit evidence for what automation did to production. title: Speculative Execution
description: Reduce latency by running multiple candidate paths concurrently and taking the first acceptable result, with explicit acceptance criteria, duplicate-write guards, and cost accounting.
body: Speculative Execution Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Speculation buys latency with resources. The skill covers choosing which steps are worth speculating, defining acceptance criteria per path before launch, launching redundant candidates against independent resources, taking the first result that passes the criteria, and cancelling the losers. Because duplicated work multiplies cost and side effects, every speculative path must be idempotent and side-effect-free until acceptance. When to Use Use when a step is both slow and uncertain: slow model calls, flaky external services, or retrieval where any of several paths can satisfy the caller. Do not speculate on steps with external side effects before acceptance. Two accepted writes is a correctness bug that costs more than the latency saved. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The slow or uncertain step eligible for speculation | | | | Yes | Independent paths expected to produce an acceptable result | | | | Yes | Pass criteria and the rule for cancelling losers | Procedure 1. Confirm the step is worth speculating: latency saved must exceed added resource cost. 2. Write acceptance criteria before launching anything, including how the winner is judged. 3. Verify every candidate path is idempotent and free of external side effects before acceptance. 4. Launch candidates concurrently against independent resources to avoid correlated failure. 5. Take the first result that passes acceptance and cancel the losers immediately. 6. Record per-path outcomes and cost so the speculation decision can be audited and retuned. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The accepted result with its path and acceptance evidence | | | | Cancelled candidates with their progress at cancellation | | | | Resource spent on losers versus latency saved | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Duplicated side effects | Candidates mutated external state pre-acceptance | Idempotent paths with side effects only after acceptance | | Winner without criteria | First finisher accepted regardless of quality | Written acceptance criteria evaluated per result | | Correlated failure | Candidates shared the same rate-limited resource | Independent resources per candidate path | | Cost runaway | Speculation applied to cheap steps | Speculate only where latency saved exceeds cost | | Zombie candidates | Losers kept running after a winner was accepted | Cancel immediately and verify cancellation | Security and Authority Boundary Speculation multiplies external calls, which multiplies exposure to rate limits and data egress. Scope candidate paths to the least privilege needed, do not speculate across security boundaries where one path has wider authority than the task requires, and audit cancelled paths for partial writes. title: Workflow Versioning
description: Version workflow definitions explicitly and record the version in every execution so in-flight runs keep a stable identity while definitions evolve without silent breakage.
body: Workflow Versioning Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A workflow definition is code that runs many times. Versioning it explicitly — semantic bumps, a recorded version per execution, and a written rule for what counts as compatible — separates "the run behaved as defined" from "the definition changed underneath the run". Executions carry their definition version, so a result can always be traced to the exact steps that produced it. When to Use Use whenever a multi-step workflow runs repeatedly and its steps, prompts, tool wiring, or output schema may change over time. Do not use one mutable definition with in-place edits; every execution should be able to name the version that produced it. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The step graph and its metadata | | | | Yes | The edits being applied to the definition | | | | No | Executions still using earlier versions | | | | Yes | What the project classifies as breaking, additive, or fix | Procedure 1. Assign each definition an explicit version; an unversioned definition is a defect, not a default. 2. Classify every change against the written rule: step removal, output schema change, or semantic edits are breaking; additive steps are additive; wording fixes are fixes. 3. Record the definition version inside every execution at start; a result without a version cannot be interpreted later. 4. Pin in-flight executions to the version they started with; migrate only between runs, never during one. 5. For breaking bumps, provide an explicit migration or a compatibility window; never change a version in place. 6. Keep the definition history queryable so any past result can be replayed against its own version. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The bumped version after applying the change set | | | | What happens to executions started under the old version | | | | Change set, bump class, and timestamp | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | In-place mutation | Definition edited while executions reference it | Versions are immutable; changes are new versions | | Unlabeled executions | Runs that cannot name their definition version | Stamp the version into every execution at start | | Silent breaking changes | Output schema edited without a major bump | Classify changes against a written rule, not mood | | Migration drift | In-flight runs partially migrated mid-run | Pin in-flight runs; migrate only between runs | | Lost history | Old definitions deleted after the switch | Keep every version queryable for replay | Security and Authority Boundary Versioning preserves the structure of orchestration; it does not pin model behavior. Two executions of the same version can still differ from model sampling — output reproducibility needs seed, prompt, and model tracking of its own. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Semantic Versioning specification (https://semver.org/). 2. Wikipedia's overview of schema evolution under version changes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schema_evolution). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Curriculum Sequencing
description: Order learning units into a dependency-respecting path — prerequisites as edges, cycle detection, mastery gates — so study plans stay coherent, individually paced, and free of impossible orders.
body: Curriculum Sequencing Category: Domain-Specific | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A curriculum is a directed graph wearing a reading list's clothes. Sequencing it means extracting prerequisite edges from stated dependencies, verifying the graph is acyclic, ordering units topologically, and placing mastery gates between a unit and everything that depends on it. Placement tests adjust the entry point by skipping proven material — not by deleting it, since a skipped unit must remain visible in the path's record. When to Use Use when a set of lessons, modules, or skills must be ordered for a learner — course assembly, onboarding plans, or personalized study paths. Do not use for a flat list with no real dependencies; sorting adds ceremony without value when the graph has no edges. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | All learning units in scope | | | | Yes | Stated edges: unit before unit | | | | Yes | Placement results per learner | Procedure 1. Extract prerequisite edges exactly as stated; an assumed-but-unstated dependency is an edge nobody can audit. 2. Detect cycles first; a cyclic curriculum has no valid order, only a hidden wrong edge to fix. 3. Produce a topological order of the units; ties break deterministically (by unit id) for reproducible plans. 4. Apply placement: units already mastered are marked skipped-in-place, never removed from the record. 5. Insert mastery gates before dependents: a unit's dependents unlock only when its gate is passed. 6. Emit the path with per-unit status (assigned, skipped, gated) and the edge set it was derived from. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The dependency-respecting order | | | | The offending units, if the graph is cyclic | | | | Units whose mastery gates downstream dependents | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Circular prerequisites | Units that depend on each other transitively | Detect cycles before ordering; fix the graph | | Hidden prerequisites | Assumed knowledge not stated as edges | Make every dependency an explicit, auditable edge | | Ungated advancement | Dependents reached before mastery | Insert mastery gates before dependents | | Placement amnesia | Skipped units vanish from records | Mark skipped-in-place; keep the full path visible | | Orphan units | Units no path can reach | Surface unreachable units for graph repair | Security and Authority Boundary Sequencing orders material; it certifies nothing about mastery. title: Customer Churn Analysis
description: Analyze why customers leave by joining behavioral signals with outcomes, scoring churn risk honestly and separating correlation from causation before acting on findings.
body: Customer Churn Analysis Category: Domain-Specific | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Churn analysis is only useful when it changes what a team does next. The skill covers defining churn operationally, joining behavioral signals with observed outcomes, building interpretable risk features, and validating that signals precede churn rather than accompany it. The deliverable is a ranked intervention list with per-signal evidence, plus the honest note that association is not a retention mechanism. When to Use Use when a subscription or recurring-revenue business must understand and predict which customers are likely to leave and why. Do not treat every correlated metric as a churn cause. Intervening on a signal that merely accompanies churn wastes retention budget and can irritate customers. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Per-account events, usage, and status changes over time | | | | Yes | Observed churn or retention outcomes per account | | | | Yes | Feature window and prediction horizon definitions | Procedure 1. Define churn operationally: cancellation event, lapse, or inactivity threshold, with the observation window. 2. Join behavioral signals with outcomes using strict temporal windows: features precede the outcome. 3. Build interpretable features: usage trend, support contacts, billing failures, and engagement drop. 4. Score accounts for churn risk with the model kept simple enough to explain per account. 5. Validate that top signals are leading, not coincident, using lagged analysis. 6. Emit a ranked intervention list with per-account evidence and stated confidence. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Per-account churn risk with top contributing signals | | | | Per-signal strength and lead time before churn | | | | Accounts ranked with suggested actions and caveats | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Coincident signals treated as causes | Interventions fired on symptoms | Lag analysis before ranking any signal | | Churn defined inconsistently | Lapse and inactivity conflated | One operational definition stated up front | | Feature leakage | Post-churn behavior used as a feature | Enforce the feature window strictly | | Retention theater | Discounts to accounts that would stay anyway | Target by risk band, not blanket offers | | Survivor bias in validation | Only completed windows evaluated | Include censored accounts in evaluation | Security and Authority Boundary Churn models segment real customers by behavior. Ensure the data use complies with privacy commitments, do not use protected attributes as features, and keep per-account risk scores need-to-know because they inform commercial decisions about individuals. body: Diagnosis Coding Category: Domain-Specific | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Diagnosis coding is a lookup task with a discipline problem: the temptation to code what a clinician probably meant. This skill pins the process to text — a code may be emitted only when the clinical text literally supports it, lookups run against a supplied code index of the declared version, and cases that cannot be resolved are flagged for a human coder. Output pairs every code with its evidence span, so nothing in the coded record is unattributable. When to Use Use when clinical notes or symptom descriptions must be converted to a standard code system (ICD or a supplied local variant) for administrative structuring. Do not use to diagnose patients, and do not emit codes for what the text implies but does not say; implication is a clinical judgment, not a coding fact. Declare the code system and version before lookup; codes from mixed versions do not merge into one record. 2. Normalize the clinical text conservatively — case and whitespace, not paraphrase; the evidence span must survive. 3. Match only against the supplied index, restricted to the declared scope if one is given. 4. Emit a code only with a literal evidence span from the source text; the span is part of the output. 5. Flag unresolved cases explicitly for human coding; a near-miss is a flag, not a code with a lower bar. 6. description: Forecast electricity or gas demand over short and medium horizons using calendar effects, weather covariates, and load history, with error bands and explicit regime awareness.
body: Energy Consumption Forecasting Category: Domain-Specific | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Load forecasting is regular until it is not. The skill covers building the baseline from calendar and weather effects, adding autoregressive load structure, handling regime changes such as holidays and extreme events, and reporting forecasts with error bands calibrated on backtests rather than assumed. The deliverable is honest: a point forecast, an interval, and the conditions under which the forecast should be distrusted. When to Use Use when operations or budgeting need expected demand: day-ahead scheduling, capacity planning, or billing projections. Do not backtest on the same period used to tune the model. Clean the load history: gaps, daylight-saving transitions, and meter rollovers handled explicitly. 2. Engineer calendar and weather features: hour, weekday, holiday, heating and cooling degrees. 3. Fit the baseline and autoregressive components on training data only. 4. Backtest on held-out recent periods and calibrate error bands from realized residuals. 5. Adjust for regime days, such as holidays and extreme weather, with dedicated handling. 6. Publish the forecast with intervals and the regime assumptions it depends on. title: Inventory Reordering
description: Compute reorder points and order quantities from demand history, lead time, and safety stock with every formula input recorded so replenishment decisions rest on stated math rather than gut feel.
body: Inventory Reordering Category: Domain-Specific | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Reordering is arithmetic pretending to be intuition. The skill makes the math explicit: demand statistics from history, a reorder point from demand rate times lead time plus safety stock, an order quantity from policy (economic order quantity or a stated rule), and a comparison against stock on hand that emits a concrete reorder list. Every input — history window, lead time, service level — is recorded with the decision, so the same numbers regenerate the same order. When to Use Use for any stocked item where running out has a cost and overstocking has another — spare parts, consumables, retail or warehouse inventory. Do not use on sparse or stale demand history; a reorder point computed from three data points is a guess with extra decimals. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Recent demand series for the item | | | | Yes | Expected replenishment delay | | | | Yes | Current available quantity | | | | Yes | Safety stock rule, service level, and order quantity rule | Procedure 1. Fix the history window and clean the series — stockouts and promotions are noted, not silently averaged in. 2. Compute demand rate and variability; record the window and both statistics with the decision. 3. Compute the reorder point as demand rate times lead time plus safety stock, from the recorded inputs only. 4. Derive the order quantity from the stated policy — economic order quantity or a rule — with its formula and inputs recorded. 5. Compare stock on hand against the reorder point; items at or below it enter the reorder list with the computed quantity. 6. Emit the decision record: item, inputs, formulas, quantities, and date, so the order is reproducible. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Items to reorder now and their quantities | | | | Computed thresholds per item | | | | Inputs, formulas, and parameters used | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Stale history | Demand from a discontinued pattern drives the point | Refresh the window; flag aged series | | Ignored lead-time variance | Only the mean lead time used | Size safety stock for lead-time variability | | Double counting | In-transit orders counted as on hand | Exclude in-transit stock from the comparison | | Seasonality blindness | An annual cycle flattened by the average | Use seasonal windows or explicit season factors | | Unrecorded inputs | The order cannot be explained later | Emit the full decision record with every run | Security and Authority Boundary Reordering math supports the operational decision; supplier risk, cash constraints, and contract terms remain with procurement.
