title: Market Research Synthesis
description: Synthesize primary and secondary market research into a decision-ready analysis with sized estimates, source hierarchy, and explicit confidence levels rather than blended opinions.
body: Market Research Synthesis Category: Domain-Specific | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Synthesis fails when it averages sources that disagree without explaining why. The skill covers inventorying sources by type and reliability, extracting findings with per-source provenance, reconciling contradictions explicitly rather than blending them, triangulating market sizes from independent methods, and grading each conclusion by the strength of what supports it. The deliverable is a decision memo with a confidence level per claim. When to Use Use when strategy, product, or investment decisions need a consolidated view of a market from mixed primary and secondary sources. Do not blend conflicting findings into a smoothed average. Contradictions between credible sources are findings, and they get surfaced, not averaged away. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Research artifacts with type, date, and methodology notes | | | | Yes | The decision questions the synthesis must answer | | | | No | Reliability ranking by source type for conflict resolution | Procedure 1. Inventory sources with type, date, and methodology; discard ones with no traceable method. 2. Extract findings per source with provenance; one row per claim, not per document. 3. Cluster findings against each decision question and surface contradictions. 4. Resolve contradictions with the source hierarchy and record why the loser lost. 5. Triangulate quantitative estimates from at least two independent methods where possible. 6. Grade every conclusion by support strength and state what would change it. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Claims with source provenance and reliability tier | | | | Answers to the decision questions with confidence grades | | | | Unresolved conflicts and their impact on conclusions | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Blended contradictions | Averaging conflicting estimates | Resolve via hierarchy or report the contradiction | | Provenance-free claims | Findings extracted without source links | One provenance row per claim | | Zombie statistics | Old estimates recycled without dates | Carry the source date with every figure | | Question drift | Synthesis answers an easier question | Cluster findings against the stated questions | | False precision | Single-method estimates presented as solid | Triangulate or grade confidence down | Security and Authority Boundary Market research includes paid and confidential data. Respect licensing terms, keep client-confidential findings out of shared artifacts, and attribute figures to sources correctly, because unlicensed reuse of syndicated data carries legal exposure. body: Patent Prior Art Search Category: Domain-Specific | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Prior art search is coverage accounting plus claim mapping. The skill covers decomposing the subject into searchable facets, running parallel queries across patent classifications and non-patent literature, mapping each hit against the claim elements, and disclosing what was searched, where, and with which queries, so a reviewer can judge coverage rather than trust a conclusion. A hit list without claim mapping is a reading list, not prior art. When to Use Use when a product idea, draft application, or existing patent must be checked against what was already published or patented. Do not present a clean result as proof of novelty. A search is a coverage statement over queries run, not a guarantee that nothing exists. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The invention description or claim set to search against | | | | Yes | Jurisdictions, date bounds, and sources to cover | | | | No | or (default) analysis depth | Procedure 1. Decompose the disclosure into claim elements and searchable technical facets. 2. Build a query matrix: facet terms across patent classifications and non-patent literature. 3. Run the matrix, logging every query, source, and date for coverage disclosure. 4. Screen hits at title and abstract level; promote relevant ones to full-text review. 5. Map each promoted hit against the claim elements it anticipates or renders obvious. 6. Emit the evidence file with citations, mappings, and the coverage statement. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Hits with citation, relevance, and claim-element mapping | | | | Sources, queries, and dates searched, and known gaps | | | | Claim elements against the hits that read on them | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | False novelty conclusion | Coverage gaps read as clean results | Disclose sources, queries, and gaps explicitly | | Keyword-only querying | Synonyms and drafting conventions missed | Classification plus synonym expansion in the query matrix | | Reading-list output | Hits collected without claim mapping | Map every promoted hit to claim elements | | Non-patent literature skipped | Search confined to patent databases | Include journals, manuals, and open repositories in scope | | Stale classifications | Reclassification shifts missed the target class | Verify current classification placement before final coverage | Security and Authority Boundary Prior art searches can reveal competitive strategy and, when run for litigation, carry privilege considerations. title: Receipt Parsing
description: Extract merchant, date, line item, tax, and total fields from raw receipt text with arithmetic cross-checks so expense records rest on validated numbers rather than best guesses.
body: Receipt Parsing Category: Domain-Specific | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A receipt is unstructured text pretending to be a table. Parsing it means segmentation (header, items, totals), normalization (dates, currencies, decimal separators per locale), and — the part that separates data from guesswork — arithmetic verification: line items must sum to the subtotal, and subtotal plus tax must match the stated total. Every extracted field carries its raw span, so any number in the structured record can be traced to where it came from. When to Use Use when receipt text (typed or OCR output) must become structured expense data — bookkeeping automation, reimbursement workflows, spend analysis. Do not use when a structured source exists instead; supplier invoices with structured input are a stricter field contract handled by invoice processing. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Raw or OCR-extracted receipt text | | | | Yes | Expected date, currency, and number formats | | | | Yes | Fields the caller needs to be present | Procedure 1. Segment the text: header block, line-item block, totals block; totals are parsed from the bottom up, where receipts are most structured. 2. Normalize numbers per locale — decimal separator, currency symbol, thousands grouping — before any arithmetic. 3. Parse line items as (quantity, description, amount) triples; wrapped descriptions are joined, not split into items. 4. Cross-check: item sum against stated subtotal; subtotal plus tax against stated total; record the verdict per check. 5. When a stated total is missing, compute it and flag it as computed, never as extracted. 6. Output the structured record with per-field raw spans and confidence; unresolved fields are flagged, not invented. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Merchant, date, items, subtotal, tax, total | | | | Arithmetic cross-check results | | | | Fields that could not be extracted | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | OCR digit noise | Misread digits pass the regex but fail arithmetic | Run cross-checks; flag records whose math fails | | Locale confusion | parsed as | Normalize per the declared locale first | | Split line items | Wrapped descriptions become two items | Join continuation lines before matching | | Missing totals | Stated total absent from the slip | Compute and mark as computed, never as extracted | | Tax-inclusive pricing | Totals include tax the parser assumed was added | Detect tax-inclusive slips and adjust the checks | Security and Authority Boundary Parsed receipts are structured data for review, not financial records of record. Reimbursement approval, tax treatment, and fraud detection remain with the accounting workflow and its human checks. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of receipts as transaction records (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receipt). 2. The Python standard library documentation for the re module (https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html). description: Screen resumes against a written rubric with per-criterion evidence spans, anchored scoring, and explicit missing-information handling so ranking decisions stay auditable and bias-controlled.
body: Resume Screening Category: Domain-Specific | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Resume screening is a judgment task wrapped in an audit problem. The skill makes the judgment mechanical and the audit trivial: criteria are written before any resume is read, each criterion is scored only against quoted evidence from the document, missing information is recorded as missing rather than punished, and protected attributes are never inferred or used. The output is a structured verdict with provenance, not a ranking by feel. When to Use Use when a stack of resumes must be reduced to a ranked or triaged shortlist against a defined role, and the decision must be explainable afterward. Do not use to make hiring decisions; screening output is decision support that humans review before any candidate outcome. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The candidate document to screen | | | | Yes | Written criteria with anchored score levels | | | | Yes | The role definition the rubric was derived from | Procedure 1. Fix the rubric before reading resumes; criteria written after reading a candidate are advocacy, not screening. 2. For each criterion, quote the evidence span from the resume that supports a score, or record it as missing. 3. Score against anchored levels defined in the rubric; two screeners should reach the same score from the same span. 4. Treat missing information as missing — a gap is not a negative unless the rubric says so explicitly. 5. Never infer protected attributes from text, dates, or names; they are out of scope by construction. 6. Emit the structured verdict with every span, score, and gap, so the decision can be reconstructed or challenged. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Per-criterion scores with anchors | | | | The quoted text supporting each score | | | | Criteria the resume left unanswered | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Unanchored scoring | Scores reflect the screener's mood | Use rubric anchors any screener can apply | | Punishing gaps | Missing information read as weakness | Record gaps as gaps unless the rubric penalizes them | | Protected-attribute inference | Dates, names, or photos used as signals | Keep protected attributes out of scope by construction | | Keyword-only matching | Exact terms trump equivalent experience | Match synonyms defined in the rubric; keep humans in review | | Decision without provenance | Verdict with no quoted evidence | Emit spans with every score or the verdict is invalid | Security and Authority Boundary Screening output is decision support for a human decision governed by employment law and fairness review. Bias auditing, adverse-impact analysis, and candidate communication remain with the hiring process, not with the screener. title: Shift Scheduling
description: Build staff shift schedules as constraint problems — coverage demand, availability, rest gaps, fairness — with every constraint explicit and every violation reported instead of hidden in an unexplained roster.
body: Shift Scheduling Category: Domain-Specific | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A roster is a set of assignments that satisfies stated constraints — or it is a wish. This skill treats scheduling as constraint programming: enumerate shifts and coverage requirements, encode hard constraints (availability, max hours, minimum rest between shifts) and soft ones (fairness in weekends and unpopular shifts), search for a feasible assignment, and report every constraint that could not be satisfied rather than quietly producing a broken roster. When to Use Use for on-call rotations, support coverage, clinical or retail staffing — any recurring horizon where people must be assigned to shifts under rules. Do not use for one-off task allocation with no recurring structure or constraints; that is task assignment, not scheduling. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | People and the shifts they can work | | | | Yes | Minimum headcount per shift | | | | Yes | Hard and soft rules with priorities | | | | Yes | The scheduling window | Procedure 1. Enumerate the shift grid across the horizon; every slot that needs coverage appears in the problem. 2. Encode hard constraints first — availability, maximum hours, minimum rest gaps; soft constraints carry explicit priorities. 3. Search for a feasible assignment; prefer solutions that minimize weighted soft-constraint violations. 4. When no feasible roster exists, report which constraints conflict and at which slots — do not silently drop coverage. 5. Compute fairness per person (shift counts, weekends, unpopular slots) and include it in the output. 6. On any later edit, revalidate the full roster; an edited roster is a new solution, not an exception to check. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The assignment per slot | | | | Unsatisfied constraints, if any | | | | Per-person load and distribution metrics | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Hidden hard constraints | Rules applied verbally after publication | Encode every constraint before solving | | Fairness ignored | One person absorbs the unpopular shifts | Track distribution and include it in the output | | Missing rest gaps | Back-to-back night-then-day assignments | Encode minimum rest as a hard constraint | | Unreported coverage gaps | Solver returns an incomplete roster silently | Emit violations with slots, always | | Unvalidated edits | Manual fixes break constraints quietly | Revalidate the full roster after any edit | Security and Authority Boundary A feasible schedule satisfies the stated constraints; labor-law compliance depends on those constraints being complete and current. title: Tax Document Preparation
description: Assemble and validate tax filings and supporting schedules from source documents, with line-level provenance, arithmetic verification, and explicit flagging of items needing professional review.
body: Tax Document Preparation Category: Domain-Specific | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Tax preparation is arithmetic under rules, and every number must trace to a source. The skill covers extracting figures from source documents into a line-level ledger, applying the relevant form logic and thresholds, verifying arithmetic through recomputation, and flagging ambiguous or unusual items for review rather than resolving them silently. The deliverable distinguishes computed values from assumptions everywhere. When to Use Use when income, deduction, and credit documents must be assembled into a draft filing or an organized preparer package. Do not silently guess at an ambiguous figure. An undocumented assumption on a filing is an error with the taxpayer’s signature on it. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Wage statements, receipts, and financial documents with figures | | | | Yes | Form line definitions, thresholds, and rates for the jurisdiction and year | | | | Yes | Filing category: individual or business, determining which form set applies | Procedure 1. Extract every figure into a line-level ledger with document provenance per entry. 2. Classify each ledger entry against the applicable form lines and schedules. 3. Apply the form logic: thresholds, rates, and phase-outs, computing rather than copying totals. 4. Recompute all arithmetic independently and require exact agreement before assembling. 5. Flag ambiguous or unusual items for review with the source image referenced. 6. Assemble the draft filing with computed values, assumptions, and flags separated. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Extracted figures with form-line classification and provenance | | | | Computed form values with recomputation evidence | | | | Ambiguous items needing professional or taxpayer confirmation | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Silent assumption | Ambiguous figure resolved without a flag | Every assumption is a review flag, never a default | | Wrong-year rules | Thresholds and rates from a prior filing year | Bind rule sets to jurisdiction and year explicitly | | Carryover errors | Prior-year values missing or double-counted | Reconcile carryovers against prior filings | | Arithmetic trust | Reported totals copied without recomputation | Independent recomputation before assembly | | Missing-document gaps | An income document absent from the ledger | Reconcile document count against ledger entries | Security and Authority Boundary Tax data is among the most sensitive personal and financial information. Restrict access, never transmit filings over unapproved channels, and ensure automation output is reviewed by a qualified preparer before submission in any regulated context. body: Alerting Design Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description An alert on every metric is a pager that cannot be trusted, and a pager that cannot be trusted gets silenced — usually right before the one that mattered. This skill designs alerting from the top down: start from what users experience, define objectives with error budgets, and alert on the burn rate of those budgets. Cause-level signals become dashboards and debug entries, not pages, because a page is a claim that a human must act now, and every unactionable claim spends trust the system needs for the real ones. When to Use Use whenever a service is on call — user-facing or internal — and especially where pages have grown noisy enough that responders pre-filter them. Do not page on individual cause metrics with no user-visible symptom; a nearly full disk at three in the morning is a dashboard, not a human. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The user-visible service level being protected | | | | Yes | How fast the error budget is being consumed | | | | Yes | The signal that measures the user experience | Procedure 1. Define the objective first — what users experience, measured as availability or latency — before writing a single alert. 2. Alert on burn rate: page when the error budget would exhaust within a bounded window, not on any single bad sample. 3. Keep causes out of the pager: route saturation and dependency signals to dashboards and debug pages, not to humans. 4. Make every page actionable: name the runbook, the owner, and the first command to run, in the alert itself. 5. Review alert performance like code: page rate, action rate, and the fraction of pages that were real become metrics. 6. Retire or repair chatty alerts immediately; a noisy alert is not a safety margin, it is a removed one. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Symptom-based, budget-burning pages with runbooks | | | | Page rate, action rate, and precision over time | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Cause paging | Humans notified of every unhealthy-looking metric | Page on symptoms and budget burn, not causes | | Unactionable pages | A page with no runbook and no owner | Name the runbook and first step in the alert | | Alert fatigue | So many pages that real ones get ignored | Retire chatty alerts; measure alert precision | | Missing objectives | Alerts exist but no user experience is defined | Define the service objective before alerting on it | | Static thresholds | A fixed line that pages nightly at low traffic | Use burn-rate windows instead of single thresholds | Security and Authority Boundary Alert content travels to the widest, least protected channel in an organization — phones and chat: alert payloads must not embed credentials, internal topology details, or user data, and access to the alerting configuration itself must be protected, because silencing rules are a prime target for an intruder who wants the quiet path. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Prometheus alerting documentation (https://prometheus.io/docs/alerting/latest/overview/). 2. The SRE Workbook chapter on alerting on service level objectives (https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/). title: Blue-Green Deployment
description: Run two production environments and switch traffic between them, so a release becomes a reversible routing change instead of a waiting period for breakage.
body: Blue-Green Deployment Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A deployment that mutates the live environment in place makes rollback a race against the damage. This skill keeps two full environments — blue, live, and green, idle — and makes the release a routing flip: the new version deploys to the idle color, is verified there, traffic switches to it, and the old color stays warm for exactly as long as the new one needs to prove itself. Rollback is then the same switch in the other direction, which is what makes the flip a decision rather than a gamble. When to Use Use for stateless or forward-compatible services where a full second environment is affordable and a fast, reversible cutover is worth the cost. Do not blue-green around breaking database changes: if the old color cannot run on the new schema, the switch is not reversible and the pattern is theater. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The version being deployed to the idle environment | | | | Yes | The traffic control between the two environments | | | | Yes | How long the old environment stays warm after the flip | Procedure 1. Keep two environments, with the idle one always ready to receive the next release. 2. Deploy the new version to the idle color only, and verify it there — health, smoke, readiness — while production is untouched. 3. Flip routing to the new color, gradually or at once by design, and watch the user-visible symptoms rather than the deploy logs. 4. Keep the old color warm for the soak period: rollback during soak is a routing change, measured in seconds. 5. Handle state carefully: the schema and its consumers must be forward-compatible with both colors, or the flip is one-way. 6. Retire the old version after soak, and immediately prepare the idle color for the next release — the pattern only works while it is always two environments. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The flip with time, direction, and verification evidence | | | | The reverse switch, ready during the entire soak | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | In-place drift | The idle environment quietly becoming non-redeployable | Rehearse deploys to the idle color regularly | | One-way schema | A migration the old color cannot survive | Forward-compatible schema changes before the flip | | Instant retirement | The old version destroyed before the soak ends | Keep the old color warm for the full soak | | Verification in production | Testing deferred until after the flip | Verify on the idle color before switching | | Stateful split | Session state trapped on the wrong color | Externalize state or drain sessions before the flip | Security and Authority Boundary The routing switch is a security boundary: whoever can flip traffic between environments can redirect production, so route changes require the same authorization and audit as production deploys, and the idle environment must hold production data protections even while idle. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Martin Fowler's article on blue-green deployment (https://martinfowler.com/bliki/BlueGreenDeployment.html). 2. Wikipedia's overview of blue-green deployment (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue-green_deployment). title: Capacity Planning
description: Forecast infrastructure capacity needs from utilization trends and growth assumptions, producing headroom recommendations with stated assumptions rather than single-point guesses.
body: Capacity Planning Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Capacity planning converts utilization history into headroom decisions. The skill covers measuring current utilization at peak rather than average, projecting demand under explicit growth scenarios, deriving resource needs with target utilization ceilings, and presenting recommendations with the assumptions attached so they can be argued with. The output is a scenario table, not one number, because the honest answer depends on inputs nobody controls. When to Use Use when compute, storage, or network capacity must be provisioned ahead of expected growth, or when recurring saturation needs a structural rather than reactive fix. Do not plan from average utilization. Peaks are what break systems, and a plan sized to averages fails precisely when it matters. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Time series of utilization for each constrained resource | | | | Yes | Plausible demand scenarios with rates and event shocks | | | | Yes | Target utilization per resource that triggers scaling | Procedure 1. Measure utilization at peak windows per resource, not period averages. 2. Define growth scenarios explicitly: trend, step events, and their probabilities. 3. Project demand per scenario over the planning horizon. 4. Derive required capacity per scenario against the target ceilings. 5. Add headroom for the noisiest scenario and state the chosen margin. 6. Publish the scenario table with assumptions, trigger thresholds, and review dates. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Required capacity per resource per scenario | | | | Chosen provisioning with the margin and rationale | | | | Utilization alarms that force a plan re-run | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Average-based sizing | Averages hide the peaks that break systems | Size to observed peak windows | | Single-point forecast | One growth number treated as fact | Scenario table with assumptions stated | | No trigger thresholds | Plan goes stale until saturation hits | Utilization alarms that force a re-run | | Hidden coupling missed | One resource sized without its dependencies | Model constrained resources together | | Correlated demand shocks | Scenarios assume independent growth | Include compound worst cases in the table | Security and Authority Boundary Capacity data reveals system architecture and business growth. Treat utilization and projection artifacts as internal, avoid exposing them in shared dashboards, and provision through the same review discipline as any production change, since headroom decisions are also availability decisions. title: Cloud Cost Optimization
description: Reduce cloud spend by right-sizing resources, eliminating idle capacity, selecting pricing models, and attributing costs per service, with savings verified after every change rather than assumed.
body: Cloud Cost Optimization Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Cost optimization is an engineering loop, not a cleanup day. The skill covers attributing spend to services with allocation tags, finding waste by comparing provisioned to observed peak utilization, right-sizing with headroom rules, committing predictable steady load to reserved or committed-use pricing, and verifying each change against the bill after it lands. Savings are measured in the billing data or they are claimed nowhere. When to Use Use when cloud spend must be reduced or held flat against growth, or when bills rise without a clear attribution of the increase. Do not cut capacity without observing utilization peaks first. An oversized instance is waste; a right-sized-away headroom is an outage with a monthly line item. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Per-resource spend with service and tag attribution | | | | Yes | Observed peak utilization for provisioned resources | | | | No | Reserved and committed-use pricing available for steady load | Procedure 1. Attribute all spend to services through allocation tags before optimizing anything. 2. Find waste: resources with observed peaks far below provisioned capacity. 3. Right-size against peak utilization with an explicit headroom rule, never averages. 4. Match pricing models to load shape: commitments for steady, on-demand for spiky. 5. Schedule or automate idle capacity, such as off-hours dev environments. 6. Verify every change against the next billing cycle and record realized savings. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Spend per service and tag with anomalies flagged | | | | Changes ranked by expected savings, with headroom rationale | | | | Realized savings per change, verified against bills | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Unattributed spend | Resources without tags bill to a mystery bucket | Tag policy enforced before optimization | | Headroom cut too thin | Right-sized away the safety margin | Peak-based sizing with an explicit headroom rule | | Commitment lock-in | Steady discount bought for spiky load | Match commitment only to demonstrably steady usage | | Savings claimed, not verified | Estimates reported as wins | Verify against billing data after every change | | Optimization by deletion | Idle-looking resources that are standby capacity | Confirm purpose before removing any resource | Security and Authority Boundary Cost dashboards expose system topology and business volume. Keep attribution data internal, be careful exporting billing detail to third-party tools, and never let optimization scripts delete resources without an approval path, because some waste-shaped resources are load-bearing. title: Container Image Tagging
description: Tag container images with immutable, traceable identifiers — semantic version tags, registry digests, and build provenance — so deployments reference an exact artifact auditable after the fact.
body: Container Image Tagging Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A tag is a label someone can move; a digest is an identity they cannot. This skill pins that difference into the pipeline: builds get version tags once, deployments reference images by digest, a tag is never reassigned to different bytes, and every artifact carries build provenance — source commit, build definition, timestamp. The result is that any deployed environment can answer "exactly which bytes are running, and where did they come from". When to Use Use for any container image that reaches a deployment — application services, tooling images, CI runner environments. Do not deploy floating tags such as or a bare branch name; a deployment that cannot name its bytes cannot be rolled back to them either. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The image being built and tagged | | | | Yes | The release version this build belongs to | | | | Yes | The content-addressed identity from the registry | | | | Yes | Source commit, build definition, and timestamp | Procedure 1. Build once per version; the artifact from one build receives all its tags at creation time. 2. Tag with the semantic version; tags are claims about content, applied once and never retagged. 3. Record the registry digest; deployments pin by digest, with the version tag kept for humans. 4. Attach provenance to the artifact — source commit, build definition, build time — as metadata or attestation. 5. Reject retag requests: a tag that points at new bytes is a new version, whatever it is called. 6. Keep tag-to-digest mappings queryable so an environment's running bytes can be resolved historically. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Version tag, digest, and provenance per image | | | | The digest deployments reference | | | | Who tagged what, when, from which build | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | in production | Environments reference a moving tag | Pin deployments to digests | | Retagged versions | The same version label naming different bytes | Refuse retags; new bytes get a new version | | Tag-only references | Digest never recorded at release time | Store tag-to-digest mappings per release | | Missing provenance | Artifact cannot be traced to source or build | Attach source commit and build definition | | Cross-registry drift | The same tag resolves differently per registry | Resolve and compare digests, not tag names | Security and Authority Boundary Tagging identifies artifacts; it does not make them safe. Vulnerability scanning and signature verification are separate steps whose verdicts attach to the digest, not to the label. title: Database Backup Automation
description: Automate database backups with declared retention, restore verification, and encryption, treating a backup as real only after a monitored restore test proves it usable.
body: Database Backup Automation Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a backup. The skill covers scheduling full and incremental backups with a retention policy that survives audit, encrypting and off-siting them, and, decisively, restoring on a schedule into an isolated environment to verify the backup is complete, current, and usable. Every backup run reports duration, size, and integrity; every restore test reports recovery time against the recovery objectives. When to Use Use when production databases need scheduled, verifiable backups with retention and off-site copies, or when an existing backup routine has never been restore-tested. Do not declare backup coverage from successful backup jobs alone. Unrestored backups fail at the worst possible moment, usually for silent corruption or version drift reasons. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Target database with size, engine, and change rate | | | | Yes | Schedule, retention tiers, and recovery objectives | | | | Yes | Isolated environment for scheduled restore verification | Procedure 1. Define the policy: full and incremental cadence, retention tiers, and recovery time and point objectives. 2. Run backups on schedule, recording duration, size, checksum, and completion status. 3. Encrypt backups at rest and in transit, and copy them off-site per policy. 4. Prune expired backups per retention tiers and log what was removed. 5. Restore on schedule into the isolated environment and verify completeness and usability. 6. Report measured recovery time against the objective and alert on drift. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Runs with size, duration, checksum, and status | | | | Latest restore verification with recovery time measured | | | | Backups held per tier and prune history | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Unrestorable backup discovered late | Restore never tested until needed | Scheduled restore verification in an isolated environment | | Silent corruption | Bit rot in stored backup files | Checksums on write and on restore | | Retention breach | Old backups kept or pruned wrongly | Tiered retention with prune logging and audit | | Credential exposure | Backup encryption keys mishandled | Key management separated from backup storage | | Version drift | Restore target newer or older than backup format | Test with the engine version used in production | Security and Authority Boundary Backups concentrate the entire database, so they inherit and exceed its sensitivity. Encrypt at rest and in transit, store keys separately from backups, restrict restore-environment access, and log every backup and restore operation for audit. title: Declarative Infrastructure
description: Define infrastructure as reviewed, versioned code — desired state, applied by a controller — so environments are reproducible, diffable, and rebuildable from source alone.
body: Declarative Infrastructure Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Infrastructure described imperatively is infrastructure nobody can rebuild: the console clicks that made it exist live in a browser history. This skill makes the desired state the source of truth: resources are declared in code, the code is reviewed and versioned, and a reconciler applies the declaration — reporting a diff between what exists and what is wanted before it changes anything. The payoff is that the environment is no longer a memory; it is a file, with a history, that can be recreated in another region on a bad day. When to Use Use for any environment expected to outlive a single change — clusters, databases, networks, queues — and for anything that must be rebuilt identically elsewhere. Do not drive one-off break-glass resources through the declarative pipeline during an incident; make the manual change, record it, and reconcile the declaration afterward. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The desired state expressed as reviewed infrastructure code | | | | Yes | The recorded actual state the controller reconciles against | | | | Yes | The preview of changes between current and desired | Procedure 1. Declare desired state in code — resources, parameters, and their relations — with nothing that exists only as a console change. 2. Store the declaration in version control with review, so every infrastructure change has an author, a diff, and a reason. 3. Preview before applying: generate the plan and read it, because the apply step is where the diff meets production. 4. Apply through the reconciler, and let it record state — never mutate resources by hand where the controller watches them. 5. Treat drift as an incident: a manual change to a managed resource gets reconciled or recorded, not ignored. 6. Rehearse the rebuild: a declaration that has never created a fresh environment is a hypothesis, not a backup. title: Dependency Auditor
description: Audit declared skill dependencies and executable examples in isolated environments, producing reproducible pass/fail evidence without silently promoting trust state.
body: Dependency Auditor Description Audit declared external dependencies and executable skill examples in isolated environments. The auditor records pass/fail evidence and proposes badge artifacts without directly changing canonical trust state. > Phase 3 of the Dependency Watchdog pipeline. > Closes the gap between Package Exists (🟡 Yellow) and Code Runs (🟢 Green). The Execution Gap The AST Sweep (Phase 1) confirms that a skill's declared packages exist on PyPI and are free of known CVEs. But existence ≠ execution. A package might: - Have breaking API changes in its latest release - Require a native system dependency (e.g. , ) absent from the runner - Conflict with another skill's dependencies when installed together - Simply have a typo in its import path in the code example The Dependency Auditor solves this by running the code, not just scanning it. --- Architecture --- Isolation Strategy Each skill runs in a completely independent virtual environment. This prevents dependency bleed between skills — Skill A's cannot shadow Skill B's . > Why not a single shared venv for all skills? > Because conflicts between skill deps would produce false results. > Skill A might pass only because Skill B's dep happened to satisfy its import. > Isolation ensures every Green badge is independently earned. --- Verdict Logic The auditor distinguishes three outcomes. The distinction between and is the single most important design decision — it keeps the CI signal clean. | Verdict | Condition | Badge Action | |---|---|---| | | Snippet exits 0, no ImportError/RuntimeError | Promote Yellow → 🟢 Green (via PR) | | | Snippet exits non-zero, or raises on import | Stays Yellow, opens issue with traceback | | | No Python snippets found, or skill has no deps declared | No badge change, not flagged as broken | --- The Human-in-the-Loop Contract The badge is not written directly into canonical skill content. A passing audit produces a proposed badge artifact on a new branch and opens a Pull Request. The exact PR HEAD is merged only when required repository CI, security, tests, and invariants pass. This is the critical security feature. Without it, a snippet that passes due to a flaky network call or a temporary PyPI outage could silently award a Green badge that isn't earned. --- Recursive Dogfooding This skill ( ) is itself subject to the badge pipeline it describes. - Its own and imports are scanned by the AST Sweep → Yellow badge - The Dependency Auditor runs its own snippets in an isolated venv - If they pass → a verification PR is opened → exact-head repository CI gates the merge → Green badge The tool that audits the repository is itself audited by the repository. This is the self-healing property of the infrastructure. --- Security: Network Constraint Model > See for the full threat model. The short version: | Risk Level | Scenario | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Low (current) | Trusted contributor PRs, reviewed before merge | Ephemeral GH runner (discarded after job) | | Medium (community PRs) | Unreviewed code execution in audit | Require maintainer approval before audit workflow runs | | High (if abuse detected) | Adversarial snippet exfiltration | Docker container for execution | For the current scope — a curated, maintainer-reviewed repository — the ephemeral runner model is the primary and sufficient containment strategy. --- Failure Modes - Verdict overreach: recording pass/fail evidence as a trust judgment; the auditor records evidence and proposes badges, it does not change canonical trust state. - Isolation leakage: network or filesystem egress from the audit environment beyond the documented constraint model invalidates that run's evidence. - Pinned-evidence drift: verdicts referencing dependency versions that no longer match the resolved lockfile at audit time; record the exact resolved versions. - Transitive blind spots: auditing declared dependencies only while the exploitable surface lives in transitive or undeclared (phantom) dependencies. - Stale advisories: advisory databases with lagging or missing entries producing false "no known issues" verdicts; record advisory database version and freshness. Related Infrastructure | Component | Role | |---|---| | | Phase 1: Extract imports, validate PyPI, write Yellow badges | | | Phase 2: Poll OSV CVE database every 15 min | | | Manual badge state transitions | | | Shared utility | | | Phase 3: CI runner for this auditor | | | Badge state machine reference | Evidence The canonical skill file is the authoritative repository implementation. Repository schema, validation workflows, and the Agent Skills projection contract define structural conformance. title: Deployment Rollback
description: Restore the last known-good release through pre-verified rollback artifacts, recorded migration state, and a rehearsed procedure so a failed deployment recovers within a bounded time budget.
body: Deployment Rollback Category: Infrastructure | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Rollback is a deployment you have already practiced — or a hope. The skill makes it an artifact: the previous release stays deployable, schema migrations carry their compensating steps, the rollback procedure is rehearsed in staging against the same artifact shape, and recovery runs in a defined order with health verification at the end. The measure of success is a bounded recovery time, not the absence of failures. When to Use Use for any release with state — services, migrations, configuration — where reverting to the previous good state must be possible within a stated time budget. Do not use rollback as the primary deployment strategy; a process that ships failures expecting to revert is a quality problem wearing recovery clothing. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The failing release and its artifacts | | | | Yes | The verified previous release, kept deployable | | | | Yes | Forward migrations with compensating steps | | | | Yes | The rehearsed recovery procedure | Procedure 1. Keep the last known-good release deployable — artifacts, configuration, and schema state — until the next one is verified. 2. Record every forward migration with its compensating step; a migration without a reverse is a decision to make rollback impossible. 3. Rehearse the rollback in staging with the same artifacts and order; an unrehearsed plan is a draft. 4. On the failure signal, execute in the recorded order: stop traffic, revert code, revert migrations step by step, restore configuration. 5. Verify health after rollback — probes, smoke checks, error rates — before declaring recovery. 6. Write the incident reference: trigger, release delta, migration state, recovery time against budget. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Whether recovery completed | | | | Each rollback step and its verification | | | | Time from signal to verified recovery | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | No retained artifact | Previous release deleted or unreferenced | Keep the last known good deployable until the next is verified | | Irreversible migrations | Forward-only schema changes | Record compensating steps with every migration | | Unrehearsed plan | Rollback procedure written during the outage | Rehearse in staging with real artifacts | | Config drift | Configuration differs between the two releases | Snapshot and restore configuration with the release | | Unverified recovery | Traffic restored without health checks | Verify probes and error rates before declaring done | Security and Authority Boundary Rollback restores service state; it does not reconcile data written by the failed release. Data repair, backfills, and customer-impact analysis stay with the data owner after service recovery. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. title: DNS Record Management
description: Manage DNS records as versioned configuration with TTL strategy, propagation verification, and change safety checks, treating record changes as production deployments with rollback plans.
body: DNS Record Management Category: Infrastructure | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description DNS is the first link in every request path, and its failure modes are slow and confusing. The skill covers expressing records as versioned configuration, choosing TTLs deliberately as a trade between change speed and resolver load, pre-validating changes against the existing zone, applying with a rollback plan, and verifying propagation from independent resolvers rather than assuming it. Record changes follow production discipline because a mistake here takes down everything. When to Use Use when zones and records must be created, modified, or migrated, or when DNS changes need controlled rollout and verification. Do not lower a TTL and change the record in the same step. The sequence is: lower the TTL, wait out the old TTL, then change the record. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Current zone records as fetched from the authoritative source | | | | Yes | Record additions, updates, and deletions to apply | | | | No | TTL defaults and the change-speed trade-off per record type | Procedure 1. Fetch the current zone state from the authoritative source and record it as the rollback point. 2. Validate the change set: conflicting records, CNAME exclusivity, and target reachability. 3. Apply the TTL strategy: lower before risky changes, restore after verification. 4. Apply changes in dependency order, with service-critical records last when migration allows. 5. Verify propagation from independent resolvers until all answer consistently. 6. Archive the applied state and confirm monitoring reflects the new topology. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Zone state after the change, archived with the change record | | | | Resolver-by-resolver verification results | | | | Exact steps to restore the pre-change zone state | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | TTL-change collision | Record changed before the old TTL expired | Sequence: lower TTL, wait, change, restore | | CNAME exclusivity broken | CNAME added beside other records | Validate the change set against zone rules | | Assumed propagation | Verified only from the local resolver | Query independent resolvers before declaring done | | Missing rollback | No archived pre-change state | Record the authoritative state before applying | | Stale delegation | Zone migration left half the NS set behind | Verify delegation glue and NS records end to end | Security and Authority Boundary DNS control is domain control: a compromised zone can redirect every service, including login flows. Keep zone configuration in version control with review, restrict API credentials tightly, enable change auditing, and treat delegation changes with the same care as certificate authority changes. title: Health Check Endpoints
description: Expose separate liveness and readiness endpoints with dependency-aware checks so orchestrators restart dead processes while temporarily unready ones simply receive no traffic.
body: Health Check Endpoints Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Liveness answers "is this process broken"; readiness answers "can it serve right now". Conflating them produces the two classic outages: restarts during a dependency blip (the process is fine, the database is not) and traffic routed to instances that cannot serve. This skill splits the endpoints, makes readiness check real dependencies with real timeouts, and degrades to unready instead of dead — because a restart loop solves nothing a moment of patience would. When to Use Use for any long-running service an orchestrator manages — web services, workers, agents behind a scheduler or platform that probes health. Do not run side effects in probes; a health check that writes, rotates, or caches changes system state on a timer nobody scheduled. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Dependency probes with timeouts for readiness | | | | Yes | How often the orchestrator checks | | | | Yes | Consecutive failures before action | | | | Yes | What liveness failure and unreadiness each do | Procedure 1. Implement two endpoints: liveness reports process health from in-process state only; readiness reports the ability to serve. 2. Make readiness walk the real dependencies with short timeouts; a dependency down means unready, not a restart. 3. Keep checks cheap and side-effect free — probing sits on the request path of every scheduling decision. 4. Tune probe intervals and thresholds above the noise floor; flapping thresholds convert blips into restart storms. 5. Degrade to unready under partial dependency failure, and report which dependency held the gate. 6. Log state transitions with the reason; restart and no-traffic events are only debuggable with that record. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Process state from in-process evidence | | | | Ability to serve, per dependency | | | | Which dependency made the instance unready | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | One endpoint for both states | Restart policy and traffic policy share one signal | Split liveness from readiness | | Dependency blip restarts | Readiness failures routed to liveness | Degrade to unready, never to dead | | Heavy probe checks | Health checks loading dependencies | Keep checks cheap, cached, and side-effect free | | Restart storms | Thresholds tuned under the noise floor | Set thresholds above transient error rates | | Silent unreadiness | Unready with no recorded reason | Log the gating dependency with every transition | Security and Authority Boundary Health endpoints report process state; they do not validate data quality, security posture, or business correctness. Those belong to monitoring, security scanning, and SLOs — separate signals with separate owners. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. title: Kubernetes Deployment
description: Build a Deployment manifest with pinned image tags, explicit resource requests and limits, distinct readiness and liveness probes, and a declared rollout strategy so container runs stay predictable.
body: Kubernetes Deployment Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A Deployment manifest is where container defaults become incidents: floating tags, unset resource bounds, identical probes, and an implicit rollout strategy. This skill defines the manifest contract: pin the image, declare requests and limits, give readiness and liveness probes distinct purposes, and state the rollout strategy and history bound explicitly. When to Use Use when authoring or reviewing a Kubernetes Deployment manifest for a long-running service. Do not use for one-off pods, batch Jobs, or StatefulSets; their lifecycle contracts differ and need their own manifests. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Deployment and label name | | | | Yes | Fully pinned image reference including registry and tag | | | | Yes | Desired replica count | | | | Yes | CPU and memory requests and limits per container | | | | Yes | Distinct readiness and liveness probe definitions | Procedure 1. Pin the image to an immutable tag or digest; latest is not a deployable version. 2. Declare resource requests and limits for every container; unbounded containers share fate with their neighbors. 3. Give readiness and liveness probes different purposes and settings; identical probes detect nothing distinct. 4. Set the replica count and the rollout strategy explicitly, including max unavailable and max surge. 5. Configure a bounded revision history so rollback targets exist without growing forever. 6. Match label selectors to the pod template exactly; a mismatch strands replicas unsupervised. 7. Validate the manifest with a dry run before applying; schema errors belong in review, not in apply output. 8. Record the deploy outcome, including revision, conditions, and observed replicas, and compare against the declared intent. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The Deployment manifest conforming to the contract | | | | Dry-run rejections with the offending field | | | | The rollout revision after apply | | | | Observed replicas and conditions versus declared intent | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Floating tag | The image reference uses latest | Pin the tag or digest | | Identical probes | Readiness equals liveness | Tune each probe for its distinct purpose | | No limits | Requests and limits are unset | Declare both requests and limits | | Selector mismatch | Labels were edited after creation | Match selectors to the pod template exactly | | Unbounded history | revisionHistoryLimit is unset | Set an explicit history limit | Security and Authority Boundary Applying a Deployment manifest grants authority only within the cluster’s own RBAC. Image registries must be trusted, and credentials are supplied through declared secrets, never in the manifest. The manifest is code: it goes through the same review path as any change, and apply happens through the platform’s normal controls. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Kubernetes Deployment controller documentation (https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/). 2. The Kubernetes documentation on managing resources for containers (https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/). title: Load Balancer Configuration
description: Configure load balancers for distribution algorithm, health checking, session handling, and TLS termination, with capacity limits and drain behavior verified before production traffic.
body: Load Balancer Configuration Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A load balancer decides who receives traffic and who gets cut off when things go wrong. The skill covers choosing the distribution strategy deliberately, wiring health checks that fail toward the safe side, handling session affinity or stickiness only when the application requires it, terminating TLS with managed certificates, and setting connection limits that protect backends. Every configuration is verified with synthetic traffic before production cutover. When to Use Use when traffic must be distributed across multiple application instances, or when an existing balancer misroutes, cuts healthy backends, or overloads them. Do not copy a health check from a template without confirming the response semantics. A check that returns success on an overloaded backend removes the balancer’s ability to protect it. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Backend pool with capacity, protocol, and health endpoints | | | | No | Distribution: (default), , or | | | | No | Certificate source and termination policy | Procedure 1. Define the backend pool with real capacity figures, protocols, and health endpoints. 2. Select the distribution strategy deliberately; affinity only with an application reason. 3. Configure health checks with thresholds tuned to fail toward removing a backend. 4. Set connection limits sized to the weakest backend, not the strongest. 5. Terminate TLS per policy with certificate renewal handled before expiry. 6. Verify with synthetic traffic: distribution, failover, and drain behavior, before cutover. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Applied balancer configuration with strategy and limits | | | | Distribution, failover, and drain test results | | | | Per-backend limits and the sizing rationale | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Healthy backend cut | Health check misreads the readiness path | Test checks against real overload conditions | | Overload funneled | Limits sized to the strongest backend | Size limits to the weakest member | | Session breakage | Affinity disabled for a session-bound app | Enable stickiness only where required and document it | | Certificate expiry | Renewal not automated | Managed renewal with alerting before expiry | | Drain surprise | Connections dropped at cutover | Verify graceful drain in the pre-production test | Security and Authority Boundary The balancer is an availability chokepoint. Restrict configuration access, prefer managed certificates over pasted ones, and log routing changes, because an unnoticed misroute is indistinguishable from an outage until someone reads the balancer. title: Secrets Management
description: Store and deliver credentials through a managed system — never in code or config files — with scoped leases, rotation, and audit, so a leak has a blast radius and an end date.
body: Secrets Management Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A credential in a config file is a credential in a repository, a backup, and a log shipper forever. This skill routes around that: secrets live in a dedicated store, workloads fetch them at start time under an authenticated identity, each credential carries a scope and a lease, and rotation is routine rather than an incident. The audit trail closes the loop — who fetched what, when, under which role — because the question after a leak is never only what got out, but what it could reach and for how long. When to Use Use for any credential a workload needs — API keys, database credentials, signing material — delivered at runtime by identity, with rotation intervals that limit the lifetime of a stolen value. Do not build home-grown encryption schemes or stash credentials in environment files that outlive their leak; the managed path exists precisely so the shortcuts do not have to. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The logical name the workload requests | | | | Yes | The authenticated workload identity making the request | | | | Yes | Scope, duration, and renewal policy for the grant | Procedure 1. Inventory the credentials first: every secret gets an owner, a scope, and a rotation interval before it gets a store entry. 2. Store values only in the secrets system, addressed by logical name, with no copies in code, config files, or CI variables. 3. Deliver at runtime: the workload authenticates as itself and receives only the entries its scope allows. 4. Lease and rotate: credentials expire by policy, and rotation is a routine operation with a tested procedure, not an emergency. 5. Audit every fetch — identity, secret, time — and route the log somewhere a compromised workload cannot edit. 6. Revoke on suspicion, and drill revocation like backups: a rotation path never exercised will fail exactly when it matters. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The scoped, time-bound credential issued to the identity | | | | Rotations and revocations with dates and owners | | | | Fetch events by identity, secret, and time | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Config-file credentials | A secret committed, backed up, and shipped in logs | Store by logical name; deliver at runtime only | | Over-scoped grants | One credential reaching everything it never needed | Scope per identity; least privilege per fetch | | Eternal credentials | Values that live until the incident that rotates them | Lease and rotate on a fixed interval | | Unexercised rotation | The rotation path fails during the real event | Drill rotation and revocation routinely | | Unaudited fetches | No answer to who read what and when | Audit every fetch to an append-only log | Security and Authority Boundary The secrets system is the highest-value target in the estate: its stores must be encrypted at rest, its access decisions must run on workload identity rather than shareable credentials, and its audit logs must live outside the reach of the identities they record. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The HashiCorp Vault documentation (https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs). 2. The twelve-factor app guidance on configuration and credentials (https://12factor.net/config). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Service Mesh Configuration
description: Configure service mesh routing, mutual TLS, retries, and traffic policy as declarative configuration with progressive rollout and verifiable policy enforcement between services.
body: Service Mesh Configuration Category: Infrastructure | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A mesh moves inter-service policy into a configurable plane, which makes it auditable and also easy to break fleet-wide. The skill covers expressing routing, mutual TLS, and resilience policy declaratively, validating configuration against a running cluster state, rolling it out progressively with traffic verification between steps, and proving enforcement rather than assuming it. Mesh configuration is production security and gets production discipline. When to Use Use when inter-service traffic needs managed routing, encryption, or resilience policy across a fleet of services without rewriting each one. Do not apply mesh policy fleet-wide in one step. A bad retry or timeout rule is a self-inflicted outage with a single commit. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Declarative routing, mTLS, and resilience policy for the services in scope | | | | Yes | Workloads the policy applies to, with ownership recorded | | | | No | Progressive stages and verification gates; defaults to staged | Procedure 1. Express routing, mutual TLS, and resilience policy as declarative configuration in version control. 2. Validate the configuration: schema, references, and a dry-run against live cluster state. 3. Apply to one service first and verify traffic, latency, and policy enforcement in practice. 4. Progress through stages, verifying enforcement at each gate before expanding scope. 5. Confirm mutual TLS end to end: certificates issued, connections actually encrypted. 6. Record the applied policy state and rollback point for incident response. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The mesh configuration now in force, per service | | | | Verified routing, mTLS, and retry behavior per service | | | | Last-known-good configuration for fast reversal | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Fleet-wide bad policy | Applied to every namespace at once | Progressive stages with verification gates | | mTLS assumed, not verified | Certificates issued but connections still plaintext | Verify encryption end to end, per service | | Retry storms | Aggressive retries amplified an outage | Conservative retry budgets with backoff and caps | | Config drift | Console edits diverging from version control | Declarative source of truth, regularly reconciled | | Ownership unknown | No one knows who owns a policy | Record service ownership with the spec | Security and Authority Boundary Mesh policy controls who may talk to whom in production. Keep the configuration in version control with review, enforce mutual TLS as the default posture, and audit policy changes, because the mesh is a privilege-escalation path if its control plane is compromised.
